# Port queue

The loop's source of truth. **State lives here, not in the conversation** — an unattended run
outlives its own context, so anything the next iteration needs to know must be written down here.

One item per iteration. Take the first `TODO`, do it, verify it, mark it, append to `Changes.md`,
stop. Do not batch items.

Status: `TODO` · `DOING` · `DONE` · `BLOCKED (why)` · `ASK (question)`

---

## Rules the loop runs under

**May decide alone** — efficiency, compatibility and best-practice calls, per the operator's
instruction. Add a dependency when it is justified, choose an internal design, reorder the queue when
sequencing is wrong, split an item that turns out to be two.

**May do without asking**
- Anything inside `/DATA/Backup/Projects/MikroDash_New`.
- Read-only reads against any router.
- **Writes against the hAP AC2 only** (`10.0.0.53`) — the operator's designated test router. Clean up
  after, and verify the cleanup by re-reading.
- Append findings to `../MikroDash/ToDo.md`. That file is the one write permitted into the live repo.

**Getting a change made in the live repo.** Default to `ToDo.md` — it is asynchronous, reviewable,
and the operator fires it off when they choose. Use `ListAgents` + `SendMessage` to a peer session in
`/DATA/Backup/Projects/MikroDash` **only when a live-repo change BLOCKS the loop** and waiting is not
an option; say exactly what is needed and why, and never ask a peer to do something this loop is not
itself allowed to do (no AX3 writes, no pushes, no version bumps).

**Must NOT do without asking**
- Write to any file in `../MikroDash` except `ToDo.md`.
- Write to the **hAP AX3** (`10.0.0.2`, the operator's home router) or the **cAP AX** (`10.0.0.4`).
  Read-only is fine on both.
- Change user-visible behaviour. Reproduce the live app's quirks; report them to `ToDo.md` instead.
- `git push`, a Docker push, or a version bump.
- Leave a fake-auth harness listening when the iteration ends.

**Must STOP and ask** (set the item to `ASK` and end the loop)
- A PLAN.md kill criterion is hit.
- A decision that is expensive to reverse and not purely technical.
- Credentials or access the loop does not have.
- A blocker that stops every remaining item, not just this one.
- The same item fails verification three times.

**Every iteration ends green.** `gofmt -l .` silent, `go vet`, `go test ./...` **with the live repo
mounted read-only at `/live` and `MIKRODASH_SRC=/live`** (without it the proplist drift gate skips,
and a gate that never runs is not a gate), the nodecheck glob, all `--check` generators, and
`tsc --noEmit`. If an iteration cannot end green, revert what it
did and mark the item `BLOCKED` with the reason.

**`tools/audit-cases.js --check` cannot run on the host** — it requires `better-sqlite3` from the
live repo's `node_modules`, which exists only inside the `mikrodash` container. Not drift and not
broken; it needs `docker exec`. Do not read its host failure as a red gate.

## UPSTREAM — A CORRECTION TO #117's CAUSE, AND A CONTRACT CHANGE (2026-08-26)

`543a93f` and `76afa49`, drift §§ 32–33. **The live session retracted part of what it had told
this port as settled**, unprompted.

**THE #117 REPORTER WAS NOT BLOCKED BY THE CONNECTION-TEST GATE.** That bug is real and its fix
stands, but the proximate fault was a **ReferenceError**: `collectModal()` called
`_selectedModalSites()`, declared in a different top-level IIFE and not in scope at the call site.
Both Save and Test Connection call `collectModal()` first, so both buttons did nothing, silently.
The first bug explained the symptom well enough to be convincing, and the diagnosis stopped there.

**AND IT WAS THE SECOND INSTANCE IN ONE SESSION.** `_syncPrimarySiteSelect` threw the same way
earlier and was patched by exporting it onto `window` — which is why its sibling was missed.
Patching a scoping bug with a global makes the next instance LESS visible.

**THIS PORT GETS THAT CHECK FROM THE COMPILER, AND THAT IS AN ADVANTAGE WORTH RECORDING AS ONE.**
A cross-module call to an undeclared function is a TypeScript error before anything runs; there is
no equivalent of an IIFE whose bindings are invisible to its siblings. The live side now has an
espree scope check to get the same guarantee, and its three refinements — collect bindings at ANY
depth, collect PARAMETERS, allowlist browser globals — are rules `tsc` already applies.

**THE CONTRACT CHANGE DOES AFFECT THIS PORT.** The device modal NO LONGER EDITS SITE MEMBERSHIP.
The multi-select is gone; only a PRIMARY picker remains, offering just the sites the device is
already in. Membership moves to Access Management — which is where the authority already lived,
since `PUT /api/routers/:id` strips the field for anyone without `system:principals`.

Two rules, each one keystroke from a destructive bug:

1. **SAVE REORDERS THE STORED LIST, IT NEVER REBUILDS IT.** The primary is position 0. Rebuilding
   from the picker's options would silently drop a site deleted since the device was filed —
   such a site has no name and is deliberately absent from the picker. Reordering cannot lose one.
2. **AN UNKNOWN DEVICE SENDS `undefined`, NOT `[]`.** The server reads absent as "leave membership
   alone"; an empty array means "remove every site this device is in". If this port's save path
   ever defaults that field, it must default to ABSENT.

This lands on top of `e76962d`, already ported. The padding contract is unchanged — server pads
with `''`, client blanks at the sink — so nothing already done needs revisiting; the modal is
simply no longer a writer of that field.

**FOLLOWED 2026-08-26, and both gates are green.** The shell was re-extracted from v0.7.37 and
the modal ported.

`web/src/pages/router-modal.ts`: the multi-select is gone; the primary picker BUILDS its options
from the device's own known sites. `siteIdsForSave` in `router-form.ts` now takes the STORED list
and returns it reordered, never rebuilt.

**AND THE DESTRUCTIVE DEFAULT WAS ALREADY IN THE PORT.** `collectRouterForm` did
`siteIdsForSave(f.siteIds ?? [], …)` — the `?? []` turning "this browser has no record for the
device" into "remove every site it is in". That is exactly the rule the live session sent, and it
was a live defect here rather than a change to adopt. Absent and empty are now different values
all the way through: `storedSiteIds` yields `undefined` only for a MISSING RECORD, and `[]` for a
known device with no sites.

**THE GATE ITSELF HAD THE FAILURE IT EXISTS TO CATCH.** `router-form-check` extracted `siteIds`
from `rtrModalSites.options` — the control 76afa49 removed. The element being gone, the extraction
returned an empty list for every case and compared it against a port that still built one. It reads
the PRIMARY PICKER'S OPTIONS now, which is what populate actually decides about sites.

Three more things the gate needed, each a real gap:

* a `document` and an `appendChild`, because the picker BUILDS options where the old control only
  marked them selected. `innerHTML` is modelled as a SETTER that clears `options`, or the
  placeholder row would accumulate across cases and the counts would drift upward silently.
* the `collectModal` anchor bound raised 3800 → 5000. It is a sanity guard on the anchor, not a
  size contract, and raising it when the function legitimately grows is the intended maintenance.
* **the absent-versus-empty rule asserted DIRECTLY**, because the comparisons cannot reach it: the
  harness always supplies a record, so a mutation turning `return undefined` into `return []`
  passed all 107 of them. It is a claim about one function's return rather than about two
  implementations agreeing, and it is now written as one.

New cases: a device in one live site and one deleted, a device whose stored primary was deleted,
and the save-side proof that a deleted site SURVIVES. Both probes verified — breaking the filter
fails 3 comparisons, breaking the absent rule fails the assertion.

## UPSTREAM — ISSUE #119, AND THIS PORT IS STRUCTURALLY IMMUNE (2026-08-26)

`1254beb`, drift § 31: the traffic dropdown lost all but one interface on a CCR2004. The live
`/interface/print` runs with `=interval=N`, so the router re-prints the whole list every cycle;
the collector accumulated into a map and, 300 ms after the last packet, replaced the live one.

**A DEBOUNCE CANNOT DELIMIT A BURST — it measures silence, not completeness.** One gap longer than
the timer inside a single cycle installs a partial snapshot as the whole truth, and the remainder
of that cycle lands in a fresh map, so the next commit is smaller still. Their fix detects a
repeated interface name: with `=interval=N` a name reappearing means the previous cycle ended.

**CORRECTED BY THAT SESSION, UNPROMPTED, AND THE CORRECTION MATTERS MORE THAN THE FIX.** They first
told this port that the stream "surfaces no cycle boundary". It does. RouterOS terminates every
interval result set with `!done` on a streaming channel, it reaches the library, and their own
vendored patch throws it away — `if (this.streaming) break;`. The patch exists BECAUSE that packet
arrives: without it the channel closed after cycle one. So the delimiter was on the wire and in
their hands the whole time, and wrap-detection reconstructs what was discarded. Their words: it is
the second-best answer, and they would rather this port had that from them than found it while
porting.

**AND IT IS NOT FREE HERE EITHER — CHECKED, NOT ASSUMED.** The obvious reading is that this port
gets the delimiter for nothing because `Do` consumes `!done` as its terminator. True, and it only
holds while the read is a `Do`. `internal/routeros`'s `Stream` ends when go-routeros closes the
channel, which it does on `!done` — so an `=interval=N` stream would look to this adapter like a
stream that ENDED after one cycle, which is precisely the failure their patch was written to fix.
CLAUDE.md already records the root of it under what the library switch knowingly gave up: "go-routeros
returns on the first `!done`, and this side cannot see block boundaries."

So if this port ever adopts `=interval=N` for these menus, it needs the same change they are
recommending upstream — surface the per-cycle `!done` as an event rather than an ending — and it
would be an adapter change, not a collector change.

**AND THEN THAT SESSION ASKED THE OBVIOUS FOLLOW-UP THIS PORT HAD NOT ASKED ITSELF:** the traffic
collector already streams `=interval=1`. If a per-cycle `!done` ends a stream here, why is it not
ending after one second, on a collector already built? Three possibilities, and the third — that it
IS ending and nobody noticed, because a stalled chart and an idle link render identically — was
worth ruling out the same day.

**RULED OUT, FROM LIVE HARDWARE, and the answer is that `=interval=` IS NOT ONE BEHAVIOUR.**
`test-results.md` already held the evidence, recorded under Claim 4 for an unrelated reason:
`/interface/monitor-traffic =interface=ether1 =interval=1` on the hAP AC2 under 7.24, cancelled
after 3.5 s, delivered

```
[   5.248ms] !re | .tag=probe1 | … | =.section=0
[1009.879ms] !re | .tag=probe1 | … | =.section=1
[2017.518ms] !re | .tag=probe1 | … | =.section=2
[3019.330ms] !re | .tag=probe1 | … | =.section=3
[3500.946ms] --> /cancel =tag=probe1
[3503.877ms] !done | .tag=probe1        ← the ONLY one, and only after cancel
```

**No `!done` between cycles.** A `monitor` command is one open result set whose sections increment;
a `print =interval=N` is a repeated print, and each repetition completes. So the claim "go-routeros
closes on `!done`" is true and the missing caveat is that `monitor-traffic` never sends one until
it is cancelled. The traffic collector is correct, and was never at risk.

**THIS CUT BOTH WAYS UPSTREAM** — their plan was to surface the streaming `!done` as a cycle event
across twelve `=interval=` collectors, which works for the `print`-shaped ones and gives
`monitor-traffic` a boundary that never fires. Sent back, along with the observation that
monitor-traffic's own marker is `=.section=N`.

**AND THAT WAS ONE SIGNAL TOO PESSIMISTIC.** They probed the AC2 with
`/interface/print =interval=3` and `.section` IS STAMPED ON THE PRINT SHAPE TOO — nine packets per
cycle, all carrying the same section, incrementing per cycle. So the split between the two shapes
is real for `!done` and irrelevant for `.section`: **one field delimits all twelve.**

Three consequences, recorded because they change what this port would do:

* **No library patch is needed on either side.** `.section` is already on the parsed packet. The
  change they were about to propose to a vendored, exact-string-fragile patch chain turned out to
  be a field both stacks had been receiving and discarding by not looking at it. Their
  `src/collectors/system.js` has *mentioned* it in a comment since it was written and used it for
  nothing.
* **Three independent implementations of "delimit this burst with a timer" existed in one stack** —
  the routeros library's own `sectionPacketSendingTimeout`, their meta commit, and the ancestor of
  their first fix. The signal was correct in all three; the delimiter was invented in all three.
* **`.section` solves what wrap-detection could not.** An interface legitimately appears several
  times in one `/ip/address/print` cycle, so a repeated key is no boundary there — which is why
  those two streams were left alone before and are now fixable. Replaced upstream in `ba24585`,
  guarded on `!== undefined` because the first cycle is section `0` and a truthiness check skips it.

**For this port:** if `=interval=N` is ever adopted for the meta menus, `.section` is the delimiter
and one rule covers both shapes — the per-stream signal declaration proposed above is not needed.
And the traffic collector is safe for a REASON rather than by luck: a monitor sends no per-cycle
`!done`, so go-routeros never sees an ending. Which also means adopting `print =interval=N`
anywhere would break this adapter immediately and visibly rather than subtly.

**Directly relevant if this port ever unifies its meta reads:** `.section` is a delimiter this port
gets for free on monitor-shaped streams and `!done` is one it gets free on `Do`. The two are
different mechanisms, and only the `print`-shaped middle case has neither today.

**This port cannot have it, and the reason is a departure made for an unrelated cause.**
`internal/collect/ifstatus.go` POLLS those three menus with ordinary prints where the Node
collector holds three `=interval=N` channels open — done because "more efficient means fewer
router channels, not faster payload assembly" and four fewer channels per router was the biggest
saving available. A `Do` returns a COMPLETE reply set terminated by the protocol's own `!done`,
so there is no burst to delimit and no debounce to be wrong.

Checked rather than assumed, on their advice to grep for the shape rather than wait to port the
fix: the only `time.AfterFunc` in `internal/collect` is `pollLoop`'s own timer, and of the three
genuine streamers (`logs`, `ping`, `traffic`) none accumulates into a map and swaps —
`Traffic.SetAvailable` takes a complete list from the interface collector's `Do`.

**A REASON FOR POLLING THAT NEITHER REPO CURRENTLY STATES.** `#104` chose fewer channels, and
completeness came along with it: **a delimited read is a completeness guarantee and a persistent
stream is not.** That is a second, independent argument for the same decision, and it is stronger
than "fewer channels" alone — it says what the caller GETS rather than what the router is spared.
Recorded here as a reason rather than left as a coincidence, at that session's suggestion.

**§35 SUPERSEDES §31, AND READING §31 ALONE WOULD MAKE THINGS WORSE.** Recorded here because the
drift file is the only durable record — the session that worked §31 out has ended. §31 concluded
"`.section` is the real cycle delimiter", which is true and was not the whole defect: a commit made
*before* the delimiter arrives is PROVISIONAL, and §31's fix moved the straggler's premature
publication from the debounce to the wrap rather than removing it. Issue #119 (a Traffic dropdown
holding one interface on a CCR2004, a late-reporting ZeroTier tunnel) survived it. The corrected rule
is that a provisional commit must COPY the batch and leave it accumulating; only a section change
hands it over. Upstream commit `272eeca`, local and unpushed as of 2026-08-27.

**NONE OF IT REACHES THIS PORT, and that is a conclusion rather than a hope.** The defect needs
provisional batch state across packets of one cycle. This port has none: `internal/collect` reads the
interface list with an ordinary `Do`, which returns a complete reply set, and `Traffic.SetAvailable`
takes that complete list. `traffic.go` does consume `.section`, but from `/interface/monitor-traffic
=interface=<list>`, which is ONE OPEN RESULT SET over a fixed list — there is no cycle of arriving
interfaces to accumulate and so no straggler to publish early. **Do not port §31.** If the three
polled menus are ever unified toward streaming, port §35 and not §31.

Worth keeping in view anyway: their §31 records that `/ip/address/print` and
`/interface/ethernet/print` have the same weakness upstream and were left alone. If the three are
ever unified here it must be **toward the `!done` cycle event**, with wrap-detection only as a
fallback if that proves unreliable — their revised advice, replacing the "unify toward
wrap-detection" they first gave. Also that
their removal-detection is deliberately delayed by up to one meta interval, pinned by its own
test so a later reader does not "fix" it back into the original defect.

The rollback mirror that leaves two `role_pages` rows per role is harmless here because

confers nothing rather than erroring.

`17127db`'s strip of `siteIds` AND `siteId` unless the caller holds `system:principals` (both
spellings — stripping only the plural lets an older client through on the scalar); `e0c8045`'s
add-or-remove-one-site semantics; and the Sites card. Building them with the gate already in
place beats adding it afterwards.

**`04f4bf9` mostly evaporates in Go** — a cancelled context gives the same fail-fast that their
per-generation rejection signal buys — with ONE exception worth checking when item 16 lands:
their `close()` returns early while still connecting and emits nothing. The Go equivalent is a
Dial in flight when Stop arrives, and the failure is an authenticated login nobody owns. That is
a LEAK, not a race, so `-race` would not find it.

**And one behavioural change that is not a bug fix:** `sendInitialState` now emits BOTH polarities
of `ros:status`. Emitting only disconnection meant a socket landing on an already-connected
session was never told so and the banner never cleared. Synthetic emits are TRUE-ONLY — a
synthetic false would dismiss the switching overlay while the new router is still connecting.

## UPSTREAM — THE LIVE REPO HAS ADOPTED TWO OF THIS PORT'S FINDINGS (2026-08-26)

`../MikroDash` has **uncommitted** work in `src/reports/pdf.js` fixing exactly the two defects this

side still passes, because it compares against the recorded corpus — which means the port currently
reproduces the OLD behaviour faithfully and the live app has moved.

**RESOLVED 2026-08-26**, after the live session committed the work (`e0dcafb`) and said so
directly. Both corpora regenerated; the port follows. Original note kept below because the
REASONING was right even though the wait was long.

**Not chased at the time, deliberately.** CLAUDE.md's own rule is that the gates lift from the
WORKING TREE and a gate can go red because of mid-edit work upstream; porting against a tree that
may still change is churn. The diff was read rather than assumed. When it lands, the port needs:

## CUTOVER QUEUE — one item per tick, in order

Added 2026-08-25 after the operator lifted the strangler rule and answered the four open decisions.
Take the first `TODO`, do it, verify it green, mark it `DONE`, append to `Changes.md`, stop.

The order is dependency-first: nothing below needs anything above it to be redone.

- [x] **DONE — 1. `backups:restore` part 2: the `/raw` route.** Token redemption, row-is-the-authority
      check, audited denial, octet-stream body. Go owns the real path per the operator's answer.

      Registered at `/api/backups/{id}/raw`, NOT behind the staging prefix — a router is handed this
      URL and cannot be told about `/next`. That is what the operator's answer bought: no flag, and
      no reinterpreting `backupBaseUrl`.

      **Redemption happens FIRST, before the id is even parsed**, so a junk id still spends the
      token. That is the delete-before-validate rule from `restoretoken.go` carried into the route:
      a token that survived a rejected read is one an attacker may keep presenting while varying the
      conditions. The mutation that validates the id first dies.

      **A refused token is 403 and audited; a missing row is 404 and is not.** A 404 for a bad token
      would tell a prober the id was wrong rather than that they held no capability, and an audit row
      for every stale URL a router retried would be noise in a trail that exists to be read.

      `remoteIP` strips the port — a comparison against `10.0.0.2:54321` never matches a token bound
      to a host, and that failure reads as a token problem rather than a parsing one. Four mutations
      killed, including both of those.
- [x] **DONE — 2. `backups:restore` part 3: the handler.** Mints a token, has the router fetch the
      file from us, loads it, and reports back — serialised through `InWriteQueue` like every other
      router write.

      **A SERIAL MISMATCH IS A REFUSAL; A VERSION MISMATCH IS A QUESTION.** Restoring one device's
      configuration onto another is not something an operator can mean, so a serial that does not
      match the row is denied AND audited. A RouterOS version difference usually is fine and the
      operator is the one who knows, so it is asked once and accepted with `acceptVersion`. Reversing
      those either blocks routine work or silently allows the unrecoverable one.

      **The audit is written BEFORE the call**, because the load reboots and the reboot takes the
      connection — a row written afterwards would be missing for exactly the restores that worked.

      **The load is not expected to answer.** Its error is dropped deliberately: reporting it would
      tell an operator their restore failed while the router was busy applying it.

      **Identity is read FRESH from the device**, not from the session's cached system payload — a
      restore is the one action where "which device is this, right now" has to be answered by the
      device. The version comparison takes the FIRST token, so `7.24 (stable)` and `7.24` are the
      same build rather than a mismatch on every stable release.

      **`backupBaseUrl` is used AS WRITTEN**, which is what the operator's answer bought: with Go
      owning the route there is one server, so the setting names it. Unset, the address comes from
      `/user/active/print` — the router telling us which of our addresses IT can reach, which beats
      anything this process could infer about its own interfaces behind NAT — plus this process's own
      listen port.

      **The live password-fallback trap is recorded rather than inherited.** `'=password=' + a || ''`
      binds `+` tighter, so the fallback is dead and a router with no backup block sends the literal
      `undefined`; RouterOS accepts it, fails to decrypt, and points the operator at their stored
      credential instead of a missing block. Go has no such trap, and the behaviour reproduced is the
      one the fixed live code produces: an empty password.

      Four mutations killed, including a URL that picked up the staging prefix — the one thing a
      router cannot be told about.

         That is why the port keeps fpdf instead of hand-writing a content stream. The gap is
         asserted to STILL EXIST, so an fpdf that learns to kern fails the suite.

         — substituting `?`, which fpdf's own translator does, would draw a mark the live app does
         not and shift everything after it half an em.

      a `save()` without its `restore()`.

      `widthOfString`, kerned, which this side cannot be. Rather than fuzz the x, the test
      accumulates the difference as a running debt from the corpus's own recorded reads and requires

      arg 1 of a `{lineBreak}`-only text, so a mis-transcribed table or chart coordinate can never

      pdfkit puts it**, and that is entirely the known kerning gap. The one 3.15 pt outlier is
      `chart kerned legend`, a case built from deliberately kern-heavy labels to prove the
      correction fires at all.

      1. **fpdf's A4 is 841.886 pt and pdfkit's is 841.89.** A PDF's y axis runs from the bottom, so
         that four-thousandth displaced every string on every page. Fixed by constructing the page
         at pdfkit's exact `SIZES.A4`.
      2. **pdfkit writes no text matrix for an empty string**, and `_render` draws one for every
         null cell. The port was emitting a mark per missing value.
      3. **The width pdfkit ALIGNS by is not `widthOfString`.** Laying out inside a `width` box it
         splits on spaces, losing a kern pair across each one: "Peak TX" measures 26.145 whole,
         26.845 as a sum of characters, and was centred as 26.495. The gate now RECOVERS the live
         width from pdfkit's own emitted x instead of recomputing it.
      4. **Helvetica has POSITIVE kern pairs** ("ry" is +0.33 pt at 11 pt), so a whole-string width
         is not always the smaller of the two. Eight corpus titles said so.

      **Five JS behaviours that a straight reading would have got wrong**, each now pinned:

      1. **A null `loss_pct` counts as a GOOD sample.** `losses` is `rows.map(r => r.loss_pct)` with
         no filter, so a null is in the denominator, sums as nothing (`0 + null` is 0) and passes
         `l < 1` (`null < 1` is TRUE). It reads as perfect in Uptime, Avg Loss and the count alike.
      2. **`rtt_ms ?? ''` is nullish, not `||`** — a 0 ms reply on a LAN renders "0", only a null
         blanks. Indistinguishable until a corpus case had `rtt_ms: 0`; the mutation survived first.
      3. **"Peak Util" is not clamped at 100%.** The live comment says over-capacity is the signal
         worth seeing, and a corpus case reads "151% / 203%".
      4. **A tie on "Top Type" resolves to the type seen FIRST.** V8's sort is stable and object
         keys iterate in insertion order; Go's map iteration is randomised, so the insertion order is
         kept explicitly — without it that case would pass or fail at random.
      5. **`Math.round` is not `math.Round`.** JS rounds a half toward +∞, Go away from zero, so
         they differ at an exact negative half — reachable here because a negative utilisation means
         a counter went backwards and the report renders it.

      it is built — `CapRows` caps the table at 5,000 rows and `Thin` caps each series at 150 points

- [x] **DONE — 7. The SMTP mailer.** `src/reports/mailer.js` — the four functions that
      decide what the message SAYS — is ported and pinned (`internal/reports/mailer.go`,
      `tools/mailer-cases.js`). All four are exported and pure, which is not an accident: the live
      header says they were split out "so the message can be built and inspected without a mail
      server, a database or a clock".

      **Two of them are security properties, not formatting, and both are pinned twice** — once
      against the corpus and once as an assertion that holds whatever the corpus says:

      1. **The subject strips CR and LF.** The schedule name is the ONLY operator-supplied string
         that reaches a message, and a newline in a Subject header is an injection. `cleanName`
         already strips it on the way in; this is the second guard, and removing it as redundant is
         how that kind of defence stops working. A run of breaks collapses to ONE space, not one
         each.
      2. **Every recipient goes in BCC**, with `to` set to the sending address. The live comment
         names the reason: these are frequently different customers, and a `to:` array would
         disclose every address to all of them. `MailEnvelope` also COPIES the slice, so a caller's
         later append cannot reach an envelope already built — mail to the wrong people is not
         retractable.

      `FitAttachments` drops the TAIL rather than the largest (canonical order means two operators
      with the same schedule get the same sections), and an oversized attachment is SKIPPED rather
      than ending the loop — a 4 MB section rejected at the message limit still leaves room for a
      10 KB one after it. Both limits are strict `>`, so a value exactly on the limit fits.

      Nine mutations, nine killed. Two "survived" on the first pass and both were faults in the
      mutation HARNESS, not the code: one test's name did not match the `-run` filter, and a shell
      quoting slip meant a mutation was never injected. Recorded because a mutation run that lies in
      that direction is worse than none.

      `Schedule` gained its `Name` field in `period.go` rather than a second Schedule type being
      declared, so a schedule cannot reach the mailer having lost fields on the way.

      **The transport is written too** (`internal/mailer`), so item 7 is complete.

      **This is the one piece with no live counterpart to port**, and that changes what "correct"
      is measured against. nodemailer assembled the MIME document AND validated the addresses;
      `net/smtp` does neither, so both jobs move here — and both are places where a mistake is a
      security bug rather than a rendering one. There is no corpus to compare against, so each one
      carries an assertion of its own instead.

      1. **BCC recipients reach the SMTP envelope and no header.** `reports.MailEnvelope`'s privacy
         property survives only as far as the MIME document; a `Bcc:` header discloses exactly the
         same set, and its name makes it look deliberate. Tested twice — the composed document must
         not contain either address anywhere, and a real in-process SMTP server must see THREE
         `RCPT TO` commands for a message with one `To` and two `Bcc`.
      2. **Addresses are rejected on CONTROL CHARACTERS.** `net/smtp` writes `RCPT TO:<addr>` with
         the string as given, so a CR is an SMTP command injection and the same string in a header
         is a header injection. Checked on control characters rather than address syntax on
         purpose: the question is whether it can escape the protocol, not whether it is deliverable.
      3. **Credentials are never offered unasked** — the live condition is
         `(smtpUser || smtpPass) ? auth : undefined`, and this additionally requires the server to
         advertise AUTH. A relay that did not ask is how a password ends up in a log.
      4. **The MIME boundary is random.** A fixed one would let an attachment whose bytes contained
         it end the message early.

      STARTTLS is opportunistic, matching nodemailer's `secure: false` default — demanding TLS would
      be a behaviour change rather than a port, and would break an install pointing at a localhost
      relay. The three live timeouts are set for the reason the live comment gives: a black-holed
      host otherwise stalls every later notification channel behind it.

      the code loosened: `X-Evil: 1` surviving as characters INSIDE `filename="..."` is inert once
      the CRLF is gone, so the test now checks it cannot START A LINE — demanding the substring
      vanish would have meant stripping colons from real filenames.

      `AttachmentFilename` and `NoSectionError`. `runOnce`'s remaining body is orchestration — it

      **`MayStillSend` is the one that matters, and it is an authorisation check.** It runs LONG
      AFTER the request that created the schedule, and it is the ONLY such check in the run path: a
      schedule mails a router's traffic to a stored recipient list every month, the router is
      stored, and the tick has no session. If the person who set it up loses access to that router,
      this is what stops the mail.

      Two failure modes, deliberately different:

      * **no `created_by` at all** — a schedule predating authentication. Refused only on an install
        that HAS authentication, because on one without it there is nobody to attribute a schedule
        to and refusing would break every schedule that exists.
      * **creator lost access** — refused outright, modern install or not.

      Both DISABLE the schedule rather than skipping the run, which is why the reason strings are
      pinned as constants: they are what the operator reads on the Reports page when a schedule has
      switched itself off, and "recreate it" is actionable where "not permitted" is not. The test
      asserts the two reasons DIFFER, and separately that a creator who lost access can never send
      — stated directly rather than left to a case name.

      `AttachmentFilename` reproduces `[^A-Za-z0-9]+ → '-'` including the parts that look like bugs:
      a run collapses to one dash, leading and trailing ones are NOT trimmed, and an accented letter
      is a separator because the class is ASCII-only ("Café" → "caf-"). A port that tidied any of
      those would name the file differently in the operator's mail client.

      Seven mutations, seven killed.

      **The route is wired and "Send now" sends** (`internal/server/reports_run.go`). It reuses
      `scheduleWriteHandler(true, …)`, so it inherits the session check, the routerId requirement,
      the write permission, the audit-unavailable refusal and the 404-on-router-mismatch.

      **Its limiter is SEPARATE and tighter: 5/min against the other three's shared 30.** The other
      three write a row; this one renders up to five PDFs and hands a message to an SMTP server, so
      30/min would be 30 outbound emails a minute to a stored recipient list from one button. A
      separate instance also means a burst of "Send now" cannot exhaust the budget for EDITING a
      schedule, which a shared limiter would do — both properties are asserted.

      **It never returns an error status for a run that did not send**, matching the live route:
      `ok:false` with an outcome and a reason, status 200. A 500 would make the browser's error
      handling swallow the reason, and the reason is the entire value of pressing the button.

      Three decisions worth naming:

      * **A missing router or a creator who lost access DISABLES the schedule**; unconfigured SMTP
        does NOT. The first two are permanent until somebody acts; SMTP is a condition of the
        install, and switching every schedule off when it is unset would leave the operator nothing
        to re-enable once they configure it.
      * **`creatorMayRead` fails CLOSED on a resolver error and OPEN when RBAC is simply absent.**
        Different situations: an unavailable resolver is install-wide and already reported at
        startup, so refusing there would disable every schedule on an install whose RBAC tables
        were never created — but an error from a resolver that IS available is a check that did not
        run, and mailing on that is worse than stopping and saying so.
      * **`isModernSession` reads the auth mode off the session, and the scheduled tick must not
        reuse it.** `false` is the PERMISSIVE answer for a schedule with no creator, so a tick that
        defaulted would let pre-authentication schedules keep mailing on an install that has since
        enabled authentication. Written down at the function rather than left to be discovered.

      `db.RecordReportRun` was added — every attempt is recorded whatever its outcome, in a `defer`
      matching the live `finally`, because a schedule failing silently for a month is visible only
      if the failures were written down.

      pinned (`internal/wifiscan/admit.go`, `tools/wifiscan-admit-cases.js`, 24 cases).

      **This is the one deliberately disruptive command the application issues**, and MikroTik's own
      words are why the guard exists at all: "Running a frequency scan will disconnect all connected
      clients, or if the interface is in station mode, it will disconnect from the AP." The live

      does not trust the router, one scan per router, and a fleet cap "so one operator cannot walk a
      building disabling every AP in it".

      even for an interface name that does not exist, because the running scan is the more useful
      fact and a caller has no business enumerating a router's interfaces through error codes. The
      corpus pins the sequence, not just the verdicts.

      * **A 64-character interface name passes the PATTERN** and fails later at the catalogue as

        pinned.
      * **The cooldown test is `last !== undefined`, not truthiness.** A timestamp of 0 is a real
        value, and `if (last)` would skip it — letting one socket scan twice in a row. The live
        comment says so and the Go test asserts it directly.

      `COOLDOWN_MS` is NOT exported by `src/wifiScan.js`, so the generator cannot lift it the way it
      lifts `FLEET_CAP`, `DURATIONS` and `MAX_CHANNELS`. The corpus records
      `cooldownMsIsNotExported: true` and a Go test asserts that flag is still there — so if the
      live module ever exports it, the test fails and says to pin it properly. If the live VALUE
      changes meanwhile, nothing will notice. That is the gap, written down rather than hidden.

      Ten mutations, ten killed.

      **The accumulator is ported too** (`internal/wifiscan/table.go`,
      `tools/wifiscan-accum-cases.js`, 9 cases). RouterOS re-sends the WHOLE table every
      freeze-frame, so rows are keyed on channel and the latest wins — without that "the graph would
      grow a duplicate bar every second".

      **The 200-channel bound is on INSERTION, not on updates, and that is the whole point of it.**
      Once the table is full a NEW channel is dropped and the scan is marked truncated, but a
      channel already in the table keeps updating. The bound exists to bound memory against a device
      reporting per-sample — and such a device would fill the table in seconds, so a cap that also
      froze updates would leave every one of the 200 channels the operator can see stuck at its
      first reading for the rest of the scan while the real measurements were discarded. It would
      look identical for the first 200 rows and be wrong for everything after. There is a corpus
      case for exactly that, and a Go test that states the rule directly.

      `SampleCount` counts every parseable row SEEN, dropped ones included: it is how many samples
      the radio produced, not how many survived.

      Five mutations, five killed. One apparent survivor was an EQUIVALENT mutant of my own making —
      moving `SampleCount++` into a `defer` still runs it on the early return — and was replaced
      with one that actually changes behaviour before being counted.

      **The lifecycle is ported** (`internal/wifiscan/registry.go`): the single-exit `Finish`, the
      fleet-wide registry, the cooldown, the dirty-flag flush, the abort paths and the
      retry-without-`=duration=` rule. Clean under `-race`.

      **`Finish` runs its body exactly once, and that is not defensive programming.** Several racing
      things can each legitimately decide a scan is over — the wall-clock stop and the stream's own
      `done` routinely fire within milliseconds of each other on a scan that ended normally. Without
      the guard the operator sees two terminal events and the registry deletes an entry twice.
      Tested with 32 concurrent callers; exactly one may report that it ended the scan.

      **Admission and registration are ONE critical section.** Checking the fleet cap and then
      inserting under a second lock lets several operators past a cap of three at the same instant —
      which is precisely the situation the cap exists for. That mutation SURVIVED forty
      unsynchronised goroutines: the window is a few instructions wide and callers spawned in a loop
      reach it at measurably different times. The test now releases 64 callers through a starting
      gate and repeats the whole scenario 200 times, and the mutation dies. **A concurrency test
      without a starting gate is not testing the race** — worth remembering for the pool in
      blocker 2.

      Two more behaviours kept because their absence is invisible: a stream that ended BY ITSELF is
      not stopped (stopping opens a new channel to write `/cancel` with a stale tag, one more write
      to a device that has just finished), and the cooldown is recorded when a scan ENDS, not when
      it starts — otherwise a 120-second scan leaves the operator free to relaunch the moment it
      finishes.

      Seven mutations, seven killed.

      **The runner is written** (`internal/wifiscan/runner.go`), so item 9 is code-complete.
      `Cmd` builds the command with `=.id=` (the manual documents `number`; the binary API rejects
      it with "missing =.id=") and the explicit proplist — without which RouterOS answers every
      freeze-frame with a bare `!empty` and never sends a row. That is not a tidy-up to drop: a
      scan missing it runs, takes the radio off the air for its full duration, and reports nothing.
      Both are asserted, including that `=number=` never appears.

      `Run` drives the select loop: the hard stop, the natural end, the flush tick, and the failure
      path. **The flush tick doubles as the liveness probe** — a router that reboots mid-scan
      otherwise leaves the entry sitting until the hard stop, blocking a retry on a radio that is
      already back. Tested by dropping the connection during a 120-second scan and asserting it
      ends in seconds rather than at the 125-second ceiling.

      **`routeros.StreamUntilDone` was added rather than changing `Stream`.** Stream's four existing
      callers are all `/listen` subscriptions, which never end by themselves — for them the callback
      would never fire. The scan is the only bounded command, and the difference between "it ended"
      and "we stopped it" decides whether a `/cancel` is written to a device that has already
      finished. `onDone` cannot fire for a stream the caller stopped: the flag is set inside the
      same `Once` that performs the cancel.

      Seven more mutations, seven killed. Clean under `-race`.

      Remaining for the FEATURE: the WebSocket wiring and the dialog, which are item 10.

      Everything below is done, and so is the layer above it: `internal/alertdispatch` holds the
      message assembly, the cooldown, the delivery and the recipient fan-out, gated by
      `tools/alert-dispatch-cases.js` (13 messages, 7 cooldown sequences, 14 mutations killed).
      `cmd/mikrodash` gained `-alert-dispatch`, **default false**, and the running app logs which
      state it is in on every start.

      **It stays off until the operator says otherwise**, for the one reason on blocker 5 that did
      not change at standalone: both engines evaluate the same conditions against the same routers
      with in-memory cooldowns neither can see, and a duplicated message cannot be un-received.
      After cutover it is simply on.

      The REQUEST SHAPES are ported and pinned
      (`internal/notify/transport.go`, `tools/notify-transport-cases.js`): Telegram, Pushbullet and
      ntfy. `Channels`, `HasConfigured` and `Reason` were already ported.

      Described rather than performed, so the shape can be compared against the live app without
      either side opening a socket. Four details are not cosmetic, and each is where a plausible
      implementation goes wrong:

      * **The Telegram token goes in the PATH** — `/bot<token>/sendMessage` — and is percent-encoded.
        It is operator-supplied text, so one containing a slash would change which endpoint is
        called. `encodeURIComponent`, NOT Go's `url.PathEscape`: the latter leaves `+ $ & , : ; = @`
        alone because they are legal in a path segment, which is correct for a URL builder and wrong
        for reproducing what the live app sends.
      * **The ntfy URL is parsed, not concatenated.** Its scheme decides the port, and its query and
        fragment must not become part of the topic — `https://ntfy.sh/topic?auth=secret` posts to
        `/topic`, and the secret does not travel. Asserted by searching the WHOLE request for it.
      * **The ntfy title is an HTTP HEADER**, so a line break in it is a header injection. Refused
        rather than sent.
      * **ntfy's Content-Length is in BYTES**, not characters. A body with any non-ASCII in it is
        longer than its string length, and a short Content-Length truncates the message.

      Nine mutations, nine killed — including both injections.

      The corpus asserts the live source still CONTAINS each transcribed marker, so it cannot
      quietly describe a request the live app stopped making. Its byte-length assertion is derived
      rather than typed: the first version said 27 and the answer is 29, which is the mistake the
      assertion exists to catch.

      merge is ported and pinned (`internal/notify/usertest.go`,
      `tools/usernotify-test-cases.js`, 18 cases).

      Pressing Test must verify what is TYPED, not only what is stored, or nobody can check a token
      without committing it first. Three rules make that safe and each looks like a detail:

      * **A MASKED value means "use the stored one".** A saved credential renders back as `••••••••`;
        taken literally, pressing Test without retyping would send eight bullet characters to
        Telegram AS THE BOT TOKEN — and the failure would read as a bad token rather than a bug.
        Asserted independently of the corpus: whatever the form sends, the mask may never appear in
        the settings a request is built from.
      * **A FALSY value means that too.** The live guard is `if (body[f] && …)`, so `0` and `false`
        are skipped. A port checking `!= null` would override with the strings "0" and "false" —
        and a chat id of "0" is a request Telegram refuses in a way the operator cannot explain.
        That mutation SURVIVED until a corpus case sent a falsy non-null value.
      * **LENGTHS ARE CAPPED** — 512 for a credential, 256 for the rest. This is the one place an
        ORDINARY ACCOUNT chooses what the SERVER connects to, which is why the install-wide switch
        ships off; the live comment says enabling it "widens what an ordinary account can make the
        server connect to". Capped BY RUNES, so a multi-byte value is not cut mid-character.

      configured" rather than the truth — and only that channel: a test of one must not enable
      another.

      `SetUserNotifyConfig`, `RemoveUserNotifyConfig` over `user_notify_config(user_id, data,
      updated_at)`, with `data` a JSON blob and `updated_at` in epoch milliseconds.

      **A corrupt blob reads as "not configured" rather than returning an error**, which is the
      live behaviour and load-bearing: this is read from inside the alert path, so an error would
      abort delivery for every OTHER recipient in the same alert. One user's unreadable row must
      cost that user their alerts and nobody else theirs. Five mutations, five killed — the first
      of them is exactly that.

      Removal exists because a personal destination must not outlive the account that owns it: a

      `tools/usernotify-save-cases.js`, 22 cases).

      `Merge` merges over the STORED blob by design, not as an optimisation: a credential the caller
      did not send keeps its existing ciphertext and is never decrypted and re-encrypted just to
      survive an edit to an unrelated field. A test counts the encryptor's calls and requires zero
      for an edit that touched no credential.

      **The save rules DIFFER FROM `MergeForTest`, and the difference is the point of the corpus:**

      |                | test merge              | save merge             |
      |----------------|-------------------------|------------------------|
      | guard          | truthy value            | key PRESENT            |
      | so an empty    | keeps the stored value  | CLEARS it              |
      | trimming       | none                    | on the string fields   |

      Both are right — a test with a blank field should verify what is stored, while a save with a
      blank field is how a channel is switched off — and "correcting" either into the other is a
      bug. `TestSaveAndTestMergeDisagreeOnPurpose` asserts both directions.

      Two more behaviours worth naming: a toggle accepts only `true` or the STRING `"true"`, so a
      form posting `"yes"` or `1` does not switch a channel on by accident; and `emailTo` is
      validated on the MERGED value, so an edit to an unrelated field on a config that already holds
      a bad address fails too.

      Eight mutations, eight killed — the first being `Public` returning the stored credential.

      install that upgraded. A non-boolean is not a yes either.

      **The rule in `alerts.go` was SATISFIED, not waived.** "A read nothing calls is a read nothing
      gates" warns against porting a query ahead of its caller because it adds code no corpus drives.
      These land WITH the corpus that drives them, so there is no window in which they exist
      unexercised; the bell (item 14) is the production caller and follows.

      Three behaviours that a reasonable implementation gets wrong:

      * **A limit of ZERO takes the default.** `limit || 200` is falsy on zero, so a caller passing
        0 gets 200 rows — a port passing it through to SQL returns an empty feed, which looks
        exactly like "no alerts".
      * **"Recent" means RESOLVED, not lately.** An open alert is never in it however recently it
        fired. Reading it the other way puts every open alert in both feeds and the bell
        double-counts. A test asserts the two feeds never share an id.

        a believability assertion REFUSES a seed where the two orders would agree.

      * **The dot means UNACKNOWLEDGED OPEN alerts.** Not "any alert" — a resolved one is history

        operator says they have seen something, and a dot that stayed lit would train them to
        ignore it.
      * **Acknowledging removes an alert from the PANEL, not from the LIST.** That is what makes
        "Clear all" clear anything. The rows stay in memory so a later resolve can find them by id.
        So an acknowledged alert that is still OPEN is invisible by design.
      * **A new alert replaces the OPEN one for the same key.** Without it a flapping interface
        fills all hundred slots in under an hour. A resolved entry for the same key is history and
        stays.
      * **A resolved row is timed from when it RESOLVED**, or it would say "3h ago" about something
        that ended a minute ago.

      `internal/collection/retune.go`: `PollRetunes(updates, saved, overrides)`. A settings save
      does not only write the file, it re-tunes the RUNNING collectors so a slider takes effect
      without a restart. Three rules, all of them about what NOT to do:

      * **A per-router override outranks the fleet default** (#105). A pinned key is SAVED and NOT
        applied — the two halves disagree on purpose. `_pinned` is `overrides[key] !== undefined`,
        so a pin of `0`, `false` or `""` still pins; a port testing truthiness un-pins exactly the
        values an operator sets to mean "off".
      * **Only keys in the UPDATES.** `saved` is the merged file, so every poll key is in it — a
        port deciding from that re-tunes all 23 collectors on every save, restarting streams
        nobody touched.
      * **The value is re-clamped to 500..600000**, which is neither the validator's range nor a
        superset of it: `pollRouting` validates at 500..300000 and `pollWifi` at 10000..600000.

      The TABLE is lifted from the route, because it is the part with a history: the live source
      records that `pollTopology`, `pollVlans` and `pollPpp` were once missing from it, so "the
      sliders existed and the bounds existed, but with no entry here the value was dropped on save
      and never reached the collector".

      **A REAL JS→GO TRAP, caught by the corpus.** `saved[key]` on a MISSING Go key yields the same
      nil as a key holding JSON null — but JavaScript tells them apart and the answers differ:
      `Number(undefined)` is NaN, so the collector is left alone, while `Number(null)` is 0, which
      is finite and clamps to the floor of **500**. Reading the one-value map form silently sped up
      a collector whose interval had never been written. The two-value lookup is now mandatory and
      `jsval.ToNumber`'s doc says so.

      **`internal/jsval` had NO TEST FILES**, and `ToNumber` was about to be the third coercion
      added to it. A shared helper with no gate is worse than a private copy — every caller
      inherits the same mistake, and each caller's corpus covers only the shapes that caller
      passes. `tools/jsval-number-cases.js` runs `Number(v)` in V8 over 29 values;
      `jsval_number_test.go` consumes it. It also pins the pair that keeps `ToNumber` and
      `store.parseIntLike` from being merged: `parseInt("25abc")` is 25 and `Number("25abc")` is
      NaN, and the settings validator uses the first while this uses the second.

      One coercion is deliberately NOT reproduced and is asserted as absent: `Number([5])` is 5 in
      JavaScript via ToPrimitive. Nothing here stores an interval as a one-element array, so
      reproducing it would be a rule with no caller.

      **14 mutations across both files, 14 killed.**
