      **PART 5 — THE MECHANISM FOR APPLYING A RETUNE.** `pollLoop.retime()`, the atomic
      `pollInterval`, and `System.SetPollMs` as the worked example.

      **`retime` exists for the PENDING timer, not the next one.** `pollLoop.delay` is a function,
      re-read on every schedule, so a changed period already affects the next tick without help.
      What it does not touch is the timer already counting down — and an operator moving a poll
      from sixty seconds to five expects five, not to wait out the remaining fifty-nine.

      **It measures from NOW, where `start` measures from `lastRun`, and that is deliberate.**
      `start` counts elapsed time because page navigation calls stop/start freely. A settings save
      is a different event: the live side does `clearInterval` + `setInterval`, a full new period
      from the save. Measuring from `lastRun` would fire IMMEDIATELY whenever the new period is
      shorter than the time already elapsed — a burst of simultaneous polls across every collector
      on every router the moment Save is pressed.

      **The interval is ATOMIC, and the reason is a survey rather than a preference.** 21 of the
      24 collectors send `pollMs` to the browser in their payload (the live ones send the value
      the route mutated), so it cannot hide inside the loop. And **three collectors — `packages`,
      `routing`, `talkers` — have NO MUTEX AT ALL**, so "guard it with the collector's lock" would
      be a rule with three exceptions, in exactly the files where a reviewer would not notice its
      absence. `TestConcurrentRetuneIsRaceFree` runs under `-race` with a starting gate.

      **8 mutations, 8 killed.** Two survived the first pass and both were my tests' fault:
      the stopped-loop test waited 300ms when `bounded` has a **500ms floor**, so a re-armed loop
      could not have fired within the window either way; and nothing observed the RE-TIME half of
      `SetPollMs`, only the stored value — the version of the bug where the number on screen looks
      right and the collector keeps polling at the old period.

      **PART 6 — EVERY RE-TUNABLE COLLECTOR NOW HAS A SETTER.** The gap recorded above is closed:
      22 collectors carry `SetPollMs`, which is ALL 23 of the live route's targets bar one.

      Done by changing the field type first and letting the compiler locate every read, rather
      than by editing 23 files from a list. Three shapes needed handling — the constructor's
      struct literal, `time.Duration(x.pollMs) * time.Millisecond`, and the bare int read — and
      four files spelled the field with different alignment, which is exactly the kind of thing a
      typed-out list gets wrong.

      **THREE COLLECTORS TURNED OUT NOT TO NEED IT, and checking beat assuming.** `dhcpleases`,
      `netwatch` and `vpn` capture their interval in a CLOSURE over a local, so it is immutable by
      construction. Only `vpn` is in the live `pollMap`; `dhcpleases` and `netwatch` are not
      re-tuned upstream either — netwatch's own comment already records that its computed interval
      "never takes effect" in the original. So `vpn` was converted and the other two were left
      alone, which is the faithful answer rather than the uniform one.

      **PING IS NOT A POLL LOOP AND ITS SETTER IS NOT `retime`.** The interval goes to the ROUTER
      as `/tool/ping =interval=N`, so changing it means restarting the stream with a new argument
      — which is what the live route does (`s.ping._restartStream()`) rather than the
      `_restartTimer` its poll-mode siblings get. A stopped stream stays stopped, which matters
      because a save re-tunes every collector including ones nobody is watching.

      **`arp` IS THE ONE TARGET WITH NO GO COUNTERPART**, and it is recorded rather than faked.
      This port has no ARP collector: the live one exists to fill a cache other collectors read
      through `getByIP`/`getByMAC`, and PORT-QUEUE already lists it beside `conns` and `traffic`
      as collectors that "fill a cache and emit elsewhere". Inventing one so the table could be
      complete would be a collector with no caller.

      **A LEDGER THAT FAILS IN BOTH DIRECTIONS**, in the manner of `wiring-audit` and its
      siblings: `TestEveryReTunedCollectorHasASetter` compares the live `pollMap` against the Go
      map and the recorded exception, and `TestEveryMappedTypeActuallyHasTheMethod` greps the
      package for the method so a renamed type fails here rather than when an operator saves.
      Four probes, all detected: dropping a mapped entry, claiming a target upstream does not
      have, excusing a target the live route DOES re-tune, and deleting a real setter.

      **PART 7 — THE WIRING, AND ITEM 15 IS DONE.** `internal/session/retune.go`:
      `Session.ApplyPollRetunes` dispatches by the LIVE collector name to the session's fields,
      and `Manager.ApplyPollRetunes` fans one save out to every live router. The settings route
      calls it instead of discarding the answer.

      **THE OVERRIDES COME FROM THE SESSION, NOT THE CALLER**, and that is the whole reason this
      could not live in the route. A fleet-wide save has ONE set of updates and as many override
      sets as there are live routers. Passing nil would silently un-pin every router the operator
      had configured specially — which is #105 restated at a different layer.

      **The target map is built PER CALL, deliberately.** A collector is nil until `Acquire` has
      connected once, and several are built only on page focus or reconnect; a map built at
      construction would capture nils and silently drop the re-tune for exactly the collectors a
      busy session has and an idle one does not.

      Four tests, each stating a rule the wiring could plausibly break: the re-tune reaches the
      collectors; a pinned key is not applied (with a believability check that an UNPINNED one
      is, or the assertion holds for a function that applies nothing); a collector this session
      never built is skipped rather than panicked on; and `KeepCurrent` does not pass its zero
      through, which would set the FLOOR on a collector nobody asked to speed up.
- [ ] **BUILT, AND IT RUNS BY DEFAULT IN STANDALONE — 16. Wire the background pool.**
      *(Corrected 2026-08-29 by measurement. This said "BUILT AND UNCONSTRUCTED" and it was wrong.)*

      **`server.go` builds the pool from `srv.standalone && !opts.NoPool`.** So a standalone process
      does pool the fleet, unless `-no-pool` is passed. The `mdtest` container had been running
      without it: the Go process held ESTABLISHED sockets to `10.0.0.4:8728` and `10.0.0.53:8729` —
      both routers nobody had open — alongside the live app's own pool, which is exactly the doubled
      background load the operator decided against.

      **Found by attributing sockets to the process rather than by reading the code.** Two earlier
      greps in the same tick said the opposite: `[pool]` matched nothing (the pool logs under
      `[overview]`), and `[overview]` matched nothing either (it only logs a capability refusal).
      `/proc/net/tcp` alone could not settle it because the container uses host networking and sees
      Node's connections too; matching socket INODES against the Go process's own fds could.

      **`mdtest` now runs with `-no-pool`, and holds no router connection when no page is open.**
      What remains open is unchanged and is the operator's: whether the pool may run during
      coexistence at all.

      `internal/routers/pool.go` holds one connection per unwatched router and the three collectors
      the live pool runs; `internal/routers/overview.go` holds its decisions as a pure `SyncPool`.
      It is CONSTRUCTED BY NOBODY on purpose — `-no-pool` exists for the same reason — because a Go
      pool during coexistence doubles the background sessions on every router, and concurrent API
      channels are the documented bottleneck.


      **PART 1 — THE SITE-NAME ALIGNMENT** (upstream `e76962d`, this port's ToDo.md §1). `BuildRow`
      pads `siteNames` with `""` per id instead of filtering, so the two arrays stay the same
      length. **The port had the bug twice** — the builder AND the consumer,
      `web/src/pages/routers.ts`, which zips them by index. That code is unchanged and correct
      once the server pads; it now carries the comment explaining why, so neither half is "fixed"
      alone. The Go test has been renamed twice as the understanding improved and records both
      renames.

      **PART 2 — THE POOL HAS A CALLER.** `internal/server/devices.go`: `buildStatsSources`
      assembles what `routers.BuildStats` needs, `syncPool` brings the pool in line with the fleet,
      and `devicesFocus`/`devicesBlur` resume it on the first watcher and suspend it on the last.
      Hooked into `pageFocus`, `pageBlur` and the socket teardown.

      Three placements that are load-bearing rather than stylistic:

      * **The assembly lives in `internal/server`, not `internal/routers`.** That package stays
        pure — no sessions, no store, no database — and its tests run without any of them.
      * **`devicesBlur` is called BEFORE `pageBlur`'s `routerID` guard.** The Devices page is
        fleet-wide and a socket can be on it with no router selected, so returning early would
        leave that connection in `devicesWatchers` for ever and the pool would never see its last
        watcher leave.
      * **And from the TEARDOWN path**, because a closed tab never sends a blur — the commonest
        way a viewer leaves is the one that would otherwise hold a connection to every router
        indefinitely.

      **`excluded` is derived on every sync rather than tracked.** A router somebody has open must
      not also get a background session: two connections is the visible cost, recording every
      up/down transition twice is the one that corrupts history. A second record of who is watching
      what is exactly the thing that drifts.

      **9 mutations, 8 killed, 1 recorded unkillable.** Four survived the first pass and all four
      needed a pool that was actually running — every test had `s.pool == nil`, where Resume,
      Suspend and `syncPool` are all no-ops. With a real pool behind a stub dialer: a disabled
      router is never connected to, an open router is excluded, and only the LAST watcher suspends.

      **One of those four then survived a second time, and the reason is worth recording:** the
      RBAC-error test never reached the erroring path. `userIDFor` returned `""` because the
      fixture had no `users.json`, `Can` answers `(false, nil)` for an empty user id, and the
      broken table was never read — so the test passed for both the original and the mutant.
      It now asserts the resolver answers YES before the break and errors after it.

      The unkillable one is `had &&` in `devicesBlur`. Dropping it survives, because the only
      thing that resumes the pool is `devicesFocus` and that always adds to the set — so an empty
      set implies already-suspended. It stays because that invariant belongs to a different
      function.

      Also added: `Pool.Suspended()` (the fleet-wide counterpart of `OverviewSession.Suspended`),
      `Session.System()` and `Manager.Live()`.

      **Ledgers updated in both directions:** `emit-audit` (`routers` moved UNPORTED → PORTED) and
      `event-audit` (`routers:stats` has an emitter). `routers:update` is now recorded as ALLOWED
      with its reason: this port serves the router LIST over HTTP, so what is missing is the
      BROADCAST, and a broadcast has nothing to announce until router administration exists.

      **PART 4 — `PUT /api/sites/:id/routers`, WHICH SATISFIES UPSTREAM `e0c8045`.**
      `internal/routers/membership.go` (the decision) and `internal/server/sites_api.go` (the route).

      **THE DECISION IS LIFTED, NOT RETYPED.** `tools/site-membership-cases.js` slices the loop out
      of `src/index.js` between two asserted anchors and evaluates it in a `vm` with
      `Routers.update` and `audit` stubbed, recording what it would have written. 12 cases. The
      reason it is lifted rather than read: the loop walks EVERY device, not the site's members,
      because a device that WAS here and is no longer listed has to be detached — and a per-member
      iteration never sees it. An implementation iterating `wanted` passes every add case and fails
      no test that does not remove something. `detachAnUnlisted` is that case.

      Two harness traps, both worth recording because they look like the generator is broken when
      it is actually being honest:

      * The slice OPENS one line above `let changed = 0;`, so prepending a declaration for the
        harness makes it a redeclaration. The slice brings its own.
      * It also opens with `const all = Routers.loadAll();`, which SHADOWS any `all` in the vm
        context. The fleet is supplied through the `Routers` stub instead.

      **16 mutations, 16 killed** — 8 on the pure decision, 8 on the route. Two needed the tests
      strengthened rather than being counted:

      * `before-aliases` (returning the record's own slice as `Before`) SURVIVED, because the test
        built the fleet from a slice LITERAL where `cap == len`, so the aliasing append reallocated
        and the scribble landed nowhere. A fleet that arrives through `append` or a decode has spare
        capacity; the test now builds one that way.
      * `db-error-is-404` and `always-broadcast` both survived a first pass with nothing observing
        them. `TestABrokenStoreIsNotReportedAsAMissingSite` closes the handle mid-test (after
        asserting the same request worked first), and the no-op test now watches a hub client for a
        `perms:changed` that must not arrive — paired with `TestARealChangeDoesBroadcastPermsChanged`
        so "broadcasts nothing" cannot hold for a route that never broadcasts.

      **The 404 comes before the body is read, and that ordering is the point.** The removal branch
      does not care whether the site exists, so an unguarded route given a typo'd id walks the fleet,
      finds nobody who should be there, and DETACHES every device carrying it — answering 200.

      **`routerIds` absent is not `[]`.** An explicit empty array is a real request ("this site has
      no devices"), so a missing field cannot default to it; the route answers 400, as the live one
      does.

      **The gate is `requireGlobalAdmin`, tested under a REAL resolver.** `AuthMode: "none"` makes
      `mayManagePrincipals` short-circuit to true, which is this port's recurring blind spot — three
      previous items had a permission check that no test reached. `TestOnlyAnAdministratorMaySet
      SiteMembership` reuses `scopedRoutersServer`, where carol holds `router:manage` on r1 and not
      `system:principals`: exactly the escalation `routers_api.go` strips the site fields for.

      **One live behaviour is deliberately NOT reproduced.** The live route calls
      `_broadcastPermsChanged()` twice on the same line; every other authorization-invalidating write
      calls it once. The port emits one and records why. Filed as `ToDo.md` §5 — if the double is
      intentional, the port will follow.

      **`memberSiteIDs` restates `store.RouterSiteIDs`** because `internal/routers` is pure and
      cannot import the store. `TestTheTwoSiteIDNormalisersAgree` holds them together, with a
      believability check that the corpus contains the case that can tell them apart: an EMPTY array
      beside a set scalar, where the array must win outright or a membership just cleared is
      resurrected from the stale `siteId` mirror.

      Also added: `db.GetSite` — `(nil, nil)` for a missing row, an error for a broken store, because
      collapsing the two tells an operator their site id is wrong when the database is unreadable.

      **PART 5 — A USER-VISIBLE DRIFT THE RENAME ARGUMENT MISSED.** The queue records that
      `063a414`'s routers → devices rename "CANNOT HURT THIS PORT, by two independent accidents of
      its design": the page catalogue is LIFTED from `src/pages.js`, and this port does not run
      migrations. Both are true and neither covers **copy inside a hand-ported renderer**. The Sites
      card's empty state read "No sites yet. Add one to group your **routers**." here and
      "…your **devices**." upstream — a rendered-page difference, which the hard constraints say is
      not a port however correct the data.

      **WHY NO GATE CAUGHT IT.** `tools/access-summary-check.js` gated `_renderSiteRow` and had done
      for several sessions. It did NOT gate `_renderSiteTable`, and the empty state is a branch a
      populated fixture never reaches — so the row was compared on every run and the sentence beside
      it never was. The lesson generalises past this string: **a gate on the row is not a gate on the
      table**, and the branches a realistic corpus never renders are exactly where copy drifts.

      Closed by extending that gate rather than adding another: `_siteIdsOf`, `_siteRouterCounts` and
      `_renderSiteTable` are now lifted alongside the row, six table cases are driven from one
      payload on both sides, and three believability checks refuse a vacuous pass (empty and
      populated must differ, the live empty state must still say "devices", and one device must not
      render the same as two). 43 cases → 49.

      **`siteRouterCounts` had no port at all** — `siteTableHtml` took the counts as a parameter and
      nobody computed them. Ported now, importing `siteIdsOf` from `routers.ts` rather than
      restating the array-wins-outright rule a third time.

      **4 mutations, 4 killed**, the first being the original bug put back.

      **PART 6 — `_parseSiteBody`, THE VALIDATION BEHIND CREATE AND EDIT.**
      `internal/sites/parse.go`, pinned by `tools/site-body-cases.js` → `parse_test.go`, 30 cases.

      **THE WHOLE DECISION IS ABSENT VERSUS NULL VERSUS SET**, and Go's `map[string]any` conflates
      the first two — `m["place"]` is nil for a missing key and for a JSON null alike. This port has
      been caught by that twice already (`collection.PollRetunes`, `store.PageSettings`), so every
      read here is `v, ok := m[k]` and `Patch` carries explicit `Has*` flags rather than relying on
      a nil. The consequence if it were got wrong is concrete: an edit that only RENAMES a site would
      blank its map pin, because absent would read as "clear the location".

      **The five location columns move together or not at all** (#96 — a location is a picked place,
      not typed coordinates). Top-level `lat`/`lon` in the body are ignored outright; a `place`
      carrying coordinates and no name is refused rather than half-written.

      **A LIVE QUIRK THAT WAS FIXED UPSTREAM, and the port followed rather than led.** A null name
      used to create a site called "null": the check was the strict `b.name === undefined`, so a JSON
      null fell through to `String(null)` — four characters, truthy, within 1-64 — while the
      description check two lines below used the loose `== null` and did not have the problem. The
      port REPRODUCED it and the corpus pinned it, deliberately, so it could not be silently
      corrected here. Filed as `ToDo.md` §6 and fixed live on 2026-08-27; the corpus regenerated, the
      pin flipped to `aNullNameIsRefused`, and `jsString` became loose to match. **That is the loop
      working as designed** — the port found it, the live repo fixed it, and the corpus is what
      carried the change across. It is also why the assertion was written to FAIL on a change rather
      than to record whatever it saw: it did, and it named the file to reread.

      **A SLICING TRAP worth recording, because it failed LOUDLY only by luck.** The signature is
      `function _parseSiteBody(body, { partial } = {}) {`, so `indexOf('{', from)` lands in the
      DESTRUCTURED PARAMETER and the depth walk closes on it — yielding a two-line "function". It was
      caught by the marker assertions (`GeoPlace.normalizePlace` was missing), which is exactly what
      they are for; without them the generator would have produced a corpus from a stub and every
      case would have agreed with a port that validated nothing. The anchor now ends at the body
      brace and the slice starts there.

      **10 mutations, 10 killed**, including both halves of the absent/null trap and the
      measure-before-trim ordering.

      **PART 7 — THE SITE WRITES, AND A BUG THE PREVIOUS PART'S OWN FIXTURE HID.**
      `internal/db/sites.go` gains `CreateSite`, `UpdateSite`, `DeleteSite` and `IsDuplicateSiteName`;
      `sites.Patch` gains `Columns()`.

      **`GetSite` WOULD HAVE 500'd ON MOST SITES.** It was written in Part 4 scanning `description`
      and the three `place_*` columns straight into Go `string`s. All four are NULLABLE in the live
      schema (migrations 4 and 10), and `description` is null for every site created without one —
      which is most of them. `database/sql` answers "converting NULL to string is unsupported", so
      the membership route would have answered 500 for a perfectly good site id.

      **It passed every test, because the test DDL declared those columns `NOT NULL DEFAULT ''`.**
      A fixture that cannot produce a NULL cannot produce the row that breaks the scan. That is the
      same shape as the Part 5 finding one tick earlier — a gate on the row is not a gate on the
      table; a fixture stricter than the schema is not a fixture. Both DDLs now match the live
      schema, `site-a` is inserted with NULL everywhere it may be, and reverting the fix reproduces
      the exact error, so the fixture is proved to catch it rather than assumed to.

      `lat`/`lon` never had the problem: they are already `*float64`, and `database/sql` sets a
      pointer destination to nil on NULL. That is also the Gulf of Guinea guard at the storage layer,
      and `TestASiteWithNoLocationHasNoCoordinates` pins both directions — an unset location reads
      back nil, and a REAL zero coordinate survives.

      **`siteWritableColumns` is an injection boundary, not tidiness.** A column name goes into SQL
      TEXT because an identifier cannot be parameterised, so the whitelist is what keeps a request
      body out of the statement. `TestOnlyWhitelistedColumnsAreWritten` sends keys containing
      `--` and `) VALUES` and asserts the statement still parses.

      **The UNIQUE index is the enforcement, not a pre-check** — the live route says so where it
      catches the constraint: two administrators creating "Depot" at the same moment both pass a
      SELECT and one still has to lose. `IsDuplicateSiteName` is asserted in BOTH directions, since
      a matcher that answered true for everything would turn every failure into a 409.

      **8 mutations, 8 killed.** One survived a first pass — `caller-supplies-id`, because nothing
      passed an `id` to `CreateSite`. It matters more than it looks: the id is what every grant,
      audit row and membership list names, so a caller choosing it could reuse the id of a site just
      deleted and silently inherit its grants.

      **PART 8 — THE DOWNGRADE MIRROR, WHICH PART 4's WRITE HAD BEEN LEAVING STALE.**
      Found while reading `Routers.clearSite` for the delete path, which keeps `siteId` true and
      prompted the question of whether `Routers.update` does too. It does:

          siteIds: _updSiteIds(data, existing),
          siteId:  _updSiteIds(data, existing)[0] || null,

      This port's `store.UpdateRouter` merged the patch and left the mirror alone. So
      `PUT /api/sites/:id/routers`, which writes `siteIds` and nothing else, produced a file Node
      would never have written.

      **WHY IT LOOKED DEAD AND IS NOT.** Every reader on both sides prefers the LIST —
      `RouterSiteIDs` here, `_normalizeSites` there — so a stale scalar changes nothing anyone can
      see today. That is precisely why it would have gone unnoticed. It matters on a DOWNGRADE: a
      pre-#117 build reads the scalar and nothing else, so a device whose membership changed under
      the new build shows up in a site it had left. This is the class of drift `cmd/compat` exists
      for — the file, not the behaviour.

      **ONE DELIBERATE DEPARTURE, and it is not laziness.** `_updSiteIds` falls back to the existing
      record, so the live function recomputes on EVERY update. Reproducing that literally would make
      a rename add `siteIds: []` and `siteId: null` to a device that has never had either — fields
      Node only writes because its record is rebuilt from a spread, where this port patches the
      decoded JSON in place. The recompute is therefore gated on the patch actually carrying one of
      the two, and `TestAnUnrelatedPatchLeavesMembershipAlone` pins both halves.

      **`cleanSiteIDs` did not dedupe** where `_cleanSiteIds` does (`out.indexOf(id) === -1`). Not
      harmless: the Sites card counts a device once per membership, so a device listed twice in one
      site reads as two devices in the only place that number is visible. Blanks were already
      dropped; the first occurrence keeps its position.

      **7 mutations, 7 killed.** All four tests failed before the fix and were written that way
      round, so none of them is a description of what the code already did.

      **PART 9 — `store.ClearSite`, THE CASCADE A DELETED SITE NEEDS.** Sites live in SQLite and
      devices in `routers.json`, so there is no foreign key and something has to walk the file.

      **ONE PASS AND ONE WRITE, not N calls to `UpdateRouter`.** Going through the patch path would
      re-read, re-decode and re-write the whole file once per device, and a failure halfway would
      leave the fleet half-detached with the site already gone.

      **The rule is deliberately NOT shared with `routers.SiteMembership`.** That package is pure and
      decides what a SAVE changes; this is a cascade with no decision in it — every device carrying
      the id loses it, and there is no "wanted" set to consult. Sharing them would mean passing an
      empty wanted set and relying on a coincidence of shape.

      **7 mutations, 7 killed.** One survived a first pass and the reason is worth recording, because
      the obvious response would have been to write it off as equivalent: `empty-id-walks` (dropping
      the `siteID == ""` guard) changes NOTHING observable through the membership, since
      `cleanSiteIDs` drops blanks and the walk reaches the same answer having done the work. What
      separates them is WHERE the guard sits — before the read, as the live one is
      (`if (!siteId) return 0;` precedes `loadAll()`). Removing `routers.json` distinguishes them: the
      guard still answers `(0, nil)` where a walk fails. The test asserts both that and, for
      believability, that a real id DOES surface the missing file.

      **A comment was corrected before it shipped.** The no-op guard's first draft said the write is
      skipped because "the file's mtime is what the live app watches" — checked, and nothing watches
      it. The real reason is coexistence: the Node process holds the same file, so a rewrite that
      changes nothing is a chance for the two to interleave for no gain.

      **PART 10 — THE FOUR HANDLERS.** `GET/POST/PUT/DELETE /api/sites`, plus the `sites:update`
      emit. `internal/server/sites_api.go`, 12 route tests.

      **`GET /api/sites` IS UNGATED BEYOND BEING SIGNED IN, AND THAT IS LOAD-BEARING.** The live
      route carries no `Rbac` middleware, and `routers_api.go` DEPENDS on that where it strips the
      site fields from a non-administrator's router write: "every site id enumerable from an ungated
      GET /api/sites". Tightening it here would make that comment wrong and the strip would read as
      belt-and-braces rather than the check it is. `TestListSitesNeedsOnlyASession` pins it, with a
      believability check that the same non-administrator IS refused the write routes on the same mux.

      **`db.SiteColumns` exists because `db.Site` collapses NULL to `""`.** That collapse is
      deliberate — `geoplace.NormalizePlace` trims and then tests, so nothing downstream can tell
      them apart — but `audit.Diff` can: the after side is `Patch.Columns()`, which writes a true nil
      for a cleared field, and comparing that against `""` reports a change on every save of a site
      that never had a description. The live route gets this for free, `_before` being the raw row.
      `Coord` is used for the two coordinates for the usual reason: a nil `*float64` in an `any` is a
      NON-NIL interface holding a nil pointer.

      **The delete's four effects are ordered, and the order is the interesting part.** Devices are
      detached FIRST — a device pointing at a site that no longer exists renders a blank chip and is
      unreachable to a site-scoped grant, and after the row goes there is no site left to name. A
      detach FAILURE refuses the request before the row goes, for the same reason. Then the row,
      then the trail while the name is still known, then the site-scoped grants.

      **TWO PRE-EXISTING GATES CAUGHT THIS WORK, which is the system doing its job:**

      * `TestNoRawErrorReachesAnHttpBody` refused both `err.Error()` calls. Every message
        `ParseSiteBody` produces is a fixed string today, so the gate is strictly-speaking early —
        and it is right anyway: the day one of them starts quoting the value it rejected is the day
        a path reaches the browser, and nobody would think to revisit here.
      * `emit-audit` and `event-audit` both went red the moment `sites:update` was emitted. `sites`
        moved UNPORTED → PORTED, and `sites:update` is recorded UNCONSUMED with its reason.

      **AND A LATENT TRAP IN AN EXISTING TEST HELPER, found by tripping it.** `routerDBDir` says it
      "remembers where each test server's database lives", but `scopedRoutersServer` swaps `auditDB`
      for a new handle in a new directory and did not update the map. A later helper adding a table
      through the map therefore created it in a database the server had already stopped using — the
      table was there, the server could not see it, and the failure read as "no such table: sites"
      for a test that had just created it. The map now follows the handle.

      **PART 11 — THE SITE FORM'S DEVICE LIST**, `siteMemberRowsHtml`. 13 cases added to
      `access-summary-check`, which now runs 62.

      **THE COPY IS THE #117 CHANGE, IN THREE WORDS.** Each row says "— also in X, Y", not
      "currently in": ticking a device here ADDS this site, where before multi-site it MOVED the
      device out of the ones it already had. That distinction lives entirely in markup, which is
      exactly what a hand-port gets subtly wrong and no fixture notices — so the gate asserts both
      that the live side still says "also in" AND that it does not say "currently in", and a
      mutation putting the old wording back is the first of nine killed.

      **The filter consults `_sitesById`, not just `id !== site.id`.** A device may carry a
      membership whose site this browser has not loaded — created by another administrator a moment
      ago, or removed while the form was open. Rendering "also in undefined" is worse than saying
      nothing, and saying nothing is what the live code does. `a membership this client cannot name`
      is the case; `renders-unknown-sites` is the mutation.

      **ONE DELIBERATE DEPARTURE FROM THE LIVE SHAPE.** The original does `filter(...).map(...)`,
      indexing `_sitesById` TWICE per id. TypeScript refuses that under
      `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, and it is right to: the two lookups agree only because nothing
      mutates the map between them, which is true and is not a property worth depending on. One
      lookup, in a loop. The output is identical — the gate compares innerHTML, so this is proved
      rather than argued.

      **The slice needed a marker rather than a spelled-out closing line.** The device list lives
      inside `showSiteForm`, and its last line is a `<span style="color:…">` full of nested quotes;
      escaping it through the generator was where the first attempt broke. It now anchors on
      `No devices configured yet.` and takes the rest of that line.

      **9 mutations, 9 killed.**

      **A THIRD LEDGER CAUGHT THIS WORK.** `attr-audit` went red on `data-site-router`: a control
      this port now renders and nothing reads. True — the renderer is ported and the form's wiring
      is not. Recorded as `UNSHIPPED` beside `site-action` and `site-id`, which are the same class
      for the same reason. Three different ledgers have now failed on this item's work in two ticks
      (`emit-audit`, `event-audit`, `attr-audit`), each naming a real gap.

      **PART 12 — WHAT PRESSING SAVE SENDS.** `siteSavePlan`, gated by `tools/site-save-check.js`,
      which LIFTS `saveSite` and RUNS it against a shimmed form and a recording `fetch` — so what is
      compared is the requests themselves, method, path and body, not a reading of the source.

      **IT IS ALWAYS TWO REQUESTS AND THE ORDER IS FORCED.** The site's fields and its membership sit
      behind different endpoints because they are different authorization decisions, and the
      membership call must go SECOND: when adding, there is no id until the create returns one. Get
      that backwards and creating a site silently drops its device assignment, with BOTH requests
      succeeding and nothing to see. The second request's path therefore carries a literal `{id}`
      placeholder when creating, modelled explicitly rather than through a callback so the decision
      stays pure — and a caller that forgets to substitute gets a 404 from a path that obviously
      names nothing, instead of writing membership to a site called "undefined".

      **THIS FORM NEVER SENDS AN ABSENT `place`, AND THE SERVER STILL MUST SUPPORT ONE.** The picker
      is read on every save, so an empty one CLEARS the location — deliberately. `ParseSiteBody`'s
      absent case exists for other callers, and a "simplification" of the server to match this client
      would break a rename made through the API. The gate asserts the live form still sends the field,
      so if that ever changes the port's note is forced to be reread rather than left lying.

      **8 mutations, 8 killed**, including the reversed order and a `place` omitted when null.

      **PART 13 — THE DELETE CONFIRMATION**, `siteDeletePrompt`, gated the same way: lifted and RUN
      with `confirm` recording what it was asked, so the string compared is the one the operator
      sees. `access-summary-check` now runs 67 cases.

      The warning is the #117 change in one sentence — "They keep any other sites, and are not
      deleted." Before multi-site a device had ONE site and deleting it left the device with none, so
      the honest warning then was about losing its only membership. A port keeping that wording would
      frighten an operator out of a safe action. Killed as `pre-117-warning`, the first of 7.

      Two smaller live behaviours are reproduced rather than tidied: no warning AT ALL for an empty

      **CLOSED — `internal/server/auth_login.go`, and this paragraph described it as open until

      holding a Go-minted cookie is unauthenticated the moment it touches a proxied page.

## OPERATOR DECISIONS — ANSWERED 2026-08-27 (SECOND ROUND)

Relayed by the live repo's session and **confirmed individually with the operator here** rather
than acted on second-hand. That mattered: the relay had one fact backwards earlier the same day and
corrected itself ten minutes later, and two of these are hard to reverse.

| question | answer |
|---|---|
| Vendor the shared assets | **YES — with licences.** ~4.2 MB: Tabler CSS, Chart.js, topojson-client, world-atlas, the logo, and 98 font files. `OFL.txt` travels with the fonts; Tabler, Chart.js and topojson need their own terms in `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md` **before** any of it is committed. |
| Fonts: all 26 families or trim | **ALL 26.** The Appearance page offers every one as a user-facing picker, so shipping fewer is a USER-VISIBLE CHANGE and the port rule forbids it. Trimming would have to be raised as a change, not slipped in as an optimisation. |
| `POST /api/account/password` | **PORT IT.** The hazard was only ever coexistence — `users.js` caches on first load, so a write from here would be reverted by Node's next save. With nothing running alongside, it is ordinary work. |
| The cutover destination | **A MERGE INTO THE LIVE REPO**, with the JS removed. The Go and TypeScript become MikroDash. |
| Does this repo become public | **NO — only the MERGED RESULT is public.** This repo's history never ships. |

**THE LAST TWO TOGETHER MEAN THE MERGE IS A FILE TRANSPLANT, NOT A GIT MERGE**, and that changes
where the credential discipline points. History is not the exposure vector; FILE CONTENT is. Nothing
credential-shaped may be in a file that transplants — which is what `assertClean()` and the
anonymisation in `tools/capture-fixtures.js` already enforce, so the discipline stands unchanged and
its stated reason needs correcting rather than its rules.

**WHAT THE MERGE DESTINATION CHANGES ABOUT THIS REPO'S ASSUMPTIONS**, none of it fatally:

- `MIKRODASH_SRC` and `../MikroDash` stop meaning anything once the two trees are one.
- The read-only rule on `../MikroDash` expires at merge — it becomes the repo this code lives in.
- The live repo's release machinery (tags, `docker-publish.yml`, GHCR) is what ships the result.

### DEFERRED, DELIBERATELY: what happens to the gates when the JS is deleted

**The operator's answer is "decide it later, near the merge". Recorded here so that decision cannot
expire quietly, which is the failure this project has now found repeatedly in a week.**

The risk, stated plainly while there is still time for it to matter: **this port's verification
apparatus is defined RELATIVE TO THE JS.** 115 differential gates, the golden payloads from
`tools/make-golden.js`, `extract-ui.js` lifting the shell and page bodies verbatim, `nodecheck/`
replaying fixtures into the OLD collectors, the proplist drift gate reading the Node source at
`/live`. Every one of them answers "does the port agree with the JS?".

Delete the JS and that question loses its subject — **at one commit, most of these go from
meaningful to unrunnable**, and the ones that keep running do so against nothing. Green, and
meaningless. That is the same quiet shape as the corpus that could not see the prune and the case
whose guard never ran.

Three questions to answer near the merge, not now:

1. Which gates convert into ordinary assertions about Go behaviour, with the golden payloads FROZEN
   as fixtures rather than regenerated from a source that no longer exists.
2. Which are inherently comparative and should be RETIRED at merge rather than ported.
3. Whether the last pre-merge run of every generator is committed as the permanent record of what
   parity meant — since afterwards there is nothing to regenerate from.

**The guard to build meanwhile**, and it is cheap: every gate that lifts from `/live` wants a
believability assertion of the kind `event-audit` already has (throw if fewer than 40 emits found).
A gate that finds an empty corpus must FAIL rather than pass over it. That is worth doing before the
source disappears, whatever is decided about the rest.

|---|---|
| Cutover plan | **Cut over after live verification.** Finish item 18 against real routers, then Node stops and Go serves everything. This is what closes the four coexistence blockers — they exist only because both apps run at once. |
| Live verification | **UNATTENDED, READ-ONLY, ALL THREE ROUTERS.** Overrides this port's own recommendation to wait for a human, and does so knowingly: the question stated that a second server opens a full `Session` (14 collectors) on a router Node is already connected to. |
| The background pool during coexistence | **NO — it waits for cutover.** `internal/routers/pool.go` stays constructed by nobody. Every router keeps ONE background connection instead of two. |
| Wiring the notification transports | **NO — they wait for cutover.** A duplicated Telegram message or email cannot be un-received, which makes this the least reversible of the four. |

**THE POOL ANSWER AND THE LIVE-VERIFICATION ANSWER ARE NOT IN CONFLICT, and the distinction is the
reason to write both down.** Both put extra collectors on a router Node is already talking to. The
difference is duration and control: live verification is transient, page-driven and watched by its
own gate, and it stops when the process does. The pool is CONTINUOUS and holds a connection to every
router in the fleet for as long as both apps run. "No to the standing load, yes to the brief one" is
a coherent position, not an inconsistency, and a later session reading only one of the two rows
would otherwise think one of them was a mistake.

**WRITES ARE STILL hAP AC2 ONLY (`10.0.0.53`).** Read-only was the answer for verification; the
standing write permission is unchanged and is not widened by it.

---

**What that unblocks**, in the order it makes sense to build:

1. `backups:restore` parts 2 and 3 — the `/raw` route with token redemption, and the handler that
   fetches and loads. Explicitly "waiting on this answer".
2. The staging prefix comes off, so the endpoints already implemented actually serve.
3. PDF export, and Send now with its mailer and report builder.
4. The Frequency Analyser runner, then its dialog.
5. The per-user notification settings, which need the transports.
6. The notification bell, which needs the alert feed — and that read now has a caller, so
   `internal/db/alerts.go`'s "a read nothing calls is a read nothing gates" rule stops applying to it.
7. The settings write path and the background pool's wiring, both of which said "waits for cutover".
8. The first-run setup wizard, whose recorded reason was that its state "cannot be reached during
   coexistence" — which is no longer the constraint it was.

**What does NOT change.** Reproducing the live app's behaviour, including its quirks; a defect found
there still goes to `ToDo.md` rather than being diverged from here. The gates, the corpora and the
mutation discipline stay exactly as they are — cutting over is a scope decision, not a licence to
ship unpinned code.

### A small protocol gap on Router Users

The live page re-emits `rosusers:caps` on every `mikrodash:pagechange`, because permission is a
property of the socket rather than of the shared payload. This port never emits it and has no
handler for it — caps arrive via `page:focus` instead, so the OUTCOME is identical and nothing
renders differently. Queues does it the live way (emit + handler, both wired). Worth making
Router Users match for protocol fidelity; not worth touching a proven page mid-item, so it is
recorded here instead.

      | after `rosusers:ok` alone | `Removed probe-user` | — (not isolable through the wrapper) |

      because `render()` runs immediately after `setStatus` in the same handler. Row 2 is the same
      fault by a slower route — `refreshNow()` guarantees a payload arrives before the 8-second timer
      expires. So PR #112 removed the crash and did not deliver the message.

      can see this class of defect, because it changes emit FREQUENCY rather than payload SHAPE.
      **A gate now exists**: `internal/collect/fingerprint_test.go` walks each payload row with
      reflection, mutates every field and asserts the fingerprint reacts, with the deliberate
      exclusions (byte counters, derived deltas) named with their reasons. A field added to a
      payload later and forgotten in the fingerprint fails on the day it is added — which a list of
      cases cannot do, because nobody writes the case they forgot.

### Why no gate caught any of this

**Two of these are invisible to every gate this port has, and that is the finding worth keeping.**
The goldens compare payload SHAPE, so §3 — which changes emit FREQUENCY, not contents — cannot show
up in one. §4 changed a proplist, which would change a payload only if a fixture held an MX, SRV or
TXT record, and the captured router holds none; that is the whole reason the defect survived on the
live side. `extract-ui --check` catches markup and `make-golden --check` catches payloads, and
neither is watching the live repo's *logic*.

There is currently **no drift gate**: nothing fails when the live repo gains a commit. Until there
is, the live repo's version is the thing to watch, and `port_drift_notes.md` is the only signal.
Proposed in PLAN.md under Verification.

### The socket sweep, and the two silences that agreed (found 2026-08-28)

`tools/live-socket-diff.js` was extended from one focused page to a sweep of all 21. It connects to
BOTH servers with one cookie, focuses each page in turn on each, and compares the event names and
payload key sets that actually arrive. **42 events on node, 39 on go, 36 in common.**

**Its first finding is closed:** `topology:update` carried no `routerId`. The live collector stamps
`routerId: this.rid` on every emit; the port declared the field, tagged it `omitempty`, and had no
constructor parameter to be told an id through — so it was never assigned and the tag hid the
missing argument.

**No gate could see it, and the reason generalises.** `nodecheck/helpers/fixture-replay.js` passed
the live collectors no `rid`, so the Node golden had no `routerId` either — `JSON.stringify` drops
undefined. The differential compared two absences and passed. The same gap ran the other way in
`ifStatus`, whose live constructor defaults `rid || ''`: its golden pinned `routerId: ''` and the Go
test passed `""` to match. **Both goldens now carry `r-fixture`.** Anything a replay declines to
supply is a field the differential silently stops pinning; that is worth a sweep of its own.

Fixed and gated — see Changes.md. Seven mutations, seven killed. The session-level gate exists
because `internal/collect`'s tests construct the collector themselves and so can never see what the
call site hands it, which is exactly the seam this shipped through.

**OPEN, recorded rather than fixed: the port's permission-denied topology payload is a shape the
live app does not emit.** `_pollOnce` sets `_permissionDenied`, warns and RETURNS; every later poll
returns at the top. So `permissionDenied: true` reaches a browser only if a rebuild was already in
flight — normally the page keeps whatever topology it had. The port builds a denied payload by hand
and emits it immediately, which shows the operator a refusal the live app does not show. It is the
better behaviour and it is still a user-visible change, which this port does not get to make on its
own. Decide it deliberately: keep it (and note the divergence), or match the live silence.

| Event | Verdict |
|---|---|
| `ros:status` | **Explained.** Merged into the port's one room-scoped `router:status`; decided, and recorded above under Part 28. |
| `interfaces:list` | **Explained.** Replaced by `ifstatus:names`. Its listener sits in `pages/interfaces.ts` rather than the shell, which is safe ONLY because every page module initialises at boot (`main.ts:415`) — worth knowing if that ever becomes lazy. |
| `ping:history`, `routers:update` | **Probe limit.** The port emits both; they answer a subscribe or an action the sweep never performed. |

The port emits the array on both paths and both its consumers guard with `Array.isArray` first. One shape where the live app has two; the inconsistency is not worth reproducing. |
| `conn:update` | **REAL — fixed 2026-08-28.** The live global emit `delete`s four heavy indexes and the replay keeps them; the port NILLED the fields, and a nil Go map marshals as `null`, so it sent `"countryDests": null` where the live payload has no key. One key set where the live app has two. `connsLight`'s `MarshalJSON` now removes them, as `geoplace.Location` does. `omitempty` would have been wrong — it drops them from the replay too, whenever the maps are empty, which is their state until someone opens the page. **RE-RUN 2026-08-28, all four fixes confirmed on the wire.** 42 events on node, 40 on go, 37 in

### `collection:config` and `collection:status`: two consumers the application never calls

The port never emits either event. Their client-side consumers — `applyCollectionConfig` and
`applyCollectionStatus` in `web/src/stale.ts` — are complete, reproduce the live behaviour, and are
pinned by `tools/stale-check.js` against the live implementation. **Nothing else calls either one.**
The gate proves them correct and says nothing about whether they run — the netwatch failure again,
in its worst form, because the gate is what makes them look covered.

**`collection:config` — CLOSED 2026-08-28.** Emitted on the router handshake where `index.js:4208`
sends it; `internal/collection/payload.go` builds it, pinned by `tools/collection-payload-cases.js`
against the live `_collectionPayload`; `main.ts` calls the consumer that was already there. `off` is
reproduced in REGISTRY order rather than sorted — the corpus carries two non-alphabetical lists so a
sorted implementation fails rather than passing by luck. Six mutations, six killed.

Three separate ledgers fired on this one change, each doing its job: `orphaned-consumer-audit` named
its own stale entry the moment the consumer gained a caller; `event-audit` catches the emit being
removed; `emit-audit` had the whole `collection` prefix recorded as UNPORTED and failed the sweep.

**`collection:status` — PART 1 DONE 2026-08-28: the state machine.** `internal/dormancy` ports
`createDormancyState` from `src/collectors/util.js` — pure, observations in and verdict out, `now`
supplied by the caller — pinned by `tools/dormancy-cases.js` over 14 ordered sequences and 65 steps,
recording all five getters after each. 11 mutations, 11 killed (three survived the first sweep and
all three were corpus gaps, now closed with believability checks over the exact properties).

**PART 2 DONE 2026-08-28: what may sleep, and what "empty" means.** The Go registry table did not
carry `emptyKey` at all — `collection-cases.js` projected the live registry to "the fields a
resolver consumes" — so the eligible set could not be derived. `emptyKey` and `sessionProp` added
and the table regenerated; **18 of 27 collectors are eligible**. `internal/collection/dormancy.go`
holds `DormancyEligible()` and `PayloadEmpty`, pinned by `tools/payload-empty-cases.js`. 8
mutations: 4 killed, 3 equivalent (verified exhaustively, recorded in the code), 1 a measured limit
— nothing today has an `emptyKey` and is NOT disableable, so that half of the filter cannot be
tested, and both the generator and a test fail if that changes.

`collection.PayloadEmptyBy` takes a lookup, the map one is pinned by the live corpus, and a test

**PART 5 DONE 2026-08-28 — DORMANCY IS WIRED AND `collection:status` IS EMITTED.** The supervisor

**CONFIRMED ON THE WIRE 2026-08-28, and the confirmation found one more defect.** The first re-run
showed `collection:status` still live-only after 90s. A diagnostic build proved the supervisor was

Three existing gates went red on the refactor and all three were right (the netwatch reachability
gate, the focus-resume gate, and the entry-point counter); each was taught the funnel rather than

`dhcpLeases` and `dhcpNetworks` to the funnel and none was in the table, so three pages would have
silently stopped collecting.

**A LATENT UPSTREAM INCONSISTENCY found while porting:** `_dormancyTick` indexes the session by
`def.sessionProp`, while `_resetDormancy` and `_wakeForFocus` index it by `key`. No collector in
today's registry has the two differ, so nothing is broken — but the registry documents them as
different concepts and one divergent row would make reset and focus probe `undefined` silently.

The original note, still true of the remaining half: `internal/session/session.go` calls its behaviour "deliberately simpler than
the Node supervisor's for now" and `internal/collect/talkers.go` says so outright. Neither statement
appeared anywhere in this file until now — a design difference recorded only in code comments, which
is the shape that goes stale unwatched. Until a supervisor exists there is nothing to report, so a
dormant card is simply never dimmed.

**`tools/orphaned-consumer-audit.js` now watches the class**, and its ledger fails in both
directions: a name that gains a caller fails, forcing the note to be deleted rather than left lying.
Four mutations, four killed.

### Initial state: the class behind the `collection:status` defect (2026-08-28)

An event can be correct on every CHANGE and absent on CONNECT, and no check this repo had could see
it — `emit-audit` asks whether an event is emitted anywhere, and it was. `tools/initial-state-audit.js`
asks whether each of `sendInitialState`'s 42 events reaches a browser at ATTACH time: on this port's
handshake, on page focus, or never.

**Seven more were missing on its first run**, all collectors that run from connect rather than page
focus, so nothing replayed them and a viewer attaching to a running session waited for the next tick
— up to a minute for netwatch and talkers. Four were router-wide chrome (`ifstatus:names`,
`system:update`, `wan:status`, `lan:wan`) and are now on the handshake; three were dashboard cards
(`netwatch:update`, `talkers:update`, `ping:update`) and are now in the dashboard focus replay.

Now: 11 on the handshake, 25 deferred by design, 6 explained. Four mutations, four killed.

**VERIFIED AGAINST A RUNNING SESSION**, not just the source: `tools/attach-probe.js` holds a session
with one socket, attaches a second, and measures what it receives. All seven arrive at ~53ms. Run
against a binary with the replays disabled, two of the seven (`lan:wan`, `netwatch:update` — both
slow pollers) NEVER arrived and the other five arrived anyway within ~1.4s, because their collectors
tick fast. So the fix closes a real hole for two and turns an accident into a contract for five;
both are worth having, and the distinction is recorded in the tool's header.

**The audit had two bugs of its own, both instructive.** Its page-focus anchor named a function that
does not exist and the fallback scanned the whole file, so everything counted as deferred; and its
list of handshake helpers was hand-written and missed the one that sends `traffic:history`. Anchors
now throw and helpers are discovered — the same two failures this repo keeps finding in its own
tools, applied to a tool written to find them.

### Page blur: three dashboard cards froze when you left their page (2026-08-28)

The port suspends a strict SUPERSET of what the live app suspends on blur (18 pages against 15,
missing none) — the right direction, fewer channels held, and the reason the live app never had this
bug. But the port's blur was PER-PAGE where the live `_updatePageStream` counts occupancy across ALL
of a collector's stream rooms. Three collectors feed a dashboard card as well as their page, and
leaving that page suspended them: `dhcpNetworks` (which also feeds the router-wide `lan:wan` chip),
`bandwidth` and `vpn`. `conns` alone had the guard.

`suspendConnsIfIdle` generalised into `suspendIfNoRoomOccupied`; `tools/blur-suspend-audit.js` reads
each collector's rooms from its own emit calls and requires a guard wherever there is more than one.
It found `vpn` on its first run. Six mutations, six killed — two survived first and both were reach
gaps: a source audit cannot see the guard's runtime behaviour (now a Go test against a real hub),
and the audit never proved its own room-reading worked (now asserted).

### Reachability: a module nothing imports (2026-08-28)

`tools/orphaned-consumer-audit.js` catches a gated FUNCTION with no caller; it cannot catch a whole
MODULE nothing imports, because that module's functions call each other and its gate passes.
`tools/module-reachability-audit.js` walks the import graph from `main.ts` — what `build.mjs`
bundles — and finds **97 of 100 modules reachable**. The three that are not are all explained by
entries already in this file: `router-form.ts` and `router-modal.ts` (the unmounted Routers page)
and `setup-overlay.ts` (the cutover-blocked wizard). No dead code, and now a gate.

Its first version called three GENERATED tables dead: this codebase writes ESM specifiers naming the
output (`'./gen/x.js'`) and the resolver dropped those edges. An unresolvable relative import is now
a hard error — a silently-failing resolver produces false positives, and a false positive is how an
audit gets ignored.

**CORRECTED 2026-08-28 — BOTH WERE FALSE POSITIVES**, and this entry claimed outstanding work that
did not exist for one tick. `drawDonutCentre` is used as a CALLBACK (`{ afterDraw: drawDonutCentre }`),
which a `name(` rule cannot see; `renderCountryList` and `renderPortList` are LIVE functions lifted
out of `public/app.js` by a differential gate and were never meant to exist here.

**The generalisation was then tried and abandoned on measurements**, recorded in the audit's header:
27 of 116 gates bundle a `web/src` module, the `m.<name>` handle is stale-check's own convention so
only 8 driven exports resolve, and a targeted scan found ZERO orphans today. It needs per-gate handle
parsing for no present yield.

What landed instead: the audit counts REFERENCES rather than calls, and — found by mutation testing
that change — strips COMMENTS first, because `stale.ts`'s own documentation mentioning a function by
name had been counting as usage, which let the deletion of a real caller survive.

### Upstream drift, caught within the hour (2026-08-28)

`d7548b0` — "The Traffic selection survives a reconnect", upstream issue #119 — landed while this
port was running its own sweep, and `tools/reset-contract-audit.js` went red on the next verify:
the live `router:switching` handler clears `_userPickedIf`, a name it could not map onto anything
here. **That is the drift gate working**, and it is the first time one has caught a live commit
rather than a stale note.

Ported the same day; `_userPickedIf` is recorded only on the change event, the restore is guarded on
the pick still being selectable, and it is cleared on a router switch but NOT on reconnect — the
asymmetry is the whole fix. `tools/traffic-pick-check.js` lifts the live condition and drives the
port's over seven cases.

**Also this tick: `docs/port-history/retired/cutover-premise-audit.js`**, which asserts that the facts holding up
blockers 5 and 6 are still true — the RBAC memo is still in-memory Maps cleared only by `bump()`,
the alerter cooldown is still a per-process `Map`. It fails when a blocker stops being true, which is
the direction nobody watches. The recorded `bump()` call-site count was 14 and is 16; substance
unchanged, and now machine-checked.

### A reconnect is not a new user — and it was moving the operator (2026-08-28)

`mikrodash-9a` sent the generalisation behind upstream `d7548b0`: per-connection state keyed on the
connection cannot outlive it, a reconnect is not a new user, and anything the operator CHOSE — an
interface, a filter, a page, a sort order — needs somewhere with a longer life than the socket.

Swept this port for the shape and found a worse instance than the one reported. `main.ts`'s
`select()` runs on EVERY connect — it must, because the server holds the router selection on the
connection — and called `showPage(socket, 'dns')` with a LITERAL. A network blip therefore moved the
operator off whatever page they were reading. Now `currentPage || 'dns'`, pinned by
`tools/reconnect-state-check.js`.

The rest of the per-connection state was checked and is sound: `trafficIf` is recovered by the
`userPickedIf` restore ported earlier today, `routerID` is re-selected on connect, room membership is
re-joined through the documented `socket:reconnect` event, and `resHist` (undo/redo) dies with the
socket deliberately, with its reason recorded in `history.go`.

**Also closed: three ledgers deferring to a group closed three days earlier.** `packages:notes` was
recorded unported in `emit-audit`, `inbound-audit` and `wiring-audit`, each pointing at "the
`upgrade dialog` group", which `wiring-audit` itself records as CLOSED on 2026-08-25.
`internal/changelog` ports the fetch — the version whitelist, the bounded cache, the streaming
size cap — and on 2026-08-28 the socket handler and the client's three rules landed too.
**All three ledger entries deleted themselves**, each audit failing on its own record the moment
the port touched what it described. `wiring-audit` is down to 9 known gaps in 2 groups: the
cutover-blocked first-run overlay, and the spectrum canvas.

### Wiring the history writers — SPECIFIED 2026-08-28, not started

Raised because the operator is about to run the port as the only app for a test window, and while
Node is stopped nothing writes `traffic_samples`, `bandwidth_usage`, `ping_samples` or
`connectivity_events`. Reports then renders a shrinking window with every DOM gate green, and
**that gap does not roll back** when Node restarts.

**I estimated "a tick's work" when I flagged it. That was wrong, and the measurement is why:**
`internal/history` ports the BUCKETING (`Writer`, `Connectivity`) and emits `Row`s — but
`internal/db/history.go` only READS. There is no insert path in this port at all.

What it actually needs, now specified rather than discovered:

1. **Four inserts in `internal/db`**, matching `src/db.js:670-674` exactly:

       INSERT INTO ping_samples        (router_id, target,    rtt_ms, loss_pct, ts) VALUES (?,?,?,?,?)
       INSERT INTO traffic_samples     (router_id, interface, rx_mbps, tx_mbps, ts) VALUES (?,?,?,?,?)
       INSERT INTO bandwidth_usage     (router_id, interface, rx_mb,   tx_mb,   ts) VALUES (?,?,?,?,?)
       INSERT INTO connectivity_events (router_id, connected, ts)                  VALUES (?,?,?)

   Note `rtt_ms` is NULL when every ping in the minute was lost — `Row.HasRTT` is that flag — and
   `connected` is an INTEGER 0/1, not a boolean.

2. **The call sites.** The live side has 7 in `index.js` and 5 in `alertSessions.js`, against a
   139-line `db-writer.js` this port has already ported the decisions of. Here they are the traffic
   and ping collectors, the bandwidth rollover, and `Session.announce` for connectivity.

3. **A STANDALONE GATE**, the same one `auth_login.go` and the account-password route use. Writing
   while Node runs would DOUBLE EVERY ROW — two processes bucketing the same samples into one
   SQLite file — which is exactly why `history.Writer` is constructed by nobody today.

4. **Flush on release**, or the last partial minute of every session is lost.

Realistically one to two iterations with a generated corpus and mutations, not one. Not started,
because the operator's test window had not been agreed and half a write path into the shared
production database is the worst possible state to leave this in.

## Standing decisions

Recorded so they are not re-litigated each iteration.

- **SQLite driver: `modernc.org/sqlite`.** Pure Go, no cgo, so the static binary survives — the
  footprint win is one of the three reasons this port exists. `mattn/go-sqlite3` is faster but needs
  cgo. The port needs SQLite regardless of audit (Reports, Audit, Alerts, stored history), so this is
  not an audit-specific cost.
- **The RouterOS client is `github.com/go-routeros/routeros/v3`, not hand-written.** Operator ruling
  after the four "protocol realities" were tested against all three routers on 7.24 and two did not
  reproduce (`test-results.md`, `PLAN.md` B1). Two conditions travel with it and must not be undone:
  **async mode is mandatory** (it is what discards a sentence for a cancelled tag — reality 4, which
  IS real), and the claims are **version-qualified** (7.23 originals, 7.24 tests).
- **A dependency is allowed when it simplifies the project or is measurably faster.** Zero-dependency
  is no longer a goal in itself. Four are in: `x/crypto`, `modernc.org/sqlite`, `coder/websocket`,
  `go-routeros/v3`. The bar is still a REASON, not convenience.
- **`packages:apply` ships as-is**, with the same confirmation the live app uses. Operator ruling.
  It reboots the router; that is what the live app does and the port reproduces behaviour.
- **Guards are ported just-in-time, with the page that needs them.** A resource declaring an unported
  guard has its writes REFUSED (`portedGuards`). Never widen that list to "get past" an item.
- **Documentation is checked before porting**, via the `rosetta` MCP server. A fixture proves what the
  code does with rows one router returned; the docs say which rows a router *may* return.
- **Markup is extracted, never retyped** (`tools/extract-ui.js`).
- **A page is done when its DOM matches the live renderer byte for byte**, via
  `tools/live-renderer.js` — not when it looks right.

## Queue

### Infrastructure — unblocks many pages at once

- [x] DONE — **diagnosed why the 7 collectors have no fixture. The original premise was wrong.**
      It is not deltas between reads. `tools/capture-fixtures.js` records at the transport by wrapping
      `ros.write()` **and does not wrap `ros.stream()`** (its own comment, line 308: "Streams are not
      recorded: a fixture is a snapshot, and a /listen channel has nothing to snapshot. The poll path
      reads the same menus."). For these seven that last sentence is false:
      - `interfaceStatus.refreshNow()` — the method `SNAPSHOT_METHODS` picks — only calls
        `_restartMetaStreams()`. It issues **no read at all**, which is exactly why ifStatus wrote an
        empty capture and was reported unsupported.
      - Its metadata comes from `/interface/print =interval=N`, a **stream**, in BOTH modes.
        `streamMode:false` replaces only the RATES poll (`_pollRatesOnce`), and even that needs
        `this._ifaces` already populated — by the stream. There is no pure-poll path.
      So no number of extra reads produces a fixture. **The recorder has to learn streams.**

- [x] DONE — **1a: streams are recorded, and replayed.** Wrap `ros.stream()` alongside
      `ros.write()`, collect the rows a stream delivers over a bounded window (a few intervals), and
      add a `streams: [{cmd, params, rows}]` section to the fixture format. Then teach
      `nodecheck/helpers/fixture-replay.js` to deliver those rows to the collector's stream callback,
      so the replay drives the same code path the router does. **One definition shared by capture and
      replay** — that rule already exists in `tools/collector-snapshot.js` and exists because
      violating it silently broke six collectors once.
      Done: `record()` wraps `ros.stream()` for both call shapes and logs each `data` packet (one
      row) through the same scrubber; `fixture-replay.js` matches a recorded stream by cmd+params and
      delivers its rows on the NEXT TICK, because a collector registers its handler after `stream()`
      returns. `collector-snapshot.js` gained a shared `settle()` — longer than the 300ms
      `_scheduleMetaCommit` debounce, and skipped entirely for poll-driven collectors so the suite
      stays fast. Proven end to end: ifStatus captured **192 stream rows** across three streams and
      replays to a 30-interface payload. Anonymisation verified on stream rows (all MACs `02:`, all
      IPs in TEST-NET-2, no credential keys). Also fixed the `ROOT` path trap at line 55.

      `isCredentialField` against the live implementation — 15 diff cases, 25 field checks — and

      capture, because `src/audit.js` requires `./db` requires `better-sqlite3`. The green check is
      therefore four generators, not three:
      `docker exec -e MIKRODASH_SRC=/app -e AUDIT_OUT=/audit-cases.json mikrodash node /tools/audit-cases.js --check`

      **One knowing divergence, pinned by a test.** `audit.js` walks `Object.keys(after)` —
      insertion order — and a Go map has none, so `Diff` sorts. Taking the random order would make
      the same write produce different bytes on different runs, which is worse than a different
      order; nothing reads `changes` positionally.

- [x] DONE — **the audit recorder is wired into the resource write path, with the type-based
      redaction.** All five audit-shaped `log.Printf` placeholders in `internal/server/resource.go`
      are gone; writes and denials now land in `audit_events` beside Node's. Denials carry the verb
      the user ATTEMPTED (`dnsStatic.update`, not "denied"), matching index.js, plus a note
      distinguishing `read-only-row` from the port-specific `guard-not-ported`.

      **`auditValues` masks by field TYPE before anything is diffed**, and that is the line that
      actually holds: a resource field is named for the form, so `wpa2PreSharedKey` matches no
      credential name pattern at all. Name matching is the second line. Both directions are pinned —
      `TestSecretsAreMaskedByTypeNotByName` asserts its own premise (that the name pattern does NOT
      match) so it cannot pass for the wrong reason.

      **Live-verified end to end against the hAP AC2**, with the server pointed at a COPY of /data so
      the operator's real trail was untouched (196 rows before and after). A create, an update and a
      delete produced three correct rows: create records the whole row with `target_id` NULL, update
      records only what moved, delete records `detail: null` and is described by its target.

      **The audit-cases `--check` needs the committed file copied IN first**, or it compares against
      nothing and calls a current file stale:
      `docker cp testdata/audit-diff-cases.json mikrodash:/audit-cases.json` then
      `docker exec -e MIKRODASH_SRC=/app -e AUDIT_OUT=/audit-cases.json mikrodash node /tools/audit-cases.js --check`

- [x] DONE — **RBAC granularity: the per-router answer, resolved from the grant graph.** The second
      cutover blocker is closed. `internal/rbac` reads grants, group_members, roles and role_pages
      out of the SQLite database Node owns — possible only once the driver landed last iteration —
      and answers `canPage(user, page, access, router)` exactly as `rbac.js` does. No live-repo
      change was needed: `/api/auth/status` withholds the user id on purpose, and `users.json`
      already carries the username→id mapping this process reads.

      **The two answers are ANDed, never substituted.** The union Node sends is a SUPERSET of the
      truth; the resolver can therefore only make the answer stricter, so a bug in the port cannot
      grant access Node would refuse. Where the database cannot be opened, the union stands alone
      and the old gap is live again — reported at startup rather than degrading silently.

      **Live-verified as a differential: 468 answers match `rbac.js` exactly** — 3 users × 3 routers
      × 26 pages × 2 access levels, on the real grant graph, including the restricted principal who
      is allowed 24 of 156. Kept as `internal/rbac/live_test.go`, skipped unless `MIKRODASH_DATA`
      (a COPY of /data) and `RBAC_NODE_ANSWERS` are set — its inputs name real ids, so they are
      generated on demand and never committed.

      `PageKeys` is a 26-string copy of `Pages.KEYS`, pinned by a drift test that skips without
      `MIKRODASH_SRC`. It exists because canPage refuses an unknown page BEFORE consulting the
      graph, which is what stops a builtin role conferring a page that does not exist.

### Drift — the Node side is moving under the port

      caught because the fixture predates the change:
      1. `internal/collect/dns.go` still sends the OLD proplist and is now behind.
      2. The DNS fixture has no rows for the new fields, so the replay silently falls back to the

      3. `dnsStatic` in `internal/resource` still offers six of the nine record types.
      Done: Go proplist extended, the `address` fallback now walks all seven properties, the resource
      carries all nine types and the seven MX/NS/SRV fields, and `resource.ts` no longer coerces an
      unlisted select value (the data-loss half, fixed generally rather than by lengthening a list).
      The AX3 fixture was re-captured — but it holds only A and FWD records, so it **cannot exercise
      the new branches**. Seeded MX/NS/SRV onto the AC2, captured a second-router fixture, and the Go
      collector reproduces the Node payload for it exactly. The corpus is now **multi-router**, which
      PLAN.md wanted anyway. AC2 restored to its single original record.

- [x] DONE — **a drift check that fails loudly.** `api-surface.js --check` caught this only by
      accident. Add a gate comparing each Go collector's proplist against the live one for the same
      menu, so a Node-side change to a ported collector fails a test instead of being noticed later.

- [x] DONE — **option pickers: a user-visible regression on two pages already marked DONE.**

      **It went unnoticed because of what the DOM gate looks at:** that comparison renders the PAGE,

- [x] **DONE — route/route6 write path, live-verified against the hAP AC2.** `TypeCidr` added
      (a slash means `ParseCIDR`, no slash means `ParseIP`, and the value is returned UNCHANGED
      rather than normalised to its network address — rewriting `198.51.100.5/24` on the way past

      live declarations under `TestPortedFieldsMatchTheirLiveDeclarations`, and declare no guard —
      which matches the live app: `selfPath` answers "which INTERFACE carries us", and a route is
      not an interface.
      Live run: create → the router held `dst=198.51.100.0/24 gw=10.0.0.2 dist=5 tbl=main
      cmt="port probe"`, every field as submitted; update → the audit row lists ONLY `disabled` and
