      **Two defects found while wiring it, both older than this item and both invisible to every
      gate the project had:**

      1. **`res:new` was never ported.** `resRow` carries the picker lists, so the EDIT form on a
         page with a picker was correct while the ADD form on the same page silently rendered a
         text box — on `vlan` and `bridgePort`, two pages already marked DONE. Every gate here
         looks at a rendered page or at a declaration; none opens a blank form. Now
         `internal/server/resource.go:resNew`, proven in a browser: the blank Add Route form
         renders `routingTable` as a `<select>` holding the router's own `["main"]`.
      2. **`resolve()` audited every denial**, including the ones that only OPEN a form. index.js
         draws the line at the mutating handlers — `res:save`/`res:remove`/`res:action` record a
         denial (6711/6782/6857) and `res:new`/`res:row`/`res:preview` refuse silently
         (6638/6659/6691). Every click of Add on a read-only page would have left a permanent
         "create denied" row in the one table that cannot be pruned selectively. Fixed by making
         the audit the caller's choice, pinned by `TestOpeningAFormIsNotAnAttemptToWriteOne`, which
         was proven to fail before being trusted.

      **And a third, cosmetic but a hard-constraint breach:** the Add buttons had been
      reimplemented per page and drifted from the live markup — `Add Port` where the live app
      renders `+ Add Bridge Port`, `Add Bridge`/`Add VLAN`/`Add DNS Entry` all missing the `+ `,
      and `padding:.3rem .7rem` against the live `.28rem .65rem`. Three copies replaced by
      `mountAdds()` in `web/src/resource.ts`, which takes the label from the fetched schema so it
      has the same single home the field list does. `mountRows()` joins it for row clicks, with the
      live rule that a row-level `data-res` beats the table's — a v6 row in the shared Routes tbody
      edits `/ipv6/route`, verified in the browser (`::1/128` opened the IPv6 Route form, read-only
      because it is connected).

- [x] **DONE — `permitted`: schema delivery moved onto the socket.** The port served schemas from
      `/next/api/resources/<key>`, and `permitted` — may THIS viewer write THIS router — depends on
      the selected router, which an HTTP request does not have. That is why index.js puts the schema
      on the socket, and now so does this. `res:schema` emits `Describe()` plus `permitted`,
      `unsupported` and `ordered`; the HTTP endpoint and its orphaned `resourceByKey` helper are
      gone, so there is one path rather than two.

      **What was actually broken:** a read-only viewer saw Add buttons on every ported page and
      found out by clicking. Verified in a browser in BOTH states against the AC2 — with
      `routing=write` the slot renders `+ Add Route` and `+ Add IPv6 Route` and rows open; with
      `routing=read` the slot is empty, the table still renders all six rows, and a row click opens
      nothing.

      `router:switched` is emitted last in `selectRouter`, named for the router ARRIVED at, because
      the browser drops every cached schema on it and re-asks — `permitted` is per-router, and
      answering during the switch would answer for the router being left.

      The check lives in `openResource` rather than in each caller as app.js has it: `dns`,
      `bridges` and `vlans` still open rows through their own per-page handlers, and putting it in
      the delegation would have left those three uncovered until they migrate. One check, all
      callers, same user-visible behaviour.

      **`Ordered` and `RequiresMenu` added to the Go `Resource`** — zero for everything ported and
      read by nothing yet. They exist so `TestPortedFieldsMatchTheirLiveDeclarations` can compare
      resource-LEVEL attributes, not just fields: nine live resources declare `requiresMenu` and
      five declare `ordered: true`, all of them ahead in this queue (wifi, capsman, veth, the four
      firewall tables), and porting one without handling them would have shipped a silent `false`
      that no gate contradicted. Both checks were proven to fail before being trusted.

- [x] **DONE — `res:history`: undo and redo, live-verified against the hAP AC2.**
      `internal/history` is the pure half (a port of `src/routeros/history.js`): every write recorded
      as the operation done plus the one that reverses it, no I/O, unit-tested — the same argument
      the guard modules make. `internal/server/history.go` applies them.

      **Per connection, per resource, in memory, dying with the socket.** "Undo" means "undo what I
      just did": a stack shared between operators would let one silently revert another's work, and
      one that outlived the session would offer to reverse something from last week. Per RESOURCE so
      undo on the Firewall card can never reach into DNS. Dropped wholesale on a router switch — a
      `.id` from one router addresses something entirely different on another, which is the one way
      an undo could destroy the wrong row.

      **An undo is a write like any other**, and the path does everything the ordinary handlers do:
      both gates, a fresh read, a staleness check, the guard, an audit row, a refresh.

      Live run, in the browser and through the socket: the empty stack refuses `nothing-to-undo`;
      create pushes `add of 198.51.100.0/24`; undo removes it and lights redo; redo re-adds it —
      finding the NEW id by diffing the table against itself rather than assuming the row is last —
      and undo removes it again, which only works because `Rebind` re-pointed the remove half at the
      id RouterOS had just assigned. The audit trail records each one as its own write
      (`route.undo|ok|…|{"undo":true,"op":"remove"}`). The AC2 finished with its original three
      dynamic routes.

      **The safety property was exercised, not just asserted.** With an entry on the stack, the row
      was deleted out of band on the router; the undo then refused `stale-history` AND dropped the
      whole stack, because if one entry no longer describes the router the ones under it are suspect
      too and leaving them is a trap for the next click.

      **`move`, `enable`, `disable` and ANCHORS are deliberately not ported.** Nothing reaches them:
      no resource declares `Ordered`, and neither `res:action` nor a move path exists on this side,
      so writing them now would be untestable code guarding a case that cannot occur.
      `TestAnActionWithNoInverseIsNotRecorded` pins that they are refused rather than half-recorded.
      They land with the firewall — the first ordered resource in the queue — and that port must
      carry the anchor rule verbatim: a position is the id of the row it sat immediately before,
      never an ordinal, and an entry whose anchor has since been deleted is REFUSED rather than
      approximated, because putting a firewall rule back in roughly the right place is worse than
      saying it cannot be done.

- [x] **DONE — `dns`, `bridges` and `vlans` migrated onto `mountRows()`.** Four per-page click
      handlers replaced by the one delegation; every ported tbody already carried `data-res-rows`,
      lifted verbatim with the markup, so nothing needed adding to reach them. The dead `regexp`
      parameter on `openResource` went too — nothing had passed it since the Add path stopped
      taking a row.

      dns was the only one doing something genuinely different: it looked the row up in the page
      payload by id, rather than round-tripping `data-identity` from the DOM. The identity is what
      lets the server refuse a write against a row that changed underneath, and taking it from a
      payload that is as stale as the last tick is a weaker claim than taking it from the row the
      operator actually clicked. It now matches app.js.

      Verified in the browser: dns opens "Edit Static DNS Entry" for `router.lan`, and BOTH bridges
      tables resolve their own key from their own tbody — `bridge` and `bridgePort` — which is the
      part a single shared handler had to get right. The vlans table has no clickable rows on the
      AC2 and that is correct rather than a regression: its VLANs have no L3 interface, so the
      renderer emits `resRow('')`, which produces no attributes — the same thing the live renderer
      does, as the DOM gate pins.

- [x] **DONE — DHCP: both collectors, the page and the write path, live-verified.** `dhcpLease` declares **no guard**.

      **Done: the `dhcpLeases` collector, matching the golden field for field** (9 of 21 goldens
      now covered). Three reads — `/ip/dhcp-server/print`, `/interface/vlan/print`, then the leases
      — in that order, because a lease carries only its SERVER NAME and the interface and VLAN
      behind it must already be resolvable when the first lease is applied. The server/VLAN read
      fails soft: leases still carry their server name, so the filter degrades to server-only
      rather than disappearing.

      **INSERTION ORDER IS PART OF THE PAYLOAD.** The Node collector emits `[...byIP.entries()]`,
      so the array is in the order the router first mentioned each address; a Go map has no order,
      and ranging one produces a different array every run. Kept explicitly, with both JavaScript
      details reproduced — re-setting a key does not move it, deleting and re-adding does. Proven
      load-bearing: ranging the Go map instead produced **223 diff lines** against the golden.
      `sort.SliceStable` for the server summary, for the same class of reason — JS sort has been
      stable since ES2019, so equal counts keep first-seen order.

      **Done: the `dhcpNetworks` collector, also matching a golden — one that did not exist.**
      The harness reported it as a collector that "fills a cache and emits elsewhere" with no
      snapshot payload to pin. **That was the harness describing a gap of its own making.**
      `_pollAllOnce()` ends in `_scheduleRebuild()`, a 10ms timer; `settle()` took its fast path
      because the collector has neither `_buildAndEmit` nor `_pollRatesOnce`, and `run()` called
      `stop()` while the timer was still pending. It builds a perfectly good payload ten
      milliseconds later. `tools/collector-snapshot.js` now waits for a scheduled build, which
      recovered **two** collectors — `dhcpNetworks` and `topology` — and took the golden set from
      21 to 23.

      Writing topology's golden exposed a second problem: it stamps `firstSeen`/`lastSeen` from
      `Date.now()` as it reads, so two replays of one fixture differ and `make-golden --check`
      would fail on every future run. They join `ts` and `deltaWindowMs` in the wall-clock set —
      **declared in three places that must agree** (`tools/make-golden.js`,
      `docs/port-history/retired/fixture-differential.test.js`, `internal/collect/fixture_test.go`), and updated in
      all three. Verified stable across repeated regenerations.

      The Go collector reproduces two things it would be tempting to correct. Pools are matched to
      subnets by whether the pool's FIRST address falls in the subnet, not by chasing
      server → interface → address. And `poolRangeSize` folds an address to a number with
      `(acc << 8) + b` under `>>> 0` — arithmetic modulo 2^32, which Go's `uint32` reproduces
      exactly, overflow included. A "fixed" version would disagree with the payload the page has
      always been given for an IPv6 range.

      **`lan:wan` is NOT emitted here.** The original sends it router-wide with just the WAN
      address; its consumers are the connections map's geo origin and the WAN readout in the
      network-devices diagram, neither ported, and this side has no router-wide emit convention.
      Whichever of those pages lands first needs both the event and the room.
      **Done: markup extracted (`web/src/ui/page-dhcp.html`, 71 lines) and the live renderer
      lifted — which needed a new extraction mode.** DHCP is the first ported page that is NOT an
      IIFE. Its renderer is top-level code in TWO regions: the subnet table and the utilisation
      gauge sit inside the `lan:overview` handler, which also draws the dashboard's LAN card, and
      the leases table is a separate block a thousand lines away.

      `tools/live-renderer.js` gained a RANGE mode alongside the IIFE one — `PAGE_REGIONS` anchors
      each region on a landmark line, with an `after` anchor for a region that has to run past the
      block it opens with (the `lan:overview` handler ends, then `renderDhcpGauge` does, and the
      region wants both). `PAGE_STATE` lifts the nine `var` lines those regions read but do not
      create, BY NAME rather than restating them here — restating would be a second copy to keep
      in step, which is the exact thing extract-never-retype exists to prevent. `PAGE_EVENT` names
      the payload event where it is not `<page>:update`: DHCP has none, so `leases:list` drives and
      `lan:overview` is passed as an `extra`, rendered first because it is the state the leases are
      drawn against.

      Both modes share `finish()`, so a range page cannot skip a check an IIFE page gets — the
      syntax parse and the undefined-helper scan both still run. Verified: 219 renderer lines with
      both regions present, nothing from the adjacent Firewall block leaked in, and all six
      existing pages still extract unchanged.

      **Done: the renderer, and the DOM comparison passes in FIVE states.**
      `web/src/pages/dhcp.ts` puts the two lifted regions back together as one page module; the
      collectors are wired into the session (dhcpLeases built first, since dhcpNetworks takes it as
      its lease source) and the page-focus replay sends `lan:overview` BEFORE `leases:list`, because
      the leases handler redraws the gauge as its last act and the pool size it divides by arrives
      with the networks.

      Both renderers driven from ONE payload — the AX3 golden, 39 leases across 3 servers — and
      compared byte for byte: **default (ip asc), sorted by name, sorted by MAC descending, a
      search filter, and a server filter. All five identical.** The comparison was proven able to
      fail first: the live renderer sorted by name against the port's default differs, as it must.

      Two things worth recording from the comparison:
      - The IP column sorts with `split('.').map(Number)`, which goes **NaN on an IPv6 address** —
        no dots to split on, so the comparator returns NaN and `sort` treats it as zero, leaving
        every IPv6 lease in input order. Reproduced, not fixed: these are IPv4 in practice and a
        corrected order would be a visible difference for a defect nobody has hit.
      - A `lan:overview` with no networks **returns early**, so a router with no DHCP networks
        leaves the subnet table on "Waiting for network data…" for ever and never updates the
        gauge. The "No DHCP networks" branch inside the subnet block is unreachable for that
        reason. Reproduced because it is visible; reported in ../MikroDash/ToDo.md.

      One harness lesson: the first cross-state run reported all five DIFFERING by four characters.
      It was `style="flex: 0 1 240px; width: 240px;"` against the markup's
      `style="flex:0 1 240px;width:240px"` — the browser re-serialising an inline style once
      `style.display` is touched. The port had already received the AC2's EMPTY payload, which hid
      the server filter; the live side started from pristine markup. Replaying the empty payload
      into the live renderer first made the two sequences comparable. **The diff was located, not
      guessed at** — the first-differing-index dump is what turned "everything is broken" into a
      four-character explanation.

      **Done: the `dhcpLease` write path, which needed two capabilities the port did not have.**

      1. **`TypeMac`** — the Node validator upper-cases before matching, and the port does too:
         the router accepts either case and returns upper, so normalising means a form submitted in
         lower case does not read as a change on the next diff. Verified live — a lease created
         with `02:aa:bb:cc:dd:ee` came back identified as `02:AA:BB:CC:DD:EE`, and `nope` was
         refused with the live message verbatim.
      2. **RESOURCE ACTIONS** (`res:action`) — named verbs beside create/update/delete. A dynamic
         lease is exactly why they exist: it cannot be edited, because it belongs to the server
         rather than to us, and the only useful thing to do with it is make it static. The form
         therefore opens read-only WITH its action bar rather than refusing to open.
         The verb is looked up in the REGISTRY, never taken from the wire — it becomes a RouterOS
         command word, so accepting one from the browser would let a caller name any command under
         the resource's menu. An invented action answers `bad-request`.

      Live on the AC2, created and cleaned up: create (MAC normalised), a bad MAC refused, the edit
      form carrying `actions: []` and a populated server picker, `makeStatic` on a STATIC row
      refused `not-applicable` and recorded as denied, an invented action refused, update, delete.
      The audit trail carries all six.

      **The one path not exercised: make-static actually reaching RouterOS.** The AC2 has no DHCP
      clients, so it has no dynamic lease to convert, and one cannot be manufactured — a lease is

      predicate is the same test the read-only rule uses, so the gap is which command word gets
      sent. Worth re-checking on a router with live clients.

      **The `resolve`-caller gate fired, as designed.** `TestOpeningAFormIsNotAnAttemptToWriteOne`
      failed the moment `resAction` appeared: "this test does not know whether it should audit a

      res:save and res:remove, so it does. That is the second forcing function this port has
      written that has since caught something real.

      **The parity gate now compares ACTIONS too** — key, verb and label against the live
      declaration, in both directions. A resource that quietly lost `makeStatic` would pass every
      field check while making a whole class of row unreachable. Proven able to fail.

      screen, so reproduced; reported in ../MikroDash/ToDo.md.

      **Done: `queueGuard`, with a SEVENTH generator pinning it against the live implementation.**

      **Why this guard gets a generator too, having argued the opposite case for `selfPath`.**
      selfPath warns and fails open, and I said that was why it did not need one. queueGuard also
      warns and also fails open — and needs one anyway, for a reason selfPath does not share: a
      wrong answer here is SILENT. A guard that refuses tells you when it is wrong, because somebody
      is locked out and says so. A guard that warns either says nothing when it should have, or
      cries wolf until the operator clicks through the one that mattered. Neither shows up in a
      screenshot, a fixture or a DOM comparison.

      **The parsers are pinned, not just the verdict.** `parseRate`/`parsePair` are what the
      COLLECTOR uses to build the payload, so a disagreement there is a wrong number on the page
      long before it is a wrong warning. The null-versus-zero distinction is the trap: RouterOS
      reads an unlimited queue back as `0/0` rather than omitting the field, so **0 means explicitly
      unlimited and absent means no value at all**, and the page renders those differently. Go has
      no `null`, so `Rate{Bps, Set}` carries it and marshals back to `null` — which the fingerprint
      needs, since it is `JSON.stringify` output that has to match byte for byte.

      **`cidrContains` is three-valued and the test compares three values.** Undecidable — an
      interface-name target, a v4/v6 mismatch — is not `false`, even though both end in no warning.
      Go returns `(contains, decided)`. The test asserts at least 5 undecidable cases and at least
      5 warning cases, because a corpus that stopped exercising either branch would pass every
      other assertion while testing a third of the module.

      **Three things the generator settled that reading could not**, all of which I had reasoned
      about wrongly first:

      1. **A bare `src-address` matches EVERY address of the same family.** `src/util/ip.js` has its
         own `parseCIDR`, and with no slash the prefix length is `parseInt(undefined, 10)` = NaN;
         ipaddr.js's `while (cidrBits > 0)` never runs and returns true. So
         `isInCidrs('8.8.8.8', ['10.0.0.5'])` is true. Reported as **`ToDo.md` item 8** — the
         reachable consequence is that `drop src-address=203.0.113.9` raises a false lockout
         warning while `…/32` correctly does not. Reproduced here, pinned by the corpus.
      2. **An over-long mask (`/33`, `/99`) does NOT match.** I had reasoned it would run off the
         end of the octet array and return true; `matchCIDR` throws and the catch makes it false.
      3. **ipaddr.js accepts the compact IPv4 forms** — `10.0`, `10.0.0`, a bare integer, hex, and
         octal, so `012.0.0.0/24` is `10.0.0.0/24` and `011.0.0.0/8` is `9.0.0.0/8`. netip parses
         none of them, so `parseAddrLenient` does. Pinned with prefixed cases, because the
         slash-less ones are all true via quirk 1 regardless of what they parse to.

      **Done: the four resource declarations — and the parity gate that covers them, which turned
      out to be mostly blind.**

      `FWFilter`, `FWNat`, `FWMangle`, `FWRaw` in `internal/resource/resource.go`, built from shared
      `fwHead`/`fwMatch`/`fwTail` groups the way the live registry is. Two registry features arrived
      with them:

      - **Composite `Identity`.** `Identity string` became `[]string`, joined with U+0001 as
        `identityOf()` does. A firewall rule has no name and nothing unique about it. The audit
        display name is empty for a composite, and that is the ORIGINAL's behaviour rather than an
        omission: `validated.values[resource.identity]` with an array subscript is a key miss in
        JavaScript, so it falls through to the round-tripped identity.
      - **`Check`**, a whole-submission rule for what per-field checks cannot express. Here it is
        RouterOS's "ports can be specified if proto is tcp,udp,udp-lite,dccp,sctp", reported against
        `protocol` — the field that is actually missing — rather than left to the router's bare
        refusal.

      **THE PARITY GATE WAS BLIND IN FOUR WAYS, and the firewall exposed all four.** Every one was
      found by mutating the port and watching the gate not react:

      1. **It never compared `identity` or `guard` at all.** A resource that lost its guard
         declaration would pass every check and simply stop being checked.
      2. **It parsed PROSE as declarations.** `resourceBody` slices from one `key:` to the next, so
         `wgPeer` carried the Firewall section's comment — which contains the literal text
         `guard: 'fwGuard'` — and the new check reported wgPeer as guarded. Fixed by reading the
         declaration with full-line comments stripped.
      3. **It could not follow the shared field groups.** The four tables declare fields as
         `..._fwHead(...)`, so a parser reading only the literal body saw two fields where there are
         fifteen, then reported all thirteen as missing live. `expandSpreads` now inlines them,
         binding parameters positionally. Same for `actions: _FW_ACTIONS`.
      4. **It checked that a picker EXISTS and never what it OFFERS.** This is the one that matters:
         truncating `protocol` from seven values to three passed silently, and so did truncating the
         DNS `type` list from nine to six — **the exact shape of §4, the defect that silently
         rewrote MX records as A.** Both spellings are now compared, `options: [...]` and
         `optionsFrom: { values: [...] }`, because the DNS field uses the first and reading only the
         second left that very field uncovered.

      Mutation-checked at each step rather than trusted: dropping `comment` from the identity,
      dropping the guard, renaming an action label, and truncating either option list all fail the
      gate now. The first run of it passed with the firewall resources **not in the loop** — there
      are two loops in that file and my edit guarded on there being one.

      compute `GuardTargets` and return early when a write named no interface. That shortcut is
      selfPath's alone: selfPath asks WHICH INTERFACE carries us, so an edit naming none cannot
      concern it. fwGuard asks whether a RULE could match our traffic, and a rule naming no
      interface is the LOUDEST case there — `chain=input action=drop` matches on all four counts.
      Keeping the shortcut would have silenced the guard on exactly the write it exists for.

      have read as an empty `srcAddress` — a guard quietly matching on nothing. Converted in
      `fwVerdict`, which is where the original does it too.

      the raw JSON because an anchor of `""` means "send it to the end", which is a real instruction
      and different from sending no anchor at all.

      **Done: `wifiGuard`, with a NINTH generator.** `internal/guard/wifiguard.go` plus
      `tools/wifiguard-cases.js` — **200 decisions, 11 warnings**, all matching.

      **Its failure mode is unusual and worth naming.** The other warn-and-fail-open guards are
      about a hazard; this one is about a SURPRISE. Overriding a shared `/interface/wifi/configuration`
      profile is a legitimate thing to do — the warning exists only because the consequence lands on
      a radio you are NOT looking at, where two SSIDs that used to move together quietly stop. So it
      deliberately stays silent for a profile only one interface uses: a prompt on every save of a
      defconf router is how a warning becomes furniture.

      **Three details would not have survived a naive translation, and the generator caught all
      three:**

      1. **ORDER.** `detail.fields` is built by walking the declaration — `Object.entries` insertion
         order — while the fingerprint sorts a copy. `Inheritable` is therefore an ordered SLICE,
         not a map. A corpus case submits `width, ssid, band` and gets back `ssid, band, width`,
         which is exactly what a Go map would randomise while every other assertion still passed.
      2. **Presence, not emptiness.** The original tests `hasOwnProperty`, so an SSID submitted as
         `''` is a value and an absent one is not. Carried as a separate `Set`, the way selfguard's
         `ValueSet` is.
      3. **The passphrase is write-only.** It is never read back, so "is it changing" cannot be
         answered by comparison: any non-empty value counts, a blank one does not.

      **Detail 3 needed a corpus case I did not have at first.** Every interface in the fixtures
      stored an empty passphrase, so comparing it gave the same answer as the special case and the
      mutation went undetected — a test that could not tell the two implementations apart. Adding a
      pair of interfaces with a STORED passphrase fixed it: re-submitting the value the router
      already holds must warn, and a plain comparison calls it "none". All four mutations bite now.

      **THE PARITY GATE WAS WRONG IN TWO MORE WAYS, and both were found by mutation:**

      1. **`guard:` can be a STRING OR AN ARRAY.** `wifiNet` declares two — selfPath and
         wifiInherit ask different questions and both can be true of one write. The gate read only
         the string form, scored it as `selfPath` alone, and would have passed a port that silently
         dropped the second guard.
      2. **Actions were read from the resource's SLICE rather than its `actions:` key.** That
         attributed somebody else's actions to `wlSecProfile`, which declares none: `resourceBody`
         slices from one `key:` to the next at indent level, and a shared actions const between two
         resources is written `{ key: 'enable', …` — preceded by a brace, so the slice ran straight
         past it into the CAPsMAN section and picked up its enable/disable pair. The gate now reads
         the key, inline or via a constant, and anything else in the slice belongs to something else.

      **Also fixed: the bounds failure message printed POINTER ADDRESSES.** `live=[<nil>,0xc00028a540]`
      names neither value. It reads `live=[none,32] port=[none,31]` now — a gate that cannot say what
      differs is only half a gate.

      Mutation-checked: dropping the second guard, renaming an inline action, and changing the SSID
      max all fail.

      as a pass. **A build failure is not "the gate is weak", it is "the experiment did not run",
      and I had been reading them as the same thing.** The harness now reports INVALID for a

      **ORDER IS PART OF THE CONTRACT and is reproduced deliberately**: nodes come out core-first,
      then neighbours in router order, then clients in bridge-table order, because JavaScript's Map
      preserves insertion order and the page renders what it is given. Go map iteration would
      reshuffle the map on every poll, so the builder carries explicit key order and the host table
      is a SLICE.

      hierarchy when something forwards LLDP that should not, so it now has a unit test on synthetic
      rows covering one, two and zero LLDP devices on a shared port, including the `shared` flag.

      **The port DECODES TopoJSON ITSELF** rather than loading `/vendor/topojson-client.min.js`.
      That is one function — an arc-delta decode, about thirty lines — and reimplementing it removes
      a script tag from the page and a dependency from the build. It is a good trade only if it is
      right, and "right" means identical outlines for the actual atlas this app ships, so
      `nodecheck/topojson-decode.test.js` decodes it BOTH ways and compares every ring of every
      country to six decimals. Removing the reversed-arc rule fails it with
      `US ring 0 point 0 differs` — verified, then reverted.

      The failure modes there are all quiet ones: a negative arc index means "this arc, backwards"
      (that is how a shared border is stored once instead of twice) and reversing it wrongly turns a
      border inside out; the first point of each arc repeats the last of the previous one, and
      keeping it leaves a zero-length segment at every join. Neither throws. Both draw a map that
      looks almost right.

      **A caveat for the DOM comparison, recorded before it surprises anyone:** the comet animations
      carry a deliberate `Math.random()` jitter in duration and start offset, so arcs drawn in one
      frame do not pulse in lockstep. Those attributes CANNOT match between two renderers, and the
      comparison has to exclude them — the same class as the Interfaces sparkline and the CAPsMAN
      render-history caveats.

      **Slice 4 done: the Sankey**, in `web/src/pages/connections-sankey.ts` — the ribbons, the node
      columns, the destination folding and the throttle.

      **THE RIBBONS ARE AN APPROXIMATION AND THE PORT SAYS SO.** There is no source-by-destination
      cross-matrix in the payload — the collector counts per source and per destination, not per
      pair, and building the matrix would mean a number for every combination. So each source's bar
      is divided across destinations by destination weight and vice versa: both COLUMN totals are
      exact, each individual ribbon is a proportional estimate. That is why hovering a ribbon names
      the pair and quotes no count, which would present an estimate as a measurement.

      Destinations FOLD onto their organisation where there is one — a diagram with nine Google rows
      tells you less than one saying Google is nine — then onto country, then the raw key.

      **The throttle is what makes this survive a three second poll**: a redraw builds up to eighty
      ribbon paths, so it happens at most every five seconds and an unchanged fingerprint skips it
      entirely. While a country or client filter is active the CALLER owns rendering — the filtered
      view comes from indexes the poll handler cannot see, and re-rendering would wipe the filter
      every few seconds — but the data is still recorded, so lifting the filter draws the latest.

      **Done: the page module and the DOM comparison.** `web/src/pages/connections.ts` holds the
      state and the wiring and nothing that draws, which is what keeps a 1,200-line page readable:
      three of the four modules are testable without a page, and the one that is not is the one
      owning live SVG nodes.

      **THE TWO FILTERS ARE MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE, deliberately.** A country filter answers "who talks
      to Germany"; a client filter answers "where does this laptop go". Both at once would ask
      whether this laptop talks to Germany — which the payload cannot answer without the
      cross-matrix nobody sends. Selecting one clears the other, in both directions.

      **DOM comparison: 30 KB, ZERO differences** — 18 Sankey nodes, 80 ribbons, 10 port rows, the
      badge and both empty states, driven from one payload.

      **Getting there took three harness corrections, all recorded because they will recur:**

      - **A throttled renderer cannot be compared against an un-throttled one.** The port's Sankey
        redraws at most every five seconds; the lifted module is a fresh module per call and always
        draws. Snapshotting straight after an emit compared two different payloads, which looked
        like an arithmetic difference and was not.
      - **A three second poll leaves no window for a five second throttle.** The fix is to LEAVE THE
        PAGE first: the collector is refcounted on the room, so with no viewer it suspends and the
        payload stops moving.
      - **Container width is part of the output.** With the page hidden the Sankey falls back to a
        600px width; with it visible it measured 758. The two renderers drew at different moments and
        so at different widths, and every X coordinate differed while every Y matched to thirteen
        significant figures. Dispatching `mikrodash:pagechange` makes the port redraw un-throttled at
        the current width, which is what finally put both on the same footing.

      **Verified against the AX3**: 383 connections, 177 country paths drawn from the port's OWN
      TopoJSON decode, 10 port rows, an 18-node Sankey, 11 clients in the picker. The country list
      reads "No geo data yet" and there are no arcs — correct, and exactly what the live app shows on
      a router without the MaxMind database.

      **Still to do (its own item):** the MaxMind reader. Until it lands `topCountries` is empty, the
      map colours nothing and no arcs are drawn — the same degradation the live app already has.
- [x] **DONE — Geo and ASN lookup.** The item the connections page left behind.

      **Reader done and gated.** `internal/geo/geoip.go` reads geoip-lite's own `geoip-city.dat`
      (24-byte range records) and `geoip-city-names.dat` (88-byte location records). The live app
      uses **geoip-lite, not MaxMind directly** — same files, same search — so any disagreement is a
      defect here and nowhere else. `tools/geo-cases.js` records geoip-lite's answers for 2,768
      synthetic addresses (fixed-seed LCG, skipping `a==0 || a==127 || a>=224`) and
      `internal/geo/geoip_test.go` replays them.

      **The case format was wrong before the reader was**, and it is the reusable lesson: it recorded
      only `country`, collapsing "no record" and "a record whose country is empty" into one row, and
      the test inferred "located" from `country != ""`. `169.51.214.0` resolves to a location with a
      timezone and coordinates and NO country code, so the gate reported a disagreement that was its
      own definition. `found` is recorded separately now — and that fix immediately caught a real
      defect: geoip-lite returns its record even when the location id is the `no location` sentinel,
      and this reader was reporting a miss for it.

      **Two mutations survive, both run down rather than left as gaps** — see the comments in
      `Lookup`, which exist so the next person to try them does not read a survival as a hole. The
      `round` midpoint is behaviour-identical to the ordinary floor (516,275 boundary lookups, both
      variants, no disagreement — the index is sorted and disjoint so they converge). The
      private-range refusal is unobservable in this data (no index record overlaps any of the seven
      private ranges); it stays as belt and braces because the data file gets refreshed.

      **IPv6 was a real gap, found by asking what the gate could NOT see.** The live app gates its
      lookups on `ipaddr.isValid`, which accepts v6, so every v6 destination is geo-located there
      through a separate 48-byte index in `geoip-city6.dat`. This reader was v4-only and returned
      nothing for all of it — and no case could notice, because every case was v4. Three reference
      behaviours are now commented so nobody "improves" them: the comparison is 64 bits wide (the
      index is ordered on the first eight bytes), `::ffff:a.b.c.d` goes to the V4 index, and there is
      no `privateRange6` so ULA and link-local are searched rather than refused.

      **The sample was widened twice, for two different reasons.** 838 v6 addresses to cover the path
      at all; then 120 more inside five real /32s, because the 32-bit-comparison mutation caught
      exactly ONE case without them — two addresses must share their top 32 bits before the width can
      matter. That mutation now fails 99 times. A gate that catches a defect once is one a data
      refresh can disarm.

      **Wired and verified live against the AX3.** `main` loads the database once (`-geo`, default
      `/app/node_modules/geoip-lite/data`), `geo.Current()` hands it to each session, and both
      collectors take `WithGeo`. 351 connections, US 130 / Germany-Bernburg 67 / Cyprus 10 / …, 177
      country paths with 11 highlighted, 11 labels, 10 arcs with comets.

      **`/api/localcc` is why the arcs were missing at first**, and it is a trap worth remembering:
      the arcs originate at the ROUTER's country, which the page fetches from that endpoint.
      Unauthenticated it 401s, `localCC` stays `'ZZ'` and no arc is drawn — which looks exactly like
      a geo defect. `tools/dev-stub-auth.mjs` answers it now (`--localcc`).

      **ASN done too**, in `internal/asn`. The table is GENERATED from the live source by
      `tools/asn-table.js` (13 orgs, 339 ranges): typing CIDRs by hand is the same class of mistake
      as retyping markup, since `104.16.0.0/13` and `/18` differ by one character and two million
      addresses. The matching has its OWN gate (`tools/asn-cases.js`, 1,604 addresses derived from
      the ranges — first, last, middle and the two just outside each) because a stale table and a
      wrong decision fail differently.

      **That gate caught two defects on its first run, both mine and both the same mistake: being
      stricter than the reference.** A `TrimSpace` before parsing — `ipaddr.parse(' 8.8.8.8 ')`
      throws and `net.isIP` returns 0, so both references answer nothing where this port answered
      Google and the United States. **`internal/geo` had the same call, and no case could see it**,
      because every geo case was well-formed; its case set now carries padded and malformed input.
      And refusing a zoned address, which both references accept and place as if the zone were
      absent — in `asn` the zone must be STRIPPED rather than tolerated, since
      `netip.Prefix.Contains` returns false for any address carrying one.

      **One divergence is documented rather than closed.** ipaddr.js implements the inet_aton
      grammar (`0x08.8.8.8`, `134744072`, `8.8.2056` are all 8.8.8.8 to it); netip takes dotted-quad
      and nothing else. RouterOS cannot emit those forms, so reproducing the grammar means a second
      IP parser for traffic that does not exist — but the gap is ASSERTED
      (`TestKnownDivergencesStillDiverge`) so closing it fails the suite and forces the note out,
      rather than being hidden by deleting the cases.

      **Verified live**: the Sankey folds onto Google and Cloudflare beside the country nodes, and

      shell redirection, so `print(... if i>0 else ...)` in a read-only Python heredoc asked
      permission to write. Shell operators now skip heredoc bodies; SCRIPT write patterns still
      scan them, because the incident the hook exists for was a heredoc that genuinely wrote. The
      fix had its own bug — `open('x')` matched because `x` is a mode letter — caught by one of the
      eight new cases; the mode must now follow a comma and look like a mode. Mode detection also
      gained `'a'` and `'r+'`, which were never caught. 32 cases, all green.

      **Part 21 DONE: `LatestFingerprint` + `RunFor`.** The fingerprint query filters on
      `fingerprint IS NOT NULL`, not the newest row: a FAILED run has none and must leave the
      last-seen configuration alone, or one unreachable minute produces a false "changed"
      notification and a redundant restore point on the next success. `RunFor` composes run →
      record → prune: every run gets a row including failures, only a CHANGED run records a stem
      (an unchanged one has a fingerprint and no stem, which is what StoredBackups filters on),
      retention runs only after a change, a failed BACKUP is not an error but a failed RECORDING
      is. Four mutations caught. Remaining for `run`: the handler's Connect closure.

      **PROTOCOL REALITY 3 IS SETTLED, and it is cheaper than assumed.** go-routeros is
      byte-transparent by construction: `readWord` does `io.ReadFull` into a `[]byte` and the
      parser does `string(b)`, which preserves bytes because Go strings are not validated UTF-8.
      **No receiver patch, no patched-library check, and no separate connection** — the live app
      opens one only because "the decode is a property of the connection", and there is no decode
      to isolate here. Proven against the real library in `internal/backups/rawbytes_test.go`
      (all 256 byte values, invalid UTF-8 forms, NUL, gzip magic, and 7-byte chunk boundaries).
      **The hazard is real on this side somewhere else:** `encoding/json` replaces invalid UTF-8
      with U+FFFD, so backup content must be carried as `[]byte` and never through a JSON string.
      Pinned by a test that asserts the corruption on purpose.

      **Drift §1 — port `isDue()` from the FIXED version, not the one in the notes' base commit.**
      The elapsed-interval gate ran before the wall-clock anchor, so a run late in the day pushed the
      next one past its own target: a manual backup at 11:45 left "daily at 08:00" not due at 08:00
      the next morning, and once it fired at 11:45 it stayed there. One router's daily schedule had
      never fired once.

      For a `daily` schedule with a chosen time, **skip the interval gate entirely** —
      `now >= target && lastRun < target` already permits exactly one run per day. Weekly and monthly
      keep it, because the "today at HH:MM" helper knows an hour and a minute but not a weekday or a
      date.

      **The trap, and it is a testing trap rather than a code one:** the live tests all placed
      `lastRun` just before the previous day's target, so a full interval had always elapsed by the
      next one and the bug could not appear. **Put `lastRun` late in the day** or this port
      reproduces the defect and its blind spot together.

  The row needs numbers for routers nobody has open. In the live app those come from
  `src/overviewSessions.js`: a pool holding a RouterOS connection per such router, running THREE
  collectors (system, interfaceStatus, dhcpLeases) to cache their payloads. Porting it is not the
  hard part; deciding when to RUN it is.

  - **The port's `Session` starts FOURTEEN collectors, not 3 — counted 2026-08-25, and this line
    said "~11" before that.** It constructs 27 and starts 14 on connect: `bridges dhcpLeases
    dhcpNetworks dns firewall ifStatus logs netwatch ping system talkers traffic vlans wan`. The
    live pool runs three (`overviewSessions.js:102-114`: system, interfaceStatus, dhcpLeases), so
    the ratio is **4.7×**, not the "roughly four times" this said — and it has been growing as the
    port progresses, because every new collector wired into `Session` lands in the background path
    too.

    The documented bottleneck is concurrent API channels on the MikroTik
    (`../MikroDash/src/collection.js:8`), so this is a measurable regression rather than a style
    point.

    **The framing matters more than the number.** This is not "a Go pool would be somewhat heavier";
    it is that the port HAS NO LIGHTWEIGHT POOL. `Session` is a full page-serving session and
    reusing it for routers nobody is looking at is the wrong object, not a tuned-down version of the
    right one. What is needed is a background mode that starts only the three — and whoever writes
    it should re-count first, because this number moved once already.
  - **Node is already running that pool against the same fleet.** A Go pool during coexistence
    DOUBLES the background sessions on every router, for a page that is not shipped yet. Same
    reasoning as the backup scheduler, already recorded above.
  - **But the page cannot ship without it.** Reporting every non-interactively-connected router as
    offline is a user-visible change, and a page that renders differently has not been ported.

  Options, in the order they seem preferable:
    1. **Proxy `routers:stats` to Node until cutover.** The page ships and renders identically; the
       Go builder above is exercised only after cutover. Costs a second socket path for one event.
    2. **Build a background-mode session (three collectors) and leave it OFF until cutover**, as the
       backup scheduler is. The page then cannot ship until cutover either.
    3. **Run it now and accept doubled background sessions** during coexistence. Cheapest to build,
       and the one that touches the documented bottleneck.

    would be TWO sessions and two connections to one router. The harness now fails on a build for a
    tracked id.
  - *A destroyed session starting on a late connect* — survived because the harness DELETED torn-down
    sessions, so the late event found nothing and never reached the guard. The live pool keeps the
    object alive; its ROS client can still deliver an in-flight `connected`. Torn sessions are now
    kept reachable, which is what makes the `destroyed` flag testable at all. **The harness was
    bypassing the exact guard the test was written for.**

    either closed without an error or errored without closing. Two cases added. The page shows the
    reason WHILE the router is down, so clearing it on the following close blanks the message it
    exists for.

  kind: the cases were present and the test could not see them fail.

      would ERROR rather than disagree, and the obvious workaround would accept a port that
      substituted a default. **Left to the write path deliberately:** `_cipherKeep`, which preserves
      undecryptable ciphertext so a later `save` cannot overwrite a credential with `''`.

  **A THIRD CUTOVER DECISION, and this one I am not asking about because it has only one answer.**
  `POST /api/settings` is NOT wired, though its validation and writer are ported and byte-compared.
  `src/settings.js` caches the settings object at first load and never re-reads the file, so during
  coexistence (a) a write from this side is invisible to the running Node app until it restarts, and
  (b) the next save from THAT side writes `{ ...its cache, ...its updates }` and silently reverts
  everything this side changed. The operator sees the change take effect here and find it gone later,
  with nothing logged. Same family as the backup scheduler and the routers pool: **the settings write
  is a cutover step.**

      two files. The purge deletes by `router_id` and would pass either way; they match now because
      **a fixture which is not the schema is not evidence**.

      **What it compares, and what it deliberately does not.** Column set, declared type, and the
      NOT NULL flag — the three that decide whether a Go scan works. NOT indexes, CHECKs, UNIQUEs or
      DEFAULTs: a fixture legitimately omits constraints on writes the port does not make, and
      requiring them would make this noise nobody reads. A column the real table has and a fixture
      omits is a NOTE, not a failure, since the audit cannot know whether a query selects it — 15
      such notes today.

      **The NOT NULL check runs in ONE direction on purpose**, and the reasoning is written at the
      comparison: a fixture stricter than the schema cannot produce the row that breaks a scan into
      a non-pointer Go type, which is precisely the `sites.description` bug. The reverse is harmless.

      **Proved against all three of the week's bugs**: reintroducing the `v` column, reverting
      `grants.id` to INTEGER, and re-declaring `sites.description` NOT NULL are each caught. A clean
      run also fails if NOTHING was compared, so a drifted matcher cannot look like a pass.

      mutation rather than the mutation. Go has no exception to unwind with, so the rollback is

      **Part 19 — A FOURTH CUTOVER BLOCKER, FOUND BY READING A COMMENT BEFORE TRUSTING IT.**
      Not a port: a constraint that was NOT recorded and that several already-ported routes sit on.

      I was about to port the three group WRITE routes. `principals_api.go`'s own header says the
      writes are deliberately absent — "Node holds `Rbac.bump()` to invalidate its own caches, and a
      write from this side would leave that stale". Checked rather than taken on trust, and it is
      exactly right: `bump()` is `_gen++; _views.clear(); _defs.clear()`, `viewFor` returns a cached
      view whenever `cached.gen === _gen`, there is NO time-based expiry, and the 14 callers are all
      in Node. A Go write to `grants` leaves Node honouring a revoked grant until something else
      bumps or the process restarts.

      **THEN THE SAME QUESTION ABOUT `routers.json`, WHICH THIS PORT HAS BEEN WRITING ALL SESSION.**
      `src/routers.js:loadAll()` is `if (_cache) return _cache;` — no watcher, no mtime check, the
      IDENTICAL pattern to `src/settings.js:366`, which this queue has recorded as a cutover blocker
      for weeks. And every Node write does `_cache = routers; _writeFile(routers)`, rebuilding the
      whole file from its stale in-memory list.

      So a Go write to `routers.json` is **invisible to the running Node app, and silently reverted
      by its next save**. That is the settings blocker, word for word, applied to a second file that
      nobody had written it down for.

      **WHICH ROUTES SIT ON IT** — all ported, all currently served by the Go mux rather than proxied:

      * `POST/PUT/DELETE /api/routers`
      * `PUT /api/sites/:id/routers` (the membership write, ported this session)
      * `DELETE /api/sites/:id`, through `store.ClearSite`

      **NOTHING IS LOST TODAY**, because the port is not cut over and the live app is not running
      behind it. What changes is the ORDER: these routes cannot be exercised during coexistence, and
      "run the Go server in front of Node and try the Devices page" would silently discard edits. The
      note now lives on both route files so a reader meets it at the code.

      **AND IT STOPS THE GROUP WRITES HERE.** Porting them would add a third family to the list,
      with the RBAC-cache half of the problem on top — a revoked grant still honoured is worse than a
      lost edit. Their validation, storage, reads and orphan guard are all ported and tested; what is
      missing is deliberately the HTTP layer, and that is now a recorded decision rather than an
      omission.

      **THE LESSON, STATED because it has now paid twice in three ticks:** a comment saying "this is
      not done because X" is a claim about the live source, and claims about the live source go
      stale. Reading it was worth the tick; the second reading — asking the same question about a
      file the comment did not mention — is what found the unrecorded one.

      **`builtin` IS NOT WRITABLE, AND IT IS A SECURITY PROPERTY.** The live comment: "`builtin` and

      take.

      **THE GRANT CHECK IS THE ENGINE'S.** `grants.role_id` is `ON DELETE RESTRICT`, so a role a
      grant still holds is refused by SQLite. `DeleteRole` deliberately does NOT re-check —
      `CountGrantsForRole` exists so the route can say HOW MANY — because a second answer to a

      **AND THAT IS WHERE `schema-audit` HAD A HOLE.** The test pinning that refusal FAILED: the

      fixture legitimately omits what constrains writes the port does not make". **That argument is
      wrong wherever the port RELIES on a constraint instead of re-checking it**, which is exactly
      this case.

      Foreign keys are now compared, with `RELIED_ON` naming the one the port leans on. **The strict
      version was written first and stepped back from**, and the reasoning is on the code: making it

      **QUEUED:** bringing those six fixtures up to the full schema, at which point the FK check can

      **Part 22 DONE: the twelve fixtures brought up, and the foreign-key rule PROMOTED from a note

      failed the moment it was corrected. It now asserts the two columns that ARE nullable (`role`,

      passing against a reader that returned nil for everything.

      **A FOURTH ENCOUNTER WITH THE BACKTICK TRAP**, in a comment I wrote this tick: SQL comments

      **Part 23 DONE: the GRANT db writers — the last principal family below the HTTP layer.**

      **THE UPSERT IS KEYED ON PRINCIPAL AND SCOPE, NOT ON ID.** Changing what somebody holds AT A
      SCOPE replaces the grant rather than stacking a second one — two rows for one principal at one
      scope would have to be resolved later, and nothing downstream resolves them.

      **A CUSTOM ROLE MIRRORS AS THE LEAST-PRIVILEGED LEGACY VALUE**, and this is the one worth
      naming. `grants.role` is read only by a downgraded (v6) binary predating the roles table, and a
      custom role has no legacy equivalent. The live comment: "a downgrade must not grant more than
      it should". Mirroring a custom role as `admin` because it happens to confer a lot would hand a
      rolled-back install more access than anybody granted. `mirror-leaks-role-name` is a killed
      mutation.

      **A GLOBAL GRANT STORES AN EMPTY STRING**, and a caller sending a scope id with a global type
      has it dropped. Both halves matter: NULL would let one principal hold two global grants,
      because SQLite treats NULLs as distinct in a UNIQUE index; a leftover id would violate the
      live CHECK. The test fixture carries BOTH constraints, which `adminDDL` omits — without the
      UNIQUE index the upsert silently becomes an insert and every "replaces" assertion would pass
      against a port that stacked rows.

      **Part 25 — WIRING THE NOTIFICATIONS IS A CUTOVER STEP, AND ITEM 11 DID NOT SAY SO.**
      Not a port. A constraint found by asking what "complete apart from wiring them to a caller"
      would actually mean.

      Item 11 ends: "item 11's transports are complete apart from wiring them to a caller." That
      reads like the remaining work is small. It is not small, and it is not safe:

      **THE CALLER DOES NOT EXIST YET.** `src/alerter.js` is 692 lines and EVENT-DRIVEN —
      `evaluate(event, data)` runs per collector event, not on a timer. This port's `internal/alert`
      holds `format.go` and `row.go` only: the rendering and the row shaping, none of the DECISION.
      Nothing here evaluates an alert or could call `notify.Send`.

      **AND WIRING IT DURING COEXISTENCE WOULD DOUBLE EVERY NOTIFICATION.** Both apps run their own
      collectors against the same routers, so both would evaluate the same conditions. The
      interlock that might have saved it does not exist: **the cooldown is an in-memory `Map`**
      (`_deliver`'s `cooldownMap`, with `.get`/`.set`/`.size`/`.clear`), not a database row — so two
      engines keep two cooldowns and neither sees the other's sends.

      **THIS IS WORSE THAN THE OTHER BLOCKERS, and the difference is worth stating.** A settings or
      `routers.json` write that gets reverted is a lost edit — annoying, recoverable, and confined
      to the app. A duplicated notification is OUTBOUND: two Telegram messages, two emails, two ntfy
      pushes per alert, to an operator who cannot un-receive them, from a system whose whole purpose
      is to be trusted about when something is wrong. An alert storm from a flapping link would
      arrive twice over.

      **So the transports stay unwired, deliberately.** They are complete, pinned by two generated
      corpora and eighteen killed mutations, and they wait on cutover exactly as the settings write
      does. `internal/notify` now carries the note at the top.

      **Item 11's own summary is corrected in place** rather than left reading as though a small
      wiring job remained.

      **Part 26 DONE: the ALERT EVALUATOR's rules, as a corpus.** `tools/alert-eval-cases.js` —
      17 cases produced by LIFTING `createEvaluator` and RUNNING it with only the delivery layer
      stubbed. This is the first of the three things `alerter-cases.js` recorded as unported ("the
      evaluator, the cooldown maps and the delivery"); the delivery stays unported for the reason in
      Part 25.

      **EDGE DETECTION IS THE WHOLE THING.** Every rule compares a reading against a threshold AND
      against its own previous verdict. `cpuGoesHighAndStaysHigh` fires ONCE across four readings —
      a port testing the level instead would page the operator every two seconds while a CPU stayed
      busy, and every other CPU case would still pass.

      **`fire` RUNS INTACT; ONLY WHAT IS BELOW IT IS STUBBED.** `fire` holds the install-wide type
      toggles, and its own comment records the bug that appeared when they were moved elsewhere — "a
      filter that does not filter what you are looking at is not a filter". Stubbing `fire` would
      take that out of the corpus.

      **THREE THINGS THE BELIEVABILITY BLOCK CAUGHT, all mine:**

      * The fixture router had no `id`, and `fire` guards its whole record-and-emit block on
        `router && router.id`. Every case evaluated every rule and emitted nothing — which reads as
        "no alert fired" and would have been recorded as the live behaviour.
      * The `db` stubs were FLAT (`hasOpenAlert: () => false`), so a recovery never resolved
        anything and never emitted. Replaced with a real little in-memory table, because `fire`
        genuinely consults that state — the dedup is half the rules.
      * The toggle key was `notifUpdate`; the live one is `notifRouterUpdate`. Every update case
        fired nothing.

      Each looked like "the live app does not do that" and was actually the harness.

      **AND A REAL FINDING, filed as `ToDo.md` §7.** The update alert's own comment says keying on
      the VERSION means "a later release still notifies instead of being swallowed as 'already
      alerting'". **Measured: it does not**, while the first alert is open. The version check passes
      and `fire` then returns at `db.hasOpenAlert`, which the comment does not account for. A router
      left un-updated across two releases is told about the one it already knew. Both sequences are
      in the corpus — suppressed while open, and firing again once the router updates — with the
      discrepancy written beside the case.

      **COVERAGE IS ONE FAMILY OF SIX, AND THE LIST IS READ FROM THE SOURCE.** `system:update` is
      covered; the interface, VPN, netwatch, ping and BGP families are recorded as uncovered with
      reasons, and a family appearing in the evaluator that is in NEITHER list fails the generator.
      A clean run here does not mean the evaluator is pinned, and the header says so.

      **The clock is PINNED rather than the timestamp dropped.** `fire` stamps `firedAt` with
      `Date.now()`, so the first version wrote a different corpus every run and `--check` called a
      freshly written file stale. Pinning keeps `firedAt` compared.

      **Part 27 DONE: the Go EVALUATOR for `system:update`.** `internal/alert/eval.go`, judged
      against last tick's corpus — 19 cases, all matching. 10 mutations: **8 killed, 2 recorded
      EQUIVALENT with a measured reason.**

      **THE TWO SURVIVORS ARE THE SAME FINDING TWICE, and it is `ToDo.md` §7.** Replacing the CPU
      rule's edge check with a bare level test survives; so does deleting the update rule's version
      check. Both survive because `emit`'s DEDUPLICATION already suppresses the repeat — the alert is
      still open, so `HasOpen` returns true and nothing fires either way.

      **Measured rather than assumed**: removing the edge check AND the dedup together fails
      `cpuGoesHighAndStaysHigh` and `aLaterReleaseWhileTheFirstIsOpen`, which is what "these two
      mechanisms overlap" predicts. So the mutants are equivalent within this rule's own dynamics,
      and they are RECORDED rather than counted.

      That overlap is exactly the inconsistency filed upstream: the update rule's comment claims the
      version keying is what lets a later release notify, and `hasOpenAlert` is what actually decides.
      A mutation surviving because two guards do the same job is the same observation from the other
      side.

      **THE PORT'S SHAPE CARRIES THE TRAPS.** `cpuLoad` is a POINTER — a plain float64 reads an
      absent reading as 0, decides the CPU recovered and fires a spurious resolution.
      `prevCPUAlert` is a `*bool` and THREE-STATE — the live value starts null, and a port
      initialising it to `true` goes silent on a first reading that is already high, which
      `firstReadingIsAlreadyHigh` pins. Both are killed mutations.

      **AND ONE THING I GUESSED RATHER THAN READ.** The resolve detail is
      `"RouterOS is up to date (" + cleanVersion + ")"`, not the bare sentence I wrote — and BOTH
      details clean the running version through
      `(data.version || '').replace(/\s*\(.*\)/, '').trim() || 'unknown'`, stripping the channel
      suffix. The corpus caught the resolve half only: the announce case had no `version` at all, so
      both sides said "unknown" and agreed by accident. Two cases added, including a version with
      two bracketed parts, because the regex is GREEDY and unanchored.

      **Part 28 DONE: the PING rule family — two of six now ported.** `Evaluator.PingUpdate`, with
      the corpus grown from 19 cases to 32. 11 mutations: **10 killed, 1 recorded EQUIVALENT.**

      **THREE FALLBACKS FROM ONE READING, AND THEY DISAGREE.** With no target at all the live rule
      produces three different answers: the state KEY is `data.target || 'host'`, the SUBJECT is
      `data.target || ''`, and the DETAIL interpolates `data.target` RAW — so the operator's email
      says "Ping loss to **undefined** is 50%". Reproduced, not tidied; `pingWithNoTarget` records
      all three, and `detail-uses-the-key` is a killed mutation.

      **TWO MUTATIONS SURVIVED THE FIRST PASS AND BOTH WERE REAL COVERAGE GAPS.**

      * `one-flag-for-all-targets` — sharing one state key across targets. Invisible while only ONE
        target is lossy, because `emit`'s dedup is keyed on the SUBJECT and separates them anyway.
        `twoTargetsBothLossy` shows it: with a shared key the second target sees "already alerting"
        and never fires. Killed once the case existed.
      * `pingWithAnEmptyTarget` — nothing sent `target: ''`, only an absent one.

      **AND THE SECOND MUTATION IS EQUIVALENT, which is the honest answer rather than a contrived
      case.** `*target != ""` cannot be observed: an empty target and an absent one both give a
      subject of `""`, and `emit` deduplicates on the SUBJECT, so a key of `""` against `"host"`
      never changes an answer. I tried three sequences to separate them — including one with a
      resolve in between — and each gives the same count either way. The guard stays because it
      matches `data.target || 'host'`, and the code now SAYS no test defends it. That is the third
      equivalent mutant in this evaluator with the same cause: the edge state and the store dedup
      overlap.

      **THE SUBJECT IS NOW COMPARED.** It decides which open alert a resolve matches — it is what
      makes ping deduplicate per target — so it was decoration until this tick and is part of the
      answer now. `no-subject-at-all` is a killed mutation.

      **A false mutation result, caught and not counted.** One anchor missed; the script wrote
      nothing, the PREVIOUS mutant was still in the file, and the run reported "KILLED". The loop now
      prints `ANCHOR MISSED` instead of a verdict — a mutation that was never applied is not a kill,
      and reporting it as one inflates the count with nothing behind it.

      **Part 29 DONE: the NETWATCH rule family — three of six.** `Evaluator.NetwatchUpdate`;
      corpus 32 cases to 43. 7 mutations: **6 killed, 1 recorded EQUIVALENT.**

      **TWO RULES THAT DIFFER FROM THE FAMILIES ALREADY PORTED, and a port reusing their shape gets
      both wrong:**

      * **THE FIRST SIGHTING NEVER FIRES.** The guard is `prev !== undefined`, so a host already
        down when the page loads is recorded silently. CPU and ping both alert on a first reading —
        reusing that here would page on every reconnect, for every host that happens to be down.
        `netwatchFirstSightDown` pins it and `first-sighting-fires` is killed.
      * **`unknown` IS SKIPPED AND DOES NOT UPDATE THE STATE.** The live `continue` jumps the `set`
        at the bottom of the loop as well, so a transient re-probe leaves the previous status intact.
        An `unknown` FIRST sighting therefore leaves the host UNSEEN, and the reading after it is
        still a first sighting — a second case, because "does not disturb" and "does not create" are
        different properties.

      The state holds the STATUS STRING rather than a boolean, since "never seen", "seen as unknown"
      and "seen as up" are three different answers.

      **THE SURVIVOR IS EQUIVALENT FOR A REASON WORTH KNOWING.** `prev == "down"` and `prev != "up"`
      are interchangeable — but only BECAUSE of the skip above. `unknown` never reaches the state, so
      a seen host is "up" or "down" and nothing else. The equivalence is not a property of that line;
      let `unknown` be stored and the two forms disagree immediately. Recorded on the code, because a
      later reader tightening the skip would silently break a line that looks unrelated.

      That is the fourth equivalent mutant in this evaluator, and the third whose cause is one rule
      standing on another.

      **Part 30 DONE: the INTERFACE rule family — four of six.** `Evaluator.IfstatusUpdate`;
      corpus 43 cases to 55. 11 mutations: **10 killed, 1 recorded EQUIVALENT.**

      **THE TICK OPENED WITH A BROKEN BUILD.** The previous one was cut off after adding the
      `Settings` fields and the `prevIfState` map but before writing `ifState` or `IfstatusUpdate` —
      `undefined: ifState`, twice. Finished first, before anything else.

      **AN ADMIN DISABLING AN INTERFACE ALSO STOPS IT RUNNING**, and that used to fire "Interface
      Down". The live comment: the disabled flag "was already being captured for exactly this purpose
      and then never read". The suppression covers BOTH directions, which is why the PREVIOUS
      reading's flag counts as well as this one's — an admin re-enabling must not produce an unpaired
      "Interface Up".

      **TWO SURVIVORS WERE REAL GAPS, AND BOTH WERE MASKED THE SAME WAY.**

      * `prev-disabled-ignored` survived the obvious re-enable sequence, because the "down" was
        suppressed so there was no open alert for the "up" to resolve and `emit` dropped it anyway.
        `ifaceDisabledWhileAlreadyDown` puts a REAL down first, so there IS one — and the mutant
        resolves it.
      * `absent-filter-means-off` could not be seen through the corpus at all: every generated case
        carries all five type filters, because the live DEFAULTS ship them. Covered by a direct Go
        test instead, which is the right tool — a map read treating a missing key as OFF would
        silence the whole family for any caller building settings from a partial object.

      **THE THIRD IS EQUIVALENT ON TWO STACKED ACCIDENTS**, recorded on the code rather than trimmed.
      Dropping the `seen` guard survives because a zero `ifState` has `Running=false` (so a first
      sighting of a DOWN interface shows no transition) AND because a first sighting of an UP one
      produces a recovery that resolves nothing. Change either and the guard starts mattering.

      That is the fifth equivalent mutant in this evaluator, and every one has the same cause: the
      edge state and the store dedup suppress the same repeats. Worth stating as a property of the
      DESIGN rather than a quirk of five separate lines.

      **Part 31 DONE: the VPN and BGP rule families — SIX OF SIX, the evaluator's rules are
      complete.** Corpus 55 cases to 111; 6 of 6 families covered and `UNCOVERED` is now empty.
      **28 mutations across the two ticks, ALL KILLED** — no equivalents this time, and the three
      that survived a first pass each named a real coverage gap rather than an untestable line.

      **VPN: THREE STATES, TWO OF WHICH MEAN THE SAME THING.** `peerState` emits
      `active | stale | never`, and only `active` is connected — so `prevVPNState` holds the STRING,
      because a change between the two disconnected values must not read as a transition. The
      discriminating case is NOT the obvious one: `never -> active` is a transition, but an UP one,
      and `emit` drops a recovery that resolves nothing, so both a correct port and one comparing
      against `"stale"` alone are silent. **`never -> stale` is what separates them** — a port
      reading "never" as connected files a spurious disconnect for a peer that has never been up.
      Two assertions of mine were wrong before the generator corrected them, both by predicting a
      fire the store swallows.

      **BGP: FOUR RULES OVER ONE EVENT, and they are independent.** state, prefix swing, flapping,
      hold timer — `bgpAllFourInOneReading` pins six events across two readings and compares the
      SEQUENCE, so a port that returned after the first match emits two. Boundaries pinned by
      mutation: the prefix threshold is `>= 0.2`, the hold timer is `> 0 && < 9`, and the keepalive
      check is the STRICT `=== 0`, so an absent keepalive is not a misconfiguration — a port
      defaulting that field to zero pages about every peer whose keepalive the router did not report.

      **THREE MUTATIONS SURVIVED A FIRST PASS. ALL THREE WERE HIDDEN BY THE STORE DEDUP, and the
      fix was a case rather than a shrug.** This is the sixth, seventh and eighth time the edge state
      and `emit`'s deduplication have overlapped in this evaluator — the difference is that these
      three CAN be separated, and the earlier five could not.

      * `pfx-alert-flag-ignored` and `settle-ignores-flag`. `prevBgpPfxAlert` is keyed on the peer's
        `key`; the alert ROW is keyed on `bgpPeer`, the peer NAME. Everywhere else that difference is
        invisible. **A RENAME separates them, and it is reachable rather than contrived**: `_peerKey`
        is `remote.address || name`, while `name` is the session's own `s.name`, so renaming a BGP
        connection in RouterOS moves the name and leaves the key alone. `bgpKeepsSwingingAcrossARename`
        kills the first. The second needed the corpus to gain PRE-SEEDED open rows —
        `bgpSteadyWithARowAlreadyOpen` — where the flag says "we never alerted" and the store says a
        row is open, and only the flag is right.
      * `capmap-never-clears`. See below; it needed 501 interfaces.

      **`_capMap` WAS NEVER PORTED AT ALL, for any family — AND PORTING IT FOUND A LIVE DEFECT
      THAT WAS FIXED THE SAME DAY.** It was BEHAVIOUR rather than a memory bound: past `STATE_MAX`
      (500) the live code CLEARED the whole map rather than trimming it, before every write, inside
      the loop. So on the reading after the 501st distinct key the first interface still saw its
      previous state and alerted, and every one after it had just been forgotten and read as
      never-seen. **One silent round for the entire fleet, from one entry over the line**, and the
      map refilled from the clear point so the split moved rather than healed. Reported upstream with
      the numbers; fixed in `07da9a9`.

      **THE OBVIOUS FIX IS BACKWARDS, and naming it as the tempting option is what got it checked.**
      `Map.set` on an EXISTING key does not move it, so insertion order is not recency — an interface
      present since startup and re-set every pass holds position 0 for ever, while the churning pppoe
      peers that caused the growth sit at the end. An oldest-first trim evicts exactly what must be
      kept. What landed instead prunes the keys ABSENT from the current payload: the only one of the
      three rules that can never forget something still live.

      **IT IS STILL GATED ON THE BOUND, and that is not an optimisation.** A payload is not always
      the whole fleet — since `272eeca` an `ifstatus:update` can carry a provisional snapshot
      mid-cycle — so pruning against a partial list would drop live state and recreate the very bug.
      Above the bound the risk is worth taking because the alternative is discarding all of it. Two
      fixes from the same afternoon that would have undone each other if either had been written
      without the other in view.

      **`prevBgpPfxAlert` WAS NEVER BOUNDED AT ALL**, upstream and here — this port mirrored the four
      maps it saw capped and inherited the omission. `TestEveryCappedMapIsActuallyPruned` is a
      ledger over all eight and fails naming the map that is missing.

      **THE CORPUS CANNOT SEE THE PRUNE, and that is why there is a Go test as well.** A churn case
      emits the same alerts whether the prune runs or not — the count is decided by the second
      payload either way — so `prune-never-runs` survives every corpus case. The map is the
      observable. Eight mutations, all killed, including the one the corpus DOES catch: NetWatch
      records its key BEFORE the `unknown` skip, because a host mid-reprobe is still live and pruning
      it throws away the state its next reading is compared against.

      `ifaceStateMapOverflows` (501 alerts from 501 live interfaces) and `ifaceStateMapJustUnderTheCap`
      (500 from 500) are a deliberate PAIR: restoring the old `clear()` fails the 501 case while the
      500 still passes, which is what says the 501 case measures the boundary and not something
      incidental. Both flipped when `07da9a9` landed, which was expected — they were written to.

      **AND A REAL DIVERGENCE THE BGP FAMILY EXPOSED: `emit` did not write to the store.** The test
      recorded open rows itself once an event had returned, which made the dedup guard blind to an
      alert fired EARLIER IN THE SAME EVENT. That is invisible for every other family — they fire at
      most one alert per subject per event — but `routing:update` carries every peer at once, and two
      peers sharing a name share an alert subject. `bgpTwoPeersOneName` found it. `Store` gained
      `Record` and `emit` calls it inline, as the live `fire` does; there is no production caller yet
      (see the alerter blocker), so this would have landed as a defect at cutover rather than now.

      **THREE UPSTREAM FIXES LANDED IN THE SAME TICK, and two of my own assertions are what caught
      them.** The live session fixed `ToDo.md` §5, §6 and §7 (commits `02df614`, `c8f87f3`,
      `b3ffec0`, local and unpushed). Both corpora that pinned the old behaviour FAILED on
      regeneration, naming the file to reread — which is exactly why those assertions were written to
      fail on a change rather than to record whatever they saw.

      * **§6 — a null name.** `aNullNameBecomesTheStringNull` is now `aNullNameIsRefused` in BOTH
        parsers; `jsName`/`jsString` became the loose `== null`. See the sites entry above.
      * **§7 — a later RouterOS release.** Fixed by SUPERSEDE, not by versioning the subject — the
        recovery resolves on `(routeros_update, "")`, so a versioned subject would match nothing and
        leave every update alert open for ever. The alert key and the resolution key are the same key.
        **AND THE TRAP: `prevUpdateVersion` is in-memory, so a REBUILT EVALUATOR STARTS EMPTY** and
        superseding unconditionally would resolve and re-file the operator's acknowledged alert on
        every restart. `supersede` is set only when an earlier version was actually observed.

        That trap is only visible against a store that ALREADY HOLDS THE ROW, which nothing in the
        corpus did — every case started empty, so a first announcement found nothing open and whether
        it would have superseded was never asked. `aFirstAnnouncementDoesNotSupersede` recorded the
        right answer for the wrong reason. The corpus gained `openAlerts` to model a restart, and
        `aRestartMeetingAnOpenUpdateAlert` (0 events — the guard stands, and `fire` returns without
        re-filing) plus `aRestartThenTwoReleases` (2) kill both survivors.

      **Part 13 DONE: THIRTEEN alert toggles the port never set.** No alert-type or interface-type

- [x] **DECIDED 2026-08-25 — a PDF dependency.** *(This entry stayed open after the decision was
      made and acted on; corrected 2026-08-29.)*

      The operator chose `github.com/go-pdf/fpdf` — MIT, pure Go, no cgo, the maintained fork of the
      archived `jung-kurt/gofpdf`. It is in `go.mod` and `internal/reportpdf` is built on it.

      It earned the fifth slot on a property MEASURED BEFORE IT WAS CHOSEN: its Helvetica metrics
      ARE pdfkit's — both take the Adobe standard-14 AFM widths and agree to 2e-13 pt across 792
      measurements. That is what decides whether the port can reproduce a document in which almost
      every x is a function of a measured string. Two things it does NOT do are pinned rather than
      discovered later: it does not kern (worst real-report position error 0.65pt, 0.23mm, on a
      CENTRED title; every right-aligned element measured exactly zero), and it walks BYTES against
      a cp1252 table, so `reportpdf.EncodeText` is mandatory on every draw AND every measurement.

      The original question, preserved:

      > `pdf.js` is built on `pdfkit`; a Go equivalent needs a PDF library, which would be the FIFTH
      dependency in a project that justifies each of its four individually. Needed for send-now AND
      for the export buttons below. Not taken unilaterally.

      thresholds, `> 90` and `> 75`, in two independent ternaries, both `>` and not `>=`: 75 is not
      warn and 90 is not crit, and the natural `>=` is wrong on two inputs in a hundred. **A
