      a `||` in the pattern, so `sed` errored and the file was untouched. Re-run through a script
      that asserts the target line exists before writing; it was caught. A mutation that does not
      apply reads exactly like a gate that does not react.

      since position is what a behavioural test through a fake cannot see.

      **`Flush` runs BEFORE the collectors stop**, and a mutant that moved it below them is
      killed. A bucket only rolls over when the next minute's first sample arrives, so after the
      stops nothing can roll it and the last minute of every session is lost — which looks like a
      quiet minute on the chart, not like an error.

      renderers on the Interfaces page build NODES, not markup strings: the list AND the tile grid

      wrong invisibly. So those two renderers, and probably the Firewall table, cannot be compared
      as things stand.

- [ ] **TODO — turning the Go backup scheduler ON is a CUTOVER step, not a porting one.**
      **ITS CONSTRUCTOR NOW EXISTS, 2026-08-29 — which was the last piece of cutover step 0.**
      `internal/server/backup_scheduler.go` builds it from `SchedDeps`, `-backup-scheduler`
      gates it and DEFAULTS FALSE, and `buildBackupScheduler(false)` returns nil. Nine mutants,
      nine killed; two of them survived their first pass and both were gaps in the TESTS rather
      than equivalent mutants — the flag test passed only because `auditDB` was nil (so the
      second guard fired and the test could not tell which one had), and the unknown-router test
      passed vacuously because no fixture router had a backup password set. Both fixtures were
      strengthened until the mutants died.

      **The design decision worth keeping: `Queue` is `Manager.Acquire` → `InWriteQueue` →
      `Release`.** `Acquire` is REF-COUNTED, so a router a browser has open returns THE SAME
      session and the backup genuinely serialises against that page's writes — which is the
      property the live comment demands ("a backup and a firewall edit on one router are not
      independent"). A bespoke connection would have been cheaper and would have silently lost it.

      **AND IT FOUND A REAL PRE-EXISTING BUG, which is the part worth reading.** `Manager.Release`
      stopped FIVE of the fourteen collectors the connect block starts. The other nine did not
      stop on their own: `pollLoop` is a self-rescheduling `time.Timer` that arms the next tick
      from inside the current one and never consults the session, so a released session kept nine
      timers alive FOREVER — each waking every 1–60s to read through a client that had just been
      closed, for every router ever acquired. It was invisible precisely because it was
      survivable: the reads fail quietly and nobody is listening to the payloads. The scheduler
      is the first caller that acquires and releases routers NOBODY IS WATCHING, on a timer, so it
      would have been the first thing to make it unbounded. Fixed, and pinned by
      `TestReleaseStopsEveryCollectorTheConnectBlockStarted`, which counts BOTH lists out of
      `session.go` and names the difference; a separate test holds the count at 14, since the
      first would stay green if a Start and its Stop were deleted together. 4 mutants, 4 killed.

      **THE SAME LENS FOUND A SECOND, USER-VISIBLE BUG ON 2026-08-29.** `session.go` holds THREE
      list pairs that must agree, and the third was also wrong: `packages` and `routing` are
      `Suspend()`ed on the disconnect path and were resumed by NOTHING on reconnect. After a
      router came back they stayed off until somebody focused their page — so a viewer already
      sitting on Routing or Packages watched a page that never updated again. Reconnects are not
      random: the usual cause is a RouterOS upgrade, which is exactly when an operator is
      watching. **The live app gets this right** — `ros.on('connected')` ends with
      `_updateAllPageStreams(session, entry)`, "restore page-aware streams for any pages still
      open after the reconnect" (`src/index.js:685`) — so this was a PORT defect, not a live one,
      and nothing goes in `../MikroDash/ToDo.md`.

      They were the only two page-gated collectors left out of the reconnect list; ten others
      (ppp, vpn, rosusers, queues, wifi, capsman, topology, wireless, bandwidth, conns) were
      already resumed unconditionally, which is what makes it an oversight rather than a policy.
      Fixed with `packages.Reconnected()` and `routing.Resume()` — different verbs deliberately:
      `Reconnected` belongs to collectors holding an absent-menu latch a reboot can invalidate,
      and Routing holds no such verdict. Pinned by
      `TestEverythingSuspendedOnDisconnectIsResumedOnReconnect` as a SUBSET (suspended ⊆ resumed),
      because netwatch/talkers/ping are resumed without being suspended and asserting equality
      would force a change that fixes nothing. 7 mutants: 5 killed, 2 recorded equivalent.

      Everything else needed already existed (`internal/backups/scheduler.go`, `RecordBackup`,
      `PruneFor`, `Run`). It remains OFF in `cmd/mikrodash`, because **the Node app is
      already scheduling backups against this fleet** — its runs are in the live /data, most
      recently 06:03 on 2026-08-23. Two schedulers on one router means two processes running
      `/export` and `/system/backup/save` on the same device, competing for flash on hardware
      whose documented limit is concurrent API channels, and two rows per run in a shared
      `config_backups`. There is no shared lock and there should not be one. Safe sequence:
      Node's scheduler OFF, then the Go one ON.

      **THE ROUTE'S SECURITY PROPERTY IS THE STORED-PASSWORD REUSE, NOT THE DIAL.** The live comment
      calls it a credential oracle if the lookup is by id alone: submit a stored id with an
      attacker-chosen host and the server posts the saved password to it. So the secret is reused
      only when `routers.SameEndpoint` matches, and being a global administrator gates the route and
      is explicitly not sufficient. Ten route mutations; the ones that matter are dropping the match
      (the oracle), decrypting before the match, and treating the mask as a real password.

      One deliberate departure from the live mechanism, same observable: `Routers.loadAll()` decrypts
      every password eagerly when it fills its cache, so the plaintext is in hand before the
      comparison happens there. This port decrypts only AFTER the match. `TestTheDialAndTheMatchUseOneCoercion`
      pins the other half — the dial config is built from the SAME coerced struct the match was
      given, because independent coercions could approve one destination and dial another, silently.

      **THE CLASSIFIER HAD NEVER BEEN EXECUTED BY EITHER REPOSITORY** — it is inline in a route
      needing a live server stack, so both sides had only ever read it. Lifting it into a `vm` found
      two defects on the first run, both fixed upstream in f4ade9e and both FOLLOWED here rather than
      reproduced:

      1. The last branch read the RAW `body.tls` where every other decision used the coerced
         `testTls`. The two disagree in both directions, and either way the sentence named a
         RouterOS service the attempt had not used.
      2. RouterOS's own words for a rejected login, `invalid user name or password`, matched none of
         the six alternatives — so the commonest failure of the button showed the raw driver message.

      **The cause is one thing.** Both were a second copy of one decision drifting from the original;
      `classifyError.js` is canonical and its own header says it was extracted from inline precisely
      so it would be reachable everywhere. `tools/test-reason-cases.js` therefore carries a DRIFT
      LEDGER comparing the two alternative sets rather than three assertions about today's strings —
      pinning the rule, so it catches the NEXT divergence.

      `tlsInsecure: "false"` (2af8164) is followed the same way: `endpointInsecure` now accepts only
      the exact word `"true"`, and `same-endpoint-cases.js` gained cases proving the exactness from
      the other side, since widening it back to truthiness re-opens the defect.

      **AND THE SAME SHAPE ON THE DATABASE SIDE (Part 125) — tables nothing on the Go side writes.**
      *(Was "four tables"; `alert_events` left that set on 2026-08-29 when the evaluator was
      wired, and `report_runs` had already left it. The table below is the current count.)* The two processes share one SQLite file; today Node writes it and Go reads it, which
      is correct during coexistence. At cutover Node stops, and a table Go reads but never writes
      stops advancing.

      Verified by hand, per table (`grep "INSERT INTO x" internal/ --include=*.go | grep -v _test`):

      | table | Go writes | Go reads | Node writes |
      |---|---|---|---|
      | `traffic_samples` | 0 | 2 | 1 |
      | `bandwidth_usage` | 0 | 2 | 1 |
      | `ping_samples` | 0 | 1 | 1 |
      | `connectivity_events` | 0 | 1 | 1 |
      | `alert_events` | **1** | **1** | 1 |  ← Go writes AND reads these as of 2026-08-29
      | `report_runs` | **1** | 0 | 1 |

      **Re-measured 2026-08-28** (`grep "INSERT INTO <t>" internal/ --include=*.go | grep -v _test`).
      Five of the six are unchanged; `report_runs` gained a Go writer in
      `internal/db/schedule_write.go`.

      **Reports is the page this costs**, and it is SHIPPED and gated. It reads the first three
      through `internal/db/history.go` (832 lines). When the writers stop, Reports keeps rendering:
      the same window, then a shrinking one, then nothing. **Every DOM gate stays green the whole
      way down**, because the markup is right and there is simply less data behind it — the same
      shape as `/api/localcc` above.

      **THE WRITERS EXIST AND ARE CONSTRUCTED BY NOBODY — the same state as `routers.Pool`, and it
      belongs on the cutover list rather than in a table.** `internal/history` holds `Writer`
      (buckets per-second traffic and ping samples into the minute rows those three tables take) and
      `Connectivity` (whose `ConnEffect` carries both the rows to write and the `router:status` to
      emit). Both are complete and pinned; nothing calls `history.NewWriter()` outside the package.

      That is deliberate during coexistence — two processes bucketing the same samples into one
      SQLite file would double every row — and it means **wiring them is a CUTOVER STEP, in the same
      breath as stopping Node.** Not before, and not after: the gap between Node stopping and the Go
      writers starting is history nobody records, and Reports renders that as a shrinking window
      with every DOM gate still green.

      `alert_events` and `report_runs` are worse in one respect and better in another: Go does not
      read them either yet, so nothing degrades visibly — but the Alerts tab and the schedule list's
      "last run" column are both rendered by the port already, against Node's rows.

      **NOT turned into an audit, deliberately.** I built one and deleted it: three attempts at
      detecting "reads but does not write" all reported English words from comments as table names
      (`guard`, `there`, `this`), because SQL keywords appear in prose about SQL. A checker that
      invents work gets ignored, and I would rather record a hand-verified table than ship a
      detector I could not get right — the same call as the Connections wiring gate in Part 120.

- 2026-08-25 — **The alerter's four PRESENTATION decisions ported (`internal/alert`). The evaluator
  and the delivery are not.**

  `alerter.js` is 692 lines of per-router state, cooldown maps and sending. Four of its functions
  hold none of that: the template renderer, the interface classifier, its settings-key map, and the
  label a stored alert type is shown under. Only `labelFor` is exported, so the other three are
  lifted by source — and the module cannot be `require`d on the host anyway, since it reaches
  `db.js`.

  **ABSENT AND NULL RENDER DIFFERENTLY, and that reaches an operator's screen.** The live guard is
  `vars[k] === undefined`, so a missing variable renders EMPTY while one present holding null renders
  the WORD "null". Reproduced deliberately; collapsing them would quietly change what a template with
  a nulled variable says. Asserted directly as well as through the corpus, because JSON cannot carry
  an `undefined` and a missing key distinctly.

  **The cap counts what SURVIVES the control-character strip**, not what arrived — 300 "x\n" pairs
  yield 200 characters of `x`, not 100. Cutting first kills 4 cases.

  **"unknown" FALLS THROUGH, an unrecognised type does not.** A type of `unknown` or none drops to
  name detection; a real but unmapped type (`pppoe`) is "other" and never reaches the name rules.
  Getting that backwards classifies a pppoe interface called `ether-wan` as an ether.

  **The name rules are ORDERED, and I got it wrong first.** I asserted `ether1.10` was a vlan; it is
  an ETHER, because `/^ether/` is tested before the dotted-suffix pattern — so the vlan rule only
  ever sees names starting with none of the earlier prefixes. The corpus refused my assertion, and it
  now carries both a dotted ether AND a dotted name that genuinely reaches the vlan rule. Reordering
  kills 4.

  Six mutations, six killed. 19 renders, 20 interfaces, 14 labels.

  **What remains unported in `alerter.js` is the evaluator, the cooldown and the delivery** — state
  and I/O. The notification bell that `wiring-audit` records as blocked needs the ALERT FEED, which
  is a database read, not these.

- 2026-08-25 — **The per-user notification config's two decisions ported (`internal/notify`), one of
  which is a SECURITY BOUNDARY.**

  `_pick` and `_withInstallMail` are module-private, so both are lifted by source. The rest of
  `userNotify.js` is database reads and decryption.

  **`_pick` IS AN ALLOWLIST and its comment says why**: "a blob written by a newer version (or
  hand-edited) cannot inject fields into what reaches notifier". The blob is a database row and the
  destination decides where to send by inspecting FIELD NAMES — so an injected `smtpHost` points one
  user's alerts at a server of somebody else's choosing, and an injected `smtpTo` redirects them
  outright. Removing the allowlist kills 6 of 18 cases, and there is a direct assertion beside the
  corpus because a corpus can be regenerated into agreement with a broken implementation.

  **The RECIPIENT is the user.** Everything else in the folded config comes from the install;
  `smtpTo` comes from the user's `emailTo`. Taking it from the install instead — the natural slip,
  since every neighbouring field does — sends every user's alerts to the administrator. It kills 4.

  **A half-configured install resolves to NOTHING**, which is the same cooldown-consuming state
  `Channels` refuses. The two are now tested together, end to end, because that pair is what a
  recipient record actually passes through.

  **`undefined` HAS NO GO EQUIVALENT, and the corpus caught it.** The live code assigns every install
  field unconditionally, so a missing one becomes `undefined` — invisible to `JSON.stringify`, so it
  never reaches a stored record. A Go map has no undefined: writing the key leaves it PRESENT holding
  nil, which a consumer testing presence reads as "configured, blank". Only the fields the install
  actually has are copied now.

  **The generator lifts the three field tables rather than typing them**, so a field added upstream
  cannot leave the corpus quietly passing — and it means the module never has to be `require`d, which
  matters because it pulls in `db.js` and `better-sqlite3` is not on the host.

  Six mutations, six killed.

  **A LIVE COMMENT SLIGHTLY OVERSTATED ITS OWN RULE, and the mutation showed it.** It says 6GHz "is
  checked first" because its numbering overlaps 5GHz's. The NUMBERING does overlap; the FREQUENCY

  separate BASE — using 5000 for a 6GHz frequency kills a case at once. The order is kept because it

- 2026-08-25 — **The notifier's two PURE decisions ported (`internal/notify`). Its transports are
  not, and that line is deliberate.**

  `hasConfiguredChannel`, which is exported, and `_reason`, which is not — so it is LIFTED by source,
  the way the gate tooling lifts a renderer. Telegram, Pushbullet, SMTP and ntfy are outbound I/O and

  **"Is any channel active?" is ONE question, and the live comment says why.** The alerter used to
  ask it from the `*Enabled` flags ALONE while `send()` checked flags PLUS credentials, so a channel

  **`_reason` has four outcomes, not two, because the `try` covers the PROPERTY ACCESS as well as
  the parse.** The corpus found both of the ones a reading misses:

  - `'"just a string"'` is valid JSON. It parses, `.description` is undefined, and the result is
    EMPTY — not the raw text. Decoding into a `map[string]any` fails there and quotes the body back
    at the operator.
  - `'null'` parses too, and then `null.description` THROWS — landing in the same catch as a parse
    failure, so the answer IS the raw text. So `null` and a JSON string, which look alike, go
    opposite ways.

  **A mutation found a corpus gap rather than a code fault.** Swapping "collapse whitespace, then
  cut at 160" for the reverse survived: every long case had no whitespace and every whitespace case
  was short, so nothing observed the ORDER. A case that is both now exists and the mutation dies.

  Six mutations, six killed. 20 reason bodies, 18 channel shapes.

  **A finding for the Send-now blocker**: its cost was recorded as needing "an SMTP mailer AND the
  report builder", and Go's `net/smtp` is STDLIB — so the mailer is not a dependency decision the way

  smaller than the PDF one, and the two should not be assumed to be the same shape.

- 2026-08-25 — **`cityIndex.js` ported (`internal/geo/cityindex.go`) — the gazetteer PLAN.md names
  as a risk. Smaller than it looked, because the binary reader was already here.**

  `PLAN.md` flags this module because it "reimplements the MaxMind binary record reader". It does —
  but `internal/geo` already reads the SAME two files with the same record geometry, so what was
  actually missing was the half geoip-lite gives no API for: ENUMERATING places and ranking them.

  **The ranking is the contract**: an exact match first; then WEIGHT descending — the number of
  address ranges pointing at a place, the only popularity signal this data carries; then the shorter
  name; then the country code.

  **TIES BEYOND THOSE FOUR KEEP INSERTION ORDER, and that needed `sort.SliceStable`.** JavaScript's
  sort is stable; `sort.Slice` is not. This was flagged as a suspicion while writing and then
  MEASURED: swapping to `sort.Slice` breaks 4 of the 28 queries. Real data ties on all four keys
  often enough that it is not theoretical.

  **The limit rules read as though 0 and -3 behave alike. They do not.**
  `Math.min(Math.max(parseInt(limit,10) || 20, 1), 50)`: zero is FALSY, so asking for none returns
  the DEFAULT of 20, while -3 parses truthy and is clamped up to 1. Measured from the corpus, not
  derived from the expression — `limit=0` returns 20 hits and `limit=-3` returns 1.

  **Two build rules a reading would miss**: coordinates come from the FIRST range seen for a
  location, not the last (the scanner returns early once `seen`); and location ids sharing a
  (name, region, cc) triple are collapsed with their weights SUMMED but the FIRST row's coordinates
  kept. Both mutations die — the first breaks 22 of 28.

  **NOTHING ASSERTS A RECORD COUNT.** The live header forbids it: counts "change with every
  geoip-lite data refresh". The corpus records ANSWERS TO QUERIES, `minRows` is a floor against a
  format change rather than an expected size, and the generator says plainly that a data refresh is
  drift to regenerate rather than a port defect.

  Six mutations, six killed. 28 queries.

  **NOT WIRED**: `/api/cities` stays on the proxied ledger. The gazetteer is the part worth having
  early — it is what `PLAN.md` called the risk, and it is now measured rather than feared.

- 2026-08-25 — **`topologyLayout.js` ported (`internal/topology`) — a validator whose whole point is
  that untrusted strings become KEYS IN A FILE, and a rounding rule no reading would have got right.**

  Found by asking which live `src/*.js` have no Go counterpart: `cityIndex`, `notifier`,
  `topologyLayout` and `wifiScan`. This was the smallest at 54 lines, and the most security-shaped —
  its own header says it was split out of `index.js` "purely so it can be unit-tested: this is the one
  place where caller-supplied strings become OBJECT KEYS in a file written to disk".

  **REJECTION IS TOTAL, and that is the rule worth having.** One banned key, one malformed key, one
  non-finite coordinate, and the whole map is refused — null meaning 400, NOT "no positions". A port
  that skipped the bad entry would persist a partial layout and report success, leaving an operator
  with a half-rearranged map and nothing to explain it. The mutation that skips instead of refusing
  kills 12 of 39 cases.

  **TWO BUGS FOUND BY THE CORPUS, ONE IN MY GENERATOR AND ONE IN MY PORT.**

  1. `{ __proto__: … }` in an object literal SETS THE PROTOTYPE rather than creating a key, so my
     case serialised to `{}` and recorded the live module refusing an EMPTY MAP — which it does not.
     The case is built with `JSON.parse` now, which creates a real own property and is also how the
     value actually arrives: as a parsed request body. The generator asserts the serialised input
     still contains `__proto__`, so the case cannot silently become a test of `{}` again.

  2. `Number(x.toFixed(1))` IS NOT Go's `%.1f`, and it is not `math.Round(x*10)/10` either. The
     multiplication is the trap: `0.15 * 10` rounds to exactly 1.5 in binary and goes UP to 0.2,
     while JavaScript reads the exact stored value (0.1499999…) and gives 0.1. The corpus caught it
     because it carries halfway values on purpose. `big.Rat` takes the exact double and makes the
     halfway decision on it — half away from zero — so 0.15 rounds down, 0.25 up, 0.05 up. A
     coordinate differing in the first decimal moves a node on the map.

  **Negative zero is normalised.** `-0.04` rounds to `-0`, which Go marshals as `-0` where
  `JSON.stringify(-0)` is `0`. Same number, different bytes in a file the Node app reads back.

  Five mutations, five killed. 39 cases, 22 of them refusals.

  **NOT WIRED**: `/api/topology-layout` is still proxied and stays on that ledger — the validator is
  the part worth having early, because it is the part a handler would be tempted to write inline.

- 2026-08-25 — **`GET /api/collectors` served in Go — and an honest correction about what that
  actually buys.**

  The endpoint was on `endpoint-audit`'s proxied list with a precise cost: without it "the dialog
  offers an EMPTY list rather than an error, so the operator sees a router with no collectors to
  choose from and no way to tell that is wrong." It became servable when #105 landed — the live route
  is three lines over the SAME registry this port now embeds, so the handler is a projection of
  generated data rather than a second source of truth.

  `label` was added to the generated tables for it, because the route sends it and typing the live
  app's own wording here is exactly what the embedded registry exists to avoid.

  **Pinned against the live route's expression, not my reading of it.** The generator now emits
  `apiCollectors` by running the original's own `.filter(disableable).map({key,label,requires})`, and
  the Go test compares the handler's payload against that.

  **A dead guard, found by a mutation that killed nothing.** The handler had `if req == nil` because
  the live route says `c.requires || []`. It cannot fire: the generator emits
  `(c.requires || []).slice()`, so every row carries an array and JSON `[]` decodes non-nil. Removed
  — unreachable defensive code reads as a hazard that exists — and the invariant asserted in the
  GENERATOR, where it can actually fail.

  **`endpoint-audit` could not see its own new route**, because it resolved only `name = "/literal"`
  consts and the path is `Prefix + "/api/collectors"`. `auditPrefix`, `reportsPrefix` and
  `principalsPrefix` have always had that shape; nothing called them from a ported page, so nothing
  noticed. It resolves chains now.

- 2026-08-25 — **#117's write-path privilege rule, ported AHEAD of the handler that needs it — with
  a tripwire so it cannot be forgotten.**

  The live `PUT /api/routers/:id` drops `siteIds` and `siteId` for anyone without
  `system:principals`. Its own comment explains why the route's normal gate is not enough: it is
  `router:manage` on the TARGET, which Devices-page write access confers and which is not
  global-only. Before #117 that let a non-administrator MOVE a device between sites — an escalation,
  but self-limiting and LOUD, because the device vanished from the old site's users. Many-to-many
  made it purely ADDITIVE: a repeatable, invisible way to inject a device into any scope, with every
  site id enumerable from an ungated `GET /api/sites`.

  **The mirror is an injection path too.** The rule deletes BOTH keys. `siteId` is the scalar the
  store keeps in step with the first entry, so dropping only `siteIds` leaves the whole escalation
  open through the older field. That is the first mutation, and it dies.

  **The fields are DROPPED, not the request refused** — the rest of the edit is legitimate and the
  original applies it. A refusal would also tell the caller which fields are privileged, which the
  live route does not.

  **This port has NO router write endpoint**, so the rule has no caller. That is precisely the
  dangerous state: a privilege check that exists, looks done, and whose handler does not yet exist to
  forget it. Ported now for the reason `portedGuards` gives — a check that must be REMEMBERED at the
  call site is the kind that gets forgotten.

  **`TestARouterWriteRouteMustStripPrivilegedFields` fails in BOTH directions.** With no route it
  passes and records that state; register any `PUT|POST|PATCH|DELETE …routers…` and it fails until
  something calls the strip. It also fails if the strip gains a caller while no route exists, which
  would mean its premise had changed. PROVEN by planting a route and watching it fail with a message
  naming the escalation — a tripwire that cannot fire is not a tripwire.

  Four mutations killed: dropping only `siteIds`, stripping nothing, stripping from administrators
  too, and reporting a key without deleting it.

  stranger, and that is exactly why it would have lasted: an operator told "no access" blames their

  router was in at most one site.

  normaliser, and the mutation that makes an empty `siteIds` fall through to the scalar mirror

  write-path privilege rule and its own unit.

  2. **`siteId`/`siteName` are backward-compatible MIRRORS of the FIRST entry**, and the geo tier

- 2026-08-25 — **`collectionFingerprint` ported — work found by asking which live files are NOT
  being edited, during the upstream rename.**

  The rename (#117) is still in flight and three gates are red for it, so porting from `app.js`,
  `index.html` or `index.js` would be reading a moving target. `src/collection.js` has not been
  touched since 2026-08-20, and `collectionFingerprint` was unported — `session.go`'s own comment
  already pointed at it as the thing that decides whether a router edit needs a session rebuild.

  A rebuild is a RECONNECT, so the fingerprint is what lets a label-only edit cost nothing.

  **It folds in six fields that are not part of `collection`** — `defaultIf` and `pingTarget` from
  the record, `topN`, `topTalkersN`, `maxConns` and `historyMinutes` from settings. None changes what
  `Resolve` returns and all change how a session is built, so two routers that resolve identically
  can still need different sessions. The corpus asserts exactly that: the `topN` case resolves
  identically to the default and must fingerprint differently.

  **The two groups coerce differently, and it is not a typo.** The record fields are `rec[k] || ''`,
  so `0` and `""` both render empty; the settings are `cfg[k] === undefined ? '' : cfg[k]`, so a `0`
  renders as `0`. A port spelling both the same way agrees on every value except zero — and zero is
  a real setting for `topN`. Both directions are pinned by cases and both mutations die.

  41 cases now (up from 29), five mutations killed: each coercion swapped for the other, the settings
  extras dropped, the poll keys left unsorted, and a float rendered with a fraction (`1500` must not
  become `1500.0` — JavaScript's `n + ''` does not).

  **NOT WIRED**: nothing compares fingerprints yet, because nothing rebuilds a session on a router
  edit. That is the Routers/Settings write path, which is blocked on the operator's decisions.

  found by the same question, and the generic test that ends the sequence.**

  Asking "who else starts a collector" caught the page-focus resumes last tick. Asked again, it
  caught two more.

  **`Reconnected()` is not the latch-clearing no-op its name suggests.** Every implementation ends
  `Tick(); loop.start()`, so an ungated one RESTARTS a collector the operator turned off — and
  reconnects are routine, the usual cause being a router upgrade. 24 calls in the reconnect branch,
  all ungated. The live side gets this free: a disabled collector there is a null stub, so calling
  anything on it does nothing.

  **`RefreshNow()` is a single `Tick`, not a loop restart** — 17 sites across five files, run after a
  WRITE so the page shows what the router did. Gated for parity: the live null stub does nothing, so
  a disabled collector's page staying stale is the behaviour, and "you turned this off" is coherent.
  The PACKAGES path is gated at the refresh only, NOT at `pkgReady` — gating there would refuse a
  package action the original still performs.

  **The test is now generic, and that is the point.** Three bypasses in three ticks is a pattern, so
  `TestEveryCollectorEntryPointIsGated` matches ANY `cn.rsession.X().Y()` where Y begins work
  (`Start|Resume|Reconnected|RefreshNow|Tick`) and requires a guard — a fourth entry point added
  later is caught without anyone remembering to list it.

  **Both of my first attempts at that test were wrong, and the mutations said so.**
  It first searched the 120 bytes BEFORE each call for the word `CollectorEnabled`, so a bare call
  sitting just after somebody else's guarded block passed — the ungating mutation survived. Rewritten
  to join gated and ungated matches by OFFSET, it then reported three correctly-gated calls as
  ungated, because I recorded the METHOD group's offset and looked it up by the ACCESSOR's. Both
  fixed; both mutations now die. A test that reports the right answer for the wrong reason is the
  thing mutation checking exists to find.

  nothing on screen explains, and the operator's setting looks intermittent rather than ignored.
  Found by asking, after the connect path landed, WHO ELSE starts a collector — which is the same
  question `lifecycle_test.go` asks about netwatch's missing Start.

  `Session.CollectorEnabled(key)` is the accessor; an unknown key reads as ENABLED, matching the
  registry's own default for a collector nobody made disableable.

  one resume, and guarding one with a different collector's key.

  have STREAMED where the operator chose to POLL. That is the kind of silent difference this port
  exists to prevent, and it was one field away from shipping.

  **The block is held as RAW JSON, and that is a robustness decision.** `Routers()` unmarshals the
  whole file in one call, so a single type mismatch anywhere loses EVERY router. The block is
  operator-editable and the live side tolerates rubbish in it (`Array.isArray(coll.off) ? … : []`),
  so a strict `Off []string` would turn `"off": "wifi"` in a hand-edited file into a total failure to
  load the fleet where the original merely ignores the field. `collection.ParseRouter` decodes it
  leniently and NEVER fails — anything it cannot make sense of is dropped, and nil resolves to the
  fleet defaults.

  **The count test defended itself against my comment.** Every `Start()` keeps its literal shape
  because `TestTheBackgroundCollectorCountIsRecorded` counts them by regex — and writing that
  pattern out in a comment made it count FIFTEEN collectors, one named after the placeholder. Exactly
  what it is for.

  **Two new tests, because "every Start is guarded" and "the guard is fed the router's own config"
  are different claims.** The first reads the source and pins that no Start loses its guard, no
  guard names the wrong key, and no constructor reverts to a hard-coded interval — with three
  declared exemptions (`NewLogs`, `NewConnTable`, `NewTraffic`), each because it has no poll interval
  to resolve. The second drives `Acquire` against a real temp store whose `routers.json` turns `wan`
  off, and only that one catches a resolution built from `nil` — which the source-reading test
  cannot see.

  **My positive-property check was better than my negative one.** The first version asserted no
  constructor ends in `, 0)`, which flagged `NewTalkers(…, Poll["talkers"], 0)` whose final zero is
  `topN`. Matching on what must BE there beat matching on what must not.

  Four mutations, four killed: ungating a Start, reverting an interval to zero, gating a collector on
  the WRONG key, and ignoring the record's block.

  Surveying what still has buildable work turned this up: `session.Session` and `routers.Pool` both

  First, my believability check demanded 25 distinct resolutions from 29 cases and FAILED on correct

  routers.json naming a collector that does not exist must be ignored, not honoured. Replaced with an
  assertion of that contract — the malformed cases must EQUAL the default, and the discriminating
  ones must differ from it — which is a statement about the code rather than a threshold.

  that turning off `conns` disables exactly `bandwidth`.

  is ONE edge deep — `bandwidth` requires `conns` — so a single pass produces the same answer and a

  papered over with a synthetic registry: the corpus is generated from the REAL one, and inventing a
  deeper graph would be testing a fixture. The Go side keeps the loop because the original has it.

- 2026-08-25 — **Routers Part 5: the payload assembler (`internal/routers/assemble.go`). Every
  dependency Part 4 was waiting on is now met.**

  `BuildRow` maps one router's data to one row; `BuildStats` decides for every router WHICH data
  that is — the interactive session's if somebody has it open, the background pool's otherwise. That
  choice is the whole file, and it has one trap worth the reading.

  **AN INTERACTIVE SESSION WINS EVEN WHEN IT KNOWS NOTHING.** The original is
  `s ? s.system.lastPayload : (bg ? bg.systemPayload : null)` — the ternary tests whether a SESSION
  EXISTS, not whether it has a payload. So a router someone just opened reports nulls until its
  first poll lands, while the background pool may still hold good numbers from a second ago. That
  reads like a bug and is not one to fix here: the two are different connections to the same router,
  and a row that mixed them would show one connection's CPU beside another's uptime. Reproduced
  deliberately and pinned — the mutation that "improves" it dies.

  **`isActive` is PRESENCE, not reachability.** It marks the router somebody is looking at, so a
  session that exists and has not connected is still active. Deriving it from `Connected` is a
  separate mutation and also dies.

  **NIL `Visible` is not EMPTY `Visible`.** Nil means unrestricted; empty means the principal may
  read nothing. Getting them the same way round either shows a locked-down user the whole fleet or
  hides the fleet from an unrestricted one. Two tests, and the mutation kills both.

  Also pinned: disabled routers are absent from the payload rather than offline rows in it; the
  default-interface precedence is router → global setting → `ether1`, each tier separately mutated;
  order is preserved (the original does not sort); open alerts are independent of `connected`.

  Six mutations, six killed — after one "survivor" that was my shell escaping again (`\&\&` reached
  Python literally, so the injected Go did not compile and a grep for `^--- FAIL` counted zero).
  Injected from a heredoc instead, it dies. That is the third time this session a bad mutation has
  briefly read as coverage; the lesson is that a mutation must be shown to BUILD before its result
  means anything.

  **What is NOT here:** the auto-geo refresh, which is a WRITE and belongs to the handler that owns
  the store. `AutoGeoAction` is already ported and pure.

  **Routers is now: everything pure and pinned, nothing wired.** `BuildStats`, `BuildRow`,
  `SyncPool`, the pool's I/O, geoplace, the two db reads. What remains is a handler and the
  operator's coexistence decision — not more porting.

- 2026-08-25 — **The background pool's I/O half is built (`internal/routers/pool.go`). Cutover
  blocker 2 is now purely the operator's decision — there is no missing code behind it.**

  `overview.go` held the decisions; this holds the sockets. One connection per unwatched router,
  three collectors on it (system, ifStatus, dhcpLeases — not `Session`'s fourteen), payloads cached
  for `BuildRow`. **Constructed by nobody**, like `history.Bucketer`: the code is needed under every
  option including "wait for cutover", so building it pre-empts nothing.

  **What is simplified, and why it is not a stub.** The live builder resolves a per-router collection
  config (#105) and must not even CONSTRUCT a disabled collector, because eleven of the sixteen open
  their streams from the constructor. The port has no `resolveCollection` at all — `session.Session`
  passes `0` for every interval too — so this pool does what the rest of the port already does rather
  than inventing half of #105 here. There are no disabled collectors to stub until that lands.

  **Two things the live code gets from its driver that Go does not.** A `close` event: go-routeros
  has none, so the loop polls `Connected()` every 500 ms and re-dials on a drop — without it a
  session sits "connected" for ever and the page reads a stale payload as current. And an errno: the
  classifier ported last tick supplies the reason instead.

  **A mutation found a real design flaw.** `destroy()` waited on the session goroutine to exit. That
  reads as tidy and is wrong: the goroutine may be inside a dial, and a dial takes until the timeout,
  so `Sync` — called from the request path — would stall the Routers page for as long as an
  unreachable router takes to fail. The live `_stopSession` does not wait. Removed; what makes it
  safe is the `destroyed` flag, and reinstating the wait now HANGS the mid-dial test, which is the
  strongest evidence available that the flag is load-bearing.

  **And my own test was wrong before the code was.** The mid-dial teardown test failed on a
  connection that was never opened: the teardown won the race to the top of the connect loop, where
  `stop` is already closed and the session returns WITHOUT dialling — correct behaviour, different
  path. It now waits until the dial is actually in flight, which is the only way that guard is
  reached.

- 2026-08-25 — **`classifyRosError` ported (`internal/routeros/classify.go`) — the piece the
  background pool needs before it is worth building.**

  Returning to buildable work, the next brick under cutover blocker 2 is the pool's I/O half. Reading
  what it needs turned up a prerequisite: `OverviewSession.OnError(reason, classified)` was ported
  with a `classified` flag **that nothing could supply**. `safe.Message` sanitises but does not

  bare-"Offline" complaint issue #92 exists about. Building the pool on that would have been a stub
  in the shape of a feature.

  **The branches port; the matches cannot.** The live matcher reads NODE's error shapes — an
  `.errno` of `-111`, the literal `ECONNREFUSED`, a `RosException` name — and Go's errors carry none
  of them: a `net.OpError` says "connection refused", "no route to host", "i/o timeout". So this
  reproduces the CONDITION → REASON mapping, not the regexes. `tools/classify-error-cases.js`
  generates the corpus by RUNNING the live module and stores BOTH spellings per case; the Go test
  feeds Go's and expects the live's answer. A port that copied the live patterns literally would
  pass a test built from the live inputs and classify nothing in production.

  **Node's `RosException` is the port's `*Trap`** — both mean "the device answered" rather than "the
  socket failed", which is what that branch turns on. Node prints the driver's errno in brackets and
  a Trap has none, so the corpus generates those cases with `errno: ''` and neither side prints a
  bracket. Nothing is fabricated.

  hole.** M2 "swapped" the order by adding an alternative to the later branch (which changes

- 2026-08-25 — **`tools/iface-tiles-check.js` (gate 104): the tile grid, and the spark that is
  REPLACED rather than rewritten.**

  The second node-building renderer on the Interfaces page — the one `interfaces-page-check` found
  out about "three runs in" when it called `appendChild`. With the list closed, the same tool closes
  this. `interfaces-page-check`'s header now records both as done and names the VIEW SWITCH as what
  remains.

  **Four promises, none of them visible to markup.** The grid ships holding a "Waiting…"
  placeholder, and the FIRST tile created clears it — a poll carrying no interfaces must not. An
  existing tile is never rebuilt: its class, dot, spark, address line and rate rows are each written
  individually, which is what stops the rate bars flashing every second. The address line is NEVER
  removed — an interface without an address keeps a U+00A0 placeholder, because dropping the line
  makes the tile a line shorter than its neighbours and the whole row comes up short. And unlike the
  list, the grid NEVER re-appends: tiles sit in creation order forever, so a reversed payload does
  not move them. That last one looks like an omission and is the design, so it is pinned.

  **The spark is the interesting part.** It is REPLACED, not rewritten: the new SVG is parsed into a
  throwaway div and `replaceChild`d over the old one, so that ONE child gets a new identity while the
  tile around it keeps its own. Nothing else in this port does that, and the picture after a replace
  is identical to the picture after an in-place rewrite. The gate reports a verdict for the tile AND
  for its spark child, from separate serial deltas.

  **Writing that assertion taught me the code takes TWO paths, not one.** `ifaceSparkSvg` returns ''
  until the history holds two points, so a tile has no spark after its first poll: the SECOND poll
  INSERTS one (`insertAdjacentHTML('afterbegin')`, no old node to replace) and only the THIRD
  replaces it. My first assertion demanded 'replaced' on the frame that inserts and failed —
  correctly. Both transitions are now asserted, and the spark case runs four polls so a replace
  following a replace is covered too.

  **Seven mutations killed, ONE genuinely equivalent and recorded as such.** Rewriting
  `replaceChild(fresh, old)` as `old.remove(); insertAdjacentHTML('afterbegin', …)` gives the spark a
  new node either way, and because the spark IS the first child it lands in the same place. No
  observable difference, here or in a browser. It is kept in the header because it stops being
  equivalent the moment the spark is not first.

  **One asymmetry had to be repaired rather than hidden.** The port's mount stamps `data-size` on the
  grid; this gate lifts the live HANDLER and not its mount, so all 26 sequences differed by that one
  attribute. The live side now replicates it — set on the LIVE side only, deliberately, because
  seeding both grids would also have hidden the port DROPPING it.

  **A real bug in `tree-shim`'s matcher, found by this renderer.** `.iface-tile[data-iface]` combines
  a CLASS and an ATTRIBUTE, and the matcher handled a tag plus one trailing part — so it read the
  whole string as a class name, matched nothing, and every frame would have looked like a first frame.
  It now parses an optional tag plus any number of `.class` / `[attr]` parts. `replaceChild` and
  `insertAdjacentHTML` were added too, the latter throwing on a position it does not model rather
  than silently dropping the insert.

  Coverage 385 → **386 of 406**; `pages/interfaces` 3 → 2, and the view switch is the last unit there.

- 2026-08-25 — **`tools/iface-list-check.js` (gate 103): the first gate here that compares NODE
  REUSE across frames — and the deferred decision it closes.**

  `interfaces-page-check`'s header recorded the gap in as many words: both big renderers on the
  Interfaces page build NODES, `dom-shim` stores markup as a STRING, and emulating identity on top of
  a string "would produce a harness sophisticated enough to be wrong in ways nobody could see — worse
  than an honest gap." It then said the fix was WRITTEN UP rather than taken, because it looked like
  it needed a dependency. It did not: `tree-shim` is that fix, built here, and this is the gate it was
  blocking. Its header now says RESOLVED, kept rather than deleted, because the reasoning is what
  produced the fix.

  **`renderIfaceList` promises three things a string cannot hold.** A row whose fingerprint is
  unchanged is left ALONE — same node, untouched — which is what keeps text selection and hover alive
  while most interfaces sit idle. A row whose data changed is rewritten IN PLACE, keeping its node.
  And because rows are reused in place, DOM order does not follow the sorted array by itself, so both
  sides re-append every row — which MOVES it — but only when the order key changed. A single-frame
  gate can see none of the three: with nothing before it, every row is new. So every case is a
  SEQUENCE, compared on picture, per-row identity verdict and move count.

  **MOVE COUNTS close a gap recorded when `sankey-check` was written.** `appendChild` on a node
  already in the tree moves it, and the picture after a move is identical to the picture without one
  when the order already matched — so "re-append every tick" and "re-append only when the order
  changed" draw the same table and differ only in churn. That was logged as an equivalent mutant.
  This gate counts moves by wrapping the tbody's `appendChild`, and the mutant now dies 10/24.

  **The believability block earned its place immediately.** The first version passed 23 sequences —
  against an EMPTY tbody on both sides. The handler renders the list only `if (_ifaceView === 'list')`

  assertion that the LIVE side alone must show reuse, a fresh rebuild after the empty state, and a
  non-zero move count on a reorder caught it. Two more preamble omissions followed from fixing it
  (`IFL_COLS` and `_iflSort`, both lifted whole rather than retyped).

  **Six mutations, six kills — with two recorded honestly rather than counted.** Dropping a field
  from the fingerprint kills 22/24, but that is CHEAP: the fingerprint is stored as `data-fp`, so it
  is in the picture and any change to it differs immediately. It is not evidence the reuse logic is
  checked. And removing the fingerprint reuse entirely was expected to be EQUIVALENT — the row is
  rewritten in place with the same values and keeps its node — but it dies 1/24, because `comment` is
  deliberately not in the fingerprint, so a reused row keeps its old `title` while a rewritten one

- 2026-08-25 — **`tools/lib/tree-shim.js`: a shim that models node IDENTITY, extracted rather than
  invented — and the reason the cheap route to closing `connections-lists-page-check` is unavailable.**

  Adopting ToDo #18's fix needs a way to compare a renderer that KEEPS its rows. I went looking for
  the shortcut first — serialise the live's built nodes back to markup and keep the existing string
  comparison — and `dom-shim`'s own header rules it out in as many words: its `createElement` and
  `appendChild` exist so a node-building renderer "runs to completion", they "do NOT model node
  identity", and "anything built that way must NOT be COMPARED — only allowed to happen." That is
  the right rule. Taking the shortcut would have compared the shim's approximation and called it the
  page.

  So the recorder `sankey-check` grew this morning is now `tools/lib/tree-shim.js`, and that gate
  uses it — 21 cases still identical, three mutations still killed, which is the migration's proof.
  It records tag, attributes in insertion order, className, dataset, style, text, children, and a
  per-node SERIAL. `insertBefore` MOVES a node, `innerHTML = ''` detaches its children, and
  `querySelector` / `closest` / `contains` walk the real tree.

  **The serial is the point, and it is off by default here.** Two renders producing identical markup
  are not the same thing if the second threw the first's nodes away — the first keeps hover, focus
  and listeners. That difference is invisible to every markup comparison in this repo and is exactly
  what #18 is about. A gate comparing two implementations at ONE instant wants serials off; a gate
  comparing one implementation across two FRAMES wants them on, and that is how "did the redraw reuse
  the row" becomes a question you can ask at all.

  **The port's defect is confirmed rather than assumed.** `connections.ts:130` assigns
  `innerHTML = countryListHTML(...)` wholesale and then re-binds a click listener PER ROW on every
  tick — both halves of what #18 describes. The live app has fixed both.

  What remains, in order: the port adopts build-and-sync (`countryRowEl` + `syncCountryRow` + a
  reconcile loop, mirroring `_ccRowEl` / `_ccRowSync`), then `connections-lists-page-check` moves onto
  this shim. Note the markup CHANGES when it does: the live skeleton always carries `.conn-map-spark`
  and `.svc-sub-rows` and HIDES them when empty, where the port's string omits them — hidden rather
  than absent, because the parent is a flex row with a gap and `.svc-sub-rows` carries a margin.

- 2026-08-25 — **CAPsMAN's configuration card was never lifted, so a third of the page had no gate —
  and reaching it took four separate harness repairs, each of which had made a mutation survive.**

  `capsman-page-check` lifted the PAGE IIFE. CAPsMAN is built from two blocks, and the configuration
  card — five tabs over five tables — is the other one. `capsCfgTabBar`, `capsCfgNote` and
  `capsAddSlot` were reported uncovered because nothing had read the region they live in.

  **Why the card matters more than a tab strip.** Switching tabs re-points the ADD SLOT at the
  resource the visible table belongs to and announces `mikrodash:resmount`. A switch that forgot it
  leaves Add creating the PREVIOUS tab's resource — pressing it on Security would make a provisioning
  rule. That is the same failure the resmount listener fixed page-wide earlier today, and this is the
  page that generates it.

  **Four repairs, each found by a surviving mutation rather than by reading:**

  1. The card's own guard is `if (!bar) return;`. Evaluated unwrapped that is an illegal return, and
     the whole block fails to PARSE rather than to run.
  2. The page and the card both subscribe `capsman:update`, and the runner's `handlers[ev] = fn` kept
     the last one — so lifting the card silently unsubscribed the page and its summary counters went
     blank. `live-renderer.js` records this identical trap for this identical page; a list per event
     now, and the gate asserts BOTH subscribed.
  3. The card names its elements three ways — `getElementById` for the bar, its own `el(...)` helper
     for the rest. Reading two spellings found ONE id, so the Add slot and the CAP note were absent
     from the document and every mutation to them compared `null` against `null`.
  4. It announces through `new CustomEvent`, which the live context did not have.

  Eight mutations killed: the Add slot keeping the previous tab's resource, always saying
  provisioning, an unknown tab accepted, the panels never hidden, all panels shown, the lit button
  frozen, `aria-selected` inverted, and the CAP note — "This router is a CAP — these are set on its
  manager" — never shown, or shown to a manager. That note exists so five empty tables do not read as
  a failure.

  Coverage 92% → 93%.

- 2026-08-25 — **`attachMapZoom` is not driven by anything, and it is 170 lines of arithmetic rather
  than browser work.** The largest ungated mechanism found by following the wiring-contract pattern.

  I went looking for other gates with the `map-fs-check` shape — a function driven with synthetic
  nodes whose page wiring nothing checks. There are fewer than expected: the port has only a handful

  entire observable output is a `transform` string and a cursor, which a string-storing shim holds
  perfectly well. It has been treated as browser work and it is not.

  **A differential is available, not just a behaviour pin.** The port zooms on wheel with
  `e.deltaY < 0 ? 1.15 : 1 / 1.15`; the live map's wheel handler uses the same factor and the same
  rule (`../MikroDash/public/app.js:4461`). The BUTTONS differ — live calls `zoomAt(1.5, …)` directly
  where the port dispatches a synthetic `WheelEvent` — which is a mechanism difference the port rules
  allow, and means the wheel path compares directly while the buttons need their own wiring check.

  So the next unit is two things, in order: a differential over `attachMapZoom`'s wheel and drag
  arithmetic, then a contract check that `mapZoomIn` dispatches a NEGATIVE `deltaY` and `mapZoomOut`
  a positive one — swapped buttons being the plausible failure, and one that no current gate would
  notice.

- 2026-08-25 — **`tools/update-seam-check.js` (gate 97): the System card's announcement and the
  Upgrade dialog's listener were each tested alone and never together.**

  Generalising the sweep — *which gates merely SURVIVE a boundary rather than drive it* — turned up
  `dispatchEvent: () => true` in four gates. One of those stubs sat on a real seam.

  `system-card-check` counts DISPATCHES: it proves the card fires once per changed row and nothing
  about WHAT it fires. `upgrade-dialog-check` never mentions the event and seeds the dialog by other
  means. So the join — installed version, latest version, channel, travelling through
  `CustomEvent.detail` — was driven by nothing, and an announcement nobody hears looks exactly like
  one nobody sends.

  **The compiler cannot cover this.** `detail` is `any` and the dialog casts it, so the two shapes
  could diverge in silence and the dialog would simply show a dash where a version belongs. They were
  two separately-declared interfaces that happened to agree — the same setup that let `GeoPlace` and
  `City` disagree earlier in this port, except there the value did not pass through an `any` and the
  compiler caught it at the call site. They now name one exported type, which closes the drift but
  not the cast.

  The gate is the browser twin of `internal/geoplace/lookup_test.go`, which exists for the same
  reason on the Go side: *"both sides pass their own tests, and the seam between them is discovered
  at the call site much later."* It drives the real card through the real socket path
  (`noteSystemUpdate` → rAF → `flushSysUpdate`, so the coalescing that decides how often the
  announcement fires is included), a real document that delivers events, and the real dialog
  listener — then presses Update and reads what the operator would read.

  Eight mutations killed: the card announcing nothing, announcing with no detail, swapping installed
  and latest, dropping the channel, announcing when no update is offered, the dialog listening for a
  near-miss event name, reading `latest` into the From field, and ignoring the detail entirely.

  It also pins the ORDER: the dialog subscribes before the card draws, as `main.ts` mounts them. A
  listener registered afterwards hears nothing, and that is a bug this gate can see.

  coverage, where a stub that breaks it gets fixed.

  Five acts share one delegated handler — edit, move, toggle, reset, remove — and only Remove asks.
  Eleven cases press them through the real listener; the snapshot carries the question and the emits.

  of the queue, the question losing "traffic it was limiting will no longer be shaped",

  the menu dropped from `resetCounters`, and an act on a row not in the payload still firing.

  **What the sweep produced, end to end.** Seven sites, three ungated when it started, and the two
  most consequential paths in the application among them — Restore, which replaces a router's whole
  configuration, and Delete, which removes files the page calls unrecoverable. Thirty-two new cases
  and twenty-eight killed mutations across three gates, from one question: *which gates drive a
  confirmation, and which merely survive one?*

  The general lesson is about stubs at a boundary. A stub for something that produces MARKUP is
  already known here to be a rewrite. A stub for something that ASKS is worse in one specific way:
  the question is the only warning the operator gets, it is invisible to every markup comparison, and
  a stub that answers it silently makes the whole path look tested.

  the gate would compare state the page never had. `dom-shim` takes an ALIAS instead —
  `'[data-rttab]': '.stab'` — so both names reach the same four buttons. Alias entries are strings

  physics ("needs a focus model", "would be inventing structure") when the truth was a missing line

- 2026-08-25 — **A recorded surviving mutation is dead: `fw-noedit` on the firewall table's parent.**
  The note explaining why it could not be killed was wrong, and wrong in an instructive way.

  `firewall-table-check` listed it among the things it could not see: the class is toggled on
  `firewallTable.parentElement`, the shim's nodes had no parent, so the toggle happened on NEITHER
  side and two empty class lists compared equal. The note said *"faking a parent would be inventing
  structure the page does not describe here."*

  and it wraps `#firewallTable` in a `<table>`. Reading a parent out of that file is not invention;
  it is the same lift-don't-retype rule the rest of the port runs on. The gate now asserts the page
  still wraps the table — so a page that stops doing it fails here rather than keeping a parent this
  tool remembers — and the parent's class list is part of the comparison.

  Inverting, dropping and misspelling the toggle all die. `fw-noedit` is what hides the write
  controls from a read-only account, so the inversion was **showing edit controls to an account that
  cannot use them** — quietly, on a page whose gate reported 45 identical cases.

  The capability is general: `dom-shim`'s `opts.parents` maps a child id to a parent name, one node
  per name, readable through `doc.parents[name]`. The firewall page is the only current user — the
  other `parentElement`/`parentNode` sites in the port are `insertBefore`/`removeChild`, which a
  string-storing shim cannot model and which belong to a browser gate. `nav-check` already built its
  own parent chain.

  It carries its own vacuity check: at least two distinct parent class-lists must occur across the
  corpus. If every case granted write access — or none did — inverting the toggle would flip both
  sides together and the mutation would survive again, while the gate looked richer for having a
  parent at all.

  `querySelector`, `querySelectorAll`, `closest`, `matches` — which reach for markup the port
  generates a few lines away. 122 selectors across 94 modules.

  **Why it matters:** a selector that matches nothing does not throw. `querySelectorAll` returns an
  empty list and the code takes its fallback path, which is usually the correct-LOOKING one. The

  class in the row template and every counter tick becomes a full rebuild: still correct, still green
  in `firewall-table-check` (which drives the REBUILD), and the flash animation now restarts on
  every poll, which is the one thing the in-place path exists to prevent. That path is named in
  `firewall-table-check`'s own "WHAT IT CANNOT SEE" list.

  **Four rounds, and the audit ran CLEAN after every one of them.** Mutation is the only thing that
  told them apart:

  1. **The haystack included the live app's stylesheets and `index.html`**, on the reasoning that the
     served page is both — and because two audits this session had produced nothing but false

     in the live markup, so the port could stop emitting it and still be "answered". Wide is right
     for `class-hook-audit`, which asks whether anything RESPONDS to a class; wrong here, where the
     question is whether the port's query matches the port's own markup.
  2. **Every selector answered ITSELF.** `querySelector('.fw-pkt')` puts `.fw-pkt` in the file being
     searched. The call sites are cut out of the haystack now.
  3. **`querySelector<HTMLElement>('.fw-pkt')`** — the type argument. A pattern demanding `(` after
     the method name skipped 34 of the 122 selectors, which were therefore never checked AND left in
     the haystack to answer themselves. Two bugs from one missing `(?:<[^>]*>)?`.
  4. **Comments answered queries.** `resource.ts` explains itself with "a `[data-res-rows]` table",
     and that sentence was enough: deleting the attribute from all 23 sites in the extracted pages
     still passed. Both comment forms are stripped now.

  Its first real run reported five missing attributes, and all five were the checker's fault — the
  DOM property form (`el.dataset.ifaceType = …`, which both codebases use to build the interface
  tiles and which never appears as a literal) and bare boolean attributes (`<span data-res-drag>`).
  Requiring `=` would have accused four working paths on the first run, which is how an audit gets
  ignored. The dataset form must be an ASSIGNMENT, though: counting `row.dataset.ruleId !== …` as

- 2026-08-25 — **The Reports pagers are driven now. Eight mutations, and the first four attempts
  all survived for reasons worth writing down.**

  `reports-tables-check`'s header said what it could not see: "the pagers' click wiring beyond the
  markup they produce". `_bwPage`/`_pingPage` outlive a render, so the rule that matters is what an
  operator on page 3 gets when a new result set arrives — which no case rendering once can reach.
  `clicks:`, `prevClicks:` and `then:` now drive both sides through their own listeners; 120 cases.

  **The page size is 100, and I assumed 50.** The first draft's "two page" set was 51 rows, so every
  Next was refused, and all five pagination mutations survived a green run. That is the whole failure
  mode of a corpus written from memory rather than from the constant, and it looked exactly like
  success.

  **Prev was never pressed.** Only Next was driven, so weakening `if (page > 0)` to `if (page >= 0)`
  survived — nothing ever went below zero. A negative index does not throw: it slices from the END of
  the array, so page zero would show the last hundred rows.

  **Two guards rescue each other and cannot be killed alone.** Next refuses to pass `pages - 1`, and
  the renderer clamps `if (page >= pages) page = pages - 1`. Weaken either and the gate stays green;
  remove both and it fails. That is a property of the code, not a hole in the corpus — recorded in
  the header rather than papered over, because a gate claiming "clamp covered" would be claiming
  something no behavioural test of this shape can. It also explains what the clamp is FOR: every new
  result set resets the index, so nothing ordinary reaches it — it exists for the moment Next has
  just overshot, which is precisely why it hides that bug.

  **A `then:` with FEWER rows cannot prove the reset either**, for the same reason: the clamp
  rescues it. `then:` with a set just as long is what kills a missing reset.

  sound and the conclusion is wrong: "manual" here means *somebody chose this value deliberately*,
  not *somebody typed it*. That is worth remembering — this was not a typo, it was a plausible
  misreading, and plausible misreadings are exactly what a differential gate is for.

  reasoned about listener registration, event ordering and the shim's `fire` before printing the

  it dangerous. A gate can be fair and vacuous at once, and only an assertion written from outside
  the harness catches it. **Rule 11 added to `tools/lib/dom-shim.js`**; all 93 gates still pass, so
  nothing was leaning on the old behaviour.

  and each is asserted still present. Weaker than lifting, and the weakness is written down.

  `showTab` was left alone deliberately. The port switches by NAME and the live by element IDENTITY

  - **An UNKNOWN dependency counts as MET.** `dep && !dep.checked` — a `requires` naming a collector
    absent from the grid disables nothing. That is the safe direction: silently switching a collector
    off would leave the operator no control to switch it back on.
  - **The pass runs ONCE, in order**, so a chain only propagates as far as the ordering allows. A
    loop-to-fixpoint would resolve chains more thoroughly than the original and disagree with the
    server in the other direction. The corpus carries the same chain in both orders.
  - **A toggle with no `requires` is SKIPPED, not processed and found met.** It never has
    `disabled = false` written to it, so once disabled it stays disabled.

  says "your shape cannot hold the rule".

- 2026-08-24 — **The WAN write path: `internal/server/wan.go`, and `wan:renew` / `wan:release`

  guard: caps → permission (with a `Denied` audit row) → bad-request → the read → row selection by
  `.id` with the interface name as a rename check → guard → ack → write → audit → `RefreshNow` → ok.

  **The parts worth stating, each straight from the original:**
  - **The connected subnets come from `/ip/address`, not the collector payload.** This is the input
    that decides whether we are cutting our own management path, so a cached answer predating the
    change would be worse than none.
  - **A DISABLED address is not a network we are attached to.** Including it would let a switched-off
    subnet make a remote session look local and silence the warning on exactly the router needing it.
  - **A missing ack writes NOTHING and audits NOTHING.** A prompt is not a refusal, and a denied row
    would misrepresent what was attempted. A WRONG ack is `stale-warning`, a different code, because
    "you have not answered" and "you answered about something else" are different facts.
  - **Renew and release are treated identically.** Both interrupt the uplink, so there is no quieter
    path to the riskier one.

  **One deliberate mechanism change, recorded in the file.** The original issues its four reads with
  `Promise.all`; this runs them in sequence. The answer is identical and the documented bottleneck
  here is CONCURRENT CHANNELS on the MikroTik rather than the latency of four prints, so sequential
  on the one channel this session already holds costs the router less — which is the direction this
  port is meant to move in.

  both collected by its Go-side scanner (verified by running its own regex, not assumed) and their

  outside that tool by the same limitation `queues:error` already sits behind — its extras

  Checked rather than assumed: `canPage` is generic over page keys, so `wan`/`write` resolves the

  renew/release permanently denied while every gate stayed green.

  the page is read-only, and it still is: nothing sends `wan:renew` yet.

  native module built only inside the app container; run there via `docker cp` into `/port`, all
  three are current. Standing rule: sweep every `--check` generator, and name the ones that need the
  container rather than letting them fail as "stale".

**Backups: what remains.** `backups:restore` only. It pushes a file back and REBOOTS the router, so
it is not to be exercised against hardware casually. The page still does not ship — `web/build.mjs`
PAGES and `main.ts` PORTED are unchanged — because a page and its endpoints cut over together.
- 2026-08-23 — **Restore, part 1: the decision.** `internal/backups/restoreguard.go` — `CheckRestore`
  plus `ShortVersion`, pure, four mutations caught. Confirm → serial → version, in that order, and
  `acceptVersion` does not override a serial mismatch. **The confirm comparison is case-SENSITIVE**,
  unlike the Packages page's `EqualFold`; the two handlers genuinely disagree in the live app and the
  difference is now pinned. **An empty value on either side is not a mismatch** — historic rows have
  no serial and CHR/x86 have no routerboard, so the alternative refuses every restore on those.
  `ShortVersion` is now the single implementation, called by `runner.go` too.
- 2026-08-23 — **`gofmt -l` exits 0 even when it names files.** Every gate command this session was
  `gofmt -l . && go vet ...`, so the `&&` guarded nothing — it printed a filename and the success
  message together. Corrected to `test -z "$(gofmt -l .)" || { gofmt -l .; exit 1; }`. Worth carrying
  into any future gate description in this file.
- 2026-08-23 — **Live-app finding, held rather than filed:** the restore handler's
  `'=password=' + (router.backup && router.backup.password) || ''` has the `||` outside the `+`, so
  it is dead and a missing `backup` block sends the literal password `undefined`. Verified by
  running it. Not reachable in ordinary use.

  **FILED as ToDo #22 on 2026-08-24 (Part 122).** It was held because "that is a write into the live
  repo and the operator was away" — the operator has since granted standing permission for that file
  and asked for findings to go there, so the reason expired and nobody went back to check. Swept the
  rest of this file for the same pattern; this was the only one.

**THE OPEN DECISION THAT BLOCKS THE REST OF RESTORE — needs the operator.**

Restore is the one direction where the ROUTER fetches from US, over plain HTTP with a capability
token, because `/tool/fetch upload=yes` refuses anything but [s]ftp and a router cannot present a
session cookie. So the URL handed to the router must point at whichever process holds the token.

- The token would be minted by the **Go** process (`internal/backups/restoretoken.go`, already
  ported), so the router must fetch from **Go's** listen port and path — `/next/api/backups/{id}/raw`
  on `-listen`, not Node's `/api/backups/:id/raw` on 3081.
- But the live app derives its base from `Settings.load().backupBaseUrl`, and that operator-set value
  **names Node's port**. Using it verbatim from Go sends the router to Node, which has never heard of
  the token — the fetch 403s and the restore fails with nothing on screen to explain why.
- Falling back to the self-address (`queueGuard.resolveSelfAddresses` over `/user/active/print`) has
  the same problem: the live code appends `process.env.PORT || 3081`.

Three ways out, and the choice is the operator's because it changes what has to be configured:

  1. **A `-backup-base` flag on the Go server**, defaulting to the discovered self-address plus the
     Go listen port. `backupBaseUrl` is ignored, with a startup log saying so.
  2. **Reuse `backupBaseUrl`'s HOST and substitute the Go port.** No new configuration, but it
     silently reinterprets a setting whose whole point is that the operator knows the reachable
     address — including its port, behind NAT.
  3. **Defer restore to cutover**, when Go owns `/api/backups/:id/raw` outright and the question
     disappears. Backups then ships without restore, which the page cannot do — its button exists.

Everything else in restore is portable without this answer, and part 1 above is done. Parts 2 and 3
— the `/raw` route with token redemption, and the handler that fetches and loads — wait on it.

## 2026-08-28 — THE STRANGLER PREFIX IS GONE, AND THE POOL RUNS

The operator: *"Remove /next/ entirely we wont use it. Then port whatever is
still missing now. This app can now run independently so we can compare it to
the live version side by side. It should run on its own with no dependencies on
the live environment."*

### Closed

- **`/next` is removed outright.** Not kept as an alias — an alias nobody uses is
  a second code path nobody tests, which is how the root answered 502 while every
  check asked for the prefix and passed. `TestTheStranglerPrefixIsGone` pins it.
- **BLOCKER 2, the Routers page's background sessions: CLOSED.**
  `internal/server/pool_wire.go` constructs `routers.Pool`. Bound to `standalone`
  rather than to a new flag, because the reason a Go pool must not run is that a
  Node pool is running and that is exactly what `-node` configures.

  **The binding's premise is knowingly false in the current setup**, and the code
  says so: this process is standalone WHILE the live app is up, on its own copy
  of /data, precisely so the two can be compared. Both pools are therefore live
  against the same three physical routers, each carrying three extra channels
  while somebody has the Devices page open. `-no-pool` drops it; the pool is
  suspended whenever nobody is on the page. That is a cost the operator has
  effectively accepted by asking for independence, not one that slipped through.
- **The Devices page is MOUNTED.** In `build.mjs` PAGES and `main.ts` PORTED; the
  `NOT_MOUNTED` entry is deleted.
- **The identity write path is ported** — `store.UpdateIdentity`,
  `collect.System.SetOnIdentity`, `server.persistRouterIdentity`. It did not
  exist, so a router added through this app would have kept an empty model column
  forever while one imported from a Node-managed /data showed a populated one.

### Two defects the port had, both silent, both found by writing the caller

The pool's `IdentityHook` was called ONCE per connection off `system.Last()`:

1. `Last()` is nil at that point — the collectors have just been started and no
   tick has run. The hook was wired and never fired on any connection.
2. It could never fire again. The OS version changes on upgrade, and the live
   comment says in as many words that this "must not be write-once".

The hook now lives on the collector with the live `_lastIdentityKey` dedupe,
fired outside the emit gate — the fingerprint excludes the serial, so a router
whose gauges are steady emits nothing and a gated identity would never be
reported on a quiet device.

### Still open, and now the whole of what is left on this page

- **The fleet map's SVG half** (`app.js:11430-11940`, ~510 lines): the
  equirectangular backdrop, marker clustering, pan/zoom, Auto Frame, the pinned
  popover. Its PURE half is ported and tested (`mapGroups`, `popHtml`,
  `groupPopHtml`, `renderTray`). Recorded in `tools/wiring-audit.js`'s EXPECTED
  against `rtrMapViewport`, `rtrMapPop` and `rtrMapAutoFrame`.

  The page does not look broken without it: `#routersMapWrap` ships `hidden` and
  `setRoutersView` already falls back from 'map' to the card grid. That fallback
  is the one visible divergence and it is deliberate.
- **The Add/Edit router modal has no opener on this page, and that is correct.**
  The Devices page has no edit affordance of its own — rows carry
  `data-router-id` and no buttons, cards carry none. The only way in is the map's
  popover and tray, which belong to the unported SVG half. `rtrAddBtn` and
  `rtrTbody` are on the SETTINGS page. Wiring `initRouterModal` from `main.ts`
  would put a dialog on a page that offers no way to open it — an earlier version
  of this change did exactly that and `tools/selector-audit.js` caught it.
- **Blockers 3, 4, 5 and 6** (settings write, routers.json cache, notification
  transports, principal writes) are unchanged as WRITTEN, but their premise has
  moved: each is phrased as "Node caches this and would revert our write", and
  this process now runs against its OWN /data. They are cutover blockers for the
  MERGED app, not blockers for the standalone one. **The notification transports
  are the exception and must stay unwired**: the channels are the operator's real
  Telegram and email, both engines evaluate the same conditions against the same
  routers, and a duplicated message cannot be un-received.
